explains: After the moves e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Nxf6+ exf6, White often plays Bd3, which is the most popular and best move. It develops quickly and targets the h7 pawn, a key weakness in Black's camp, especially since Black often castles kingside.
teaches: In the Caro-Kann, White's bishop on d3 can put immediate pressure on h7, forcing Black to address the threat.
plans: Black should respond with Re8, gaining a tempo on the king, and then prepare to castle or address the pressure.

explains: After Bd3, Black castles and White plays Qc2, creating a battery on the b1-h7 diagonal. This is a common setup, but Black can easily resolve the pressure with Re8, which also gains a tempo.
teaches: Recognizing common attacking setups and finding active defensive moves that also create counterplay.
plans: Black plays Re8, forcing White to address the check, and then proceeds with development.

explains: At move 9, Black has a choice between h6 and g6. g6 is the main move, but it has a downside: it weakens the kingside pawn structure and gives White a target for a pawn storm with h4 and h5. However, the position remains equal if Black knows how to respond.
teaches: Fianchettoing the bishop can be double-edged; it provides support but also creates a target for pawn advances.
plans: If Black plays g6, White should play h4 to start an attack. Black should respond with Be6, preparing to meet h5 with f5, defending the point.

explains: After g6, h4, Be6, h5, f5, Black has defended the kingside. White may try Bxh6, but it has no targets because Black's dark-square bishop, knight, and queen can defend the dark squares. Black can play Qf6, solidifying the kingside, and then develop the knight to d7.
teaches: When facing a pawn storm, it's important to keep the king safe and coordinate pieces to defend key squares.
plans: Black plays Qf6 and Nd7, while White castles queenside and continues with f3 and g4 to open the position.

explains: This line is a great weapon for Black because it is easy to learn and leads to at least equality. White's attacking plans are obvious, but Black's defensive resources are sufficient, and Black can counter on the queenside with b5 and a5.
teaches: Choosing a solid, forcing line that minimizes the need to learn many sidelines can be practical, especially for beginners.
plans: Black should aim to play b5 and a5 to open the queenside, while White tries to break through on the kingside with f3 and g4.

explains: After White plays f3, Black should not chase the knight away with g5, as that would be bad after Ne2, when the b6 pawn falls and the position crumbles. Instead, Black should maintain the pawn structure.
teaches: Don't weaken your pawn structure without good reason. Avoid pawn moves that create weaknesses, especially when they don't achieve a concrete goal.
plans: Develop normally, play b5, and prepare to exchange the active knight with Nb6 or Nd5 if appropriate.

explains: In the position after Nxf6, Black has two main defensive setups: g6 or h6. g6 provokes h4-h5, which weakens Black's kingside, while h6 prevents the h4-h5 plan because if White plays h5, it does nothing. After h6, White will likely castle kingside and play g4-g5, but Black has enough defenders on g5.
teaches: When choosing between defensive moves, consider how they affect your opponent's plans. A move like h6 can stop a pawn storm, while g6 may invite weaknesses.
plans: After h6, Black plays Qc7, then b6, aiming to get the bishop pair striking at the king. White may play h3 to avoid weakening, but Black's position is solid.

explains: If White plays c4 to close down the bishop on b7, Black must not play c5, as after d5 Black would be losing. Instead, Black should develop normally with Nd7, and can expand on the queenside with a5, double rooks on the e-file, or play Nf8-e6 to provoke d5.
teaches: When your opponent tries to restrict your bishop, don't fall into pawn traps. Develop your pieces and find active squares for them, even if it means rerouting.
plans: Develop the knight to d7, then consider a5, Rfe8, or Nf8-e6. The bishop on b7 can be activated later.

explains: In the Korchnoi Variation of the Caro-Kann, after e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Nxf6+ exf6, Black's h7 pawn is a target. White often plays Bd3 and Qc2 to attack it. Black can defend with h6 or g6, each with different consequences.
teaches: In this structure, be aware of the weakness on h7 and choose your defensive setup based on whether you want to provoke h4-h5 or prevent it.
plans: Choose between h6 and g6 based on your preference. If h6, White will castle kingside and play g4-g5, but Black has enough defenders. If g6, White may play h4-h5, but Black can handle the resulting weaknesses.

explains: After the early exchanges, Black's h7-pawn is a recurring target. White often follows with c3, Bd3, and Qc2 to attack along the b1-h7 diagonal.
teaches: When your king's bishop is developed to d3 and the queen to c2, the h7-pawn becomes a focal point of attack.
plans: Black must be ready to defend h7, either by playing h6 or g6, depending on the desired pawn structure.

explains: Black has two defensive moves against the h7 pressure: h6 or g6. Playing h6 keeps the kingside pawn structure intact and invites White to castle kingside. Playing g6 weakens the kingside pawns and invites White to castle queenside and launch an attack with h4-h5.
teaches: The choice between h6 and g6 determines the nature of the game: h6 leads to a kingside castling race, while g6 invites a queenside attack and a weakened king position.
plans: If Black plays h6, White castles kingside and Black can counterattack with Qc7 and Bd6, aiming at h2. If Black plays g6, White castles queenside and pushes h4-h5.

explains: In the resulting pawn structure, Black's pawns on f6 and c6 are weaker than White's pawns on e4 and d4. If pieces are exchanged, White's pawn majority and advanced pawns give a clear endgame advantage.
teaches: In endgames, pawn structure is decisive. A healthy pawn majority and advanced passed pawns are a long-term asset.
plans: White's endgame plan is to bring the king to the center and push the d-pawn. Black should avoid unnecessary exchanges and seek active piece play.

explains: While the endgame favors White, Black has good attacking chances in the middlegame, especially if the queens stay on and the kingside is weakened.
teaches: A pawn structure that is worse in the endgame can still offer dynamic attacking opportunities in the middlegame.
plans: Black should aim for active piece play and an attack on the kingside, while White should try to simplify to reach a favorable endgame.

explains: After Bg6, White plays h4 to threaten trapping the bishop. Black must respond with h6 (not h5) to give the bishop a retreat square on h7. h5 is worse because it weakens the g5 square and the kingside pawn structure.
teaches: When your bishop is attacked by a pawn advance, choose a retreat that preserves the bishop's activity and doesn't create weaknesses. Avoid pawn moves that give up key squares.
plans: Black plays h6, then after White's h5, the bishop goes to h7. White will later develop the knight to f3, building pressure.

explains: After the early trades, White often tries h4 to trap the bishop on g6. Black must respond accurately; h6 is better than h5 because h5 weakens the g5 square and, after the bishop trade, leaves the h5 pawn as a target.
teaches: When a bishop is attacked by a pawn advance, choose the defensive move that gives away the fewest squares and doesn't create future weaknesses.
plans: Black plays h6, maintaining the bishop on g6, and prepares to meet White's next moves.

explains: White delays Bf3 until after Nf3, aiming to trade the light-squared bishops so the knight can settle on e5. If Black allows it, the knight on e5 supported by f4 exerts strong pressure.
teaches: Trading a bishop to open a square for a knight is a common strategic idea; the knight on a strong outpost can dominate the position.
plans: Black plays Nbd7 to prevent Ne5, forcing White to find another plan.

explains: In the alternative plan, White tries to bring a knight to f4 (via h3 or e2) to attack the bishop on g6. If Black is forced to play h6 while the knight is on f4, the resulting pawn structure is bad for Black.
teaches: When the opponent threatens to plant a knight on a strong square, be ready to trade it off before it becomes entrenched.
plans: Black plays e6 to prepare Bf8-d6, so that when the knight arrives on f4, Black can capture it.

explains: White can also choose a quiet setup without immediate h4-h5 or knight maneuvers. In that case, Black develops naturally, and the position becomes a typical Caro-Kann structure with no theory, just strategic play.
teaches: Not every position requires sharp tactics; sometimes simple development leads to an equal middlegame where understanding the pawn structure matters more.
plans: Black develops pieces, castles, and aims for a solid position with no weaknesses.

explains: After the early exchanges, Black has a solid structure with pawns on e6 and c6, and the light-squared bishop is developed outside the pawn chain, so there are no weaknesses or bad pieces. The position is balanced and strategic.
teaches: In the Caro-Kann, once Black has solved the problem of the light-squared bishop, the resulting structures are equal and require strategic understanding rather than memorized theory.
plans: Both sides should aim to castle and then proceed with typical plans: White may expand on the kingside or center, while Black will seek counterplay on the queenside or in the center.

explains: In the main line, after Nf3, Black's best move is Nd7 to prevent Ne5. Alternatives like e6 or Nf6 allow Ne5, which gives White a strong central outpost. If Black plays e6, White can exchange on h7 and then play f4, gaining a favorable structure.
teaches: Preventing the opponent's knight from reaching a strong central square is often more important than developing a piece to a natural square. The move Nd7 is prophylactic, stopping Ne5.
plans: Black should prefer Nd7 to maintain the bishop on g6 and avoid allowing White's knight to e5. If Black plays Nf6, White can still consider Ne5, but Black gets dynamic play.

explains: In this Caro-Kann Classical structure, Black's knight on f6 invites White to jump to e5, which would attack the d4 pawn and the bishop on h7. However, allowing Ne5 also weakens the c5 square, making it easier for Black to play ...c5 later. This trade-off is why ...Nf6 has become a modern main line.
teaches: When deciding whether to allow a knight to an outpost like e5, weigh the immediate pressure it creates against the long-term weaknesses it leaves behind, such as a weakened c5 square.
plans: Black should be ready to meet Ne5 with ...Bh7, keeping the bishop and preparing to challenge the knight or exploit c5.

explains: After ...Nd5, White's most natural move is Bb3, keeping the bishop on the f7 diagonal and freeing the c-pawn. Black can then play ...a5, provoking a4, which weakens the b4 square and creates a hook for a future ...b5 break if White castles queenside.
teaches: When facing a bishop on b3, a timely ...a5 can create long-term weaknesses in White's camp: the b4 square becomes available for a knight, and the a4 pawn becomes a target for undermining with ...b5.
plans: Black should follow up with ...Nd7, ...Qb6, and prepare ...c5 or ...b5 depending on White's castling choice.

explains: If White tries Qf3 instead of Bb3, there is again a threat on f7. Black must defend with ...Qe7 rather than ...Qc7, because ...Qe7 keeps the d7 square available for the knight, allowing ...Nd7 to meet a future Ne5.
teaches: When choosing a defensive move, consider which squares it leaves available for your other pieces. A queen on e7 may be more flexible than on c7 if you need to develop the knight to d7.
plans: After ...Qe7 and ...Nd7, Black has a solid position with chances to play ...c5 or ...b5.

explains: After e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6 Nxf6+ exf6, Black's pawn structure is compromised but the f8 bishop is free. White's bishop often goes to d3 to target the h7 bishop, which is Black's only well-placed piece.
teaches: In the Caro-Kann, Black's light-squared bishop is a key piece; White often aims to exchange it to leave Black with a passive position.
plans: Black should develop harmoniously, often with ...Nd7, ...Qc7, and ...Bd6, preparing to castle queenside or challenge White's center.

explains: If Black plays ...Nf6 and White plays Bc4, Black can respond with ...Nd7, attacking the bishop. If White plays Bd3 instead, Black must be careful: taking on d4 is bad because Nf7! wins material. So Black should take on d3, allowing White to recapture with the queen, but then White has gained time.
teaches: When a bishop is placed on an attacking square, consider counterplay against it; also, don't grab pawns if it opens you to tactics.
plans: After ...Bxd3, Qxd3, Black can continue with ...Nd7, ...e6, and ...Bd6, aiming for a solid setup.

explains: In the ...Nf6 line, after White plays Bd3 and Black takes, White often plays Qxd3. Then White has a choice: Bd2 or Bf4. Bd2 supports the e5 knight with f4, while Bf4 supports it with a piece. Black should be ready to challenge the knight with ...Nd7 or ...c5.
teaches: Supporting a knight with a pawn vs. a piece has different implications; the choice affects future pawn breaks and piece placement.
plans: White may play Qf3, supporting f5 and preparing a kingside attack. Black should aim for ...Qc7, ...c5, and ...Nbd7 to counter.

explains: In the main line with ...Nd7, White often plays h5 before Bd3 to gain space and fix Black's h-pawn. After ...Bh7, Bd3, Black trades, and White recaptures with the queen. White has gained three tempi (bishop moved once vs. Black's four), but Black's structure is solid.
teaches: Gaining tempi in the opening can be valuable, but a slightly compromised structure may be acceptable if it leads to a favorable endgame.
plans: Black can play ...e6, ...Qc7, ...Bd6, and castle queenside, aiming for counterplay on the queenside.

explains: Black's choice of ...e6 over ...Nf6 is to free the f8 bishop, enabling ...Bb4 to disrupt White's queenside castling plans. If White plays Bd2, it transposes, but if Bf4, Black needs ...Bb4 to create weaknesses.
teaches: Developing with a pawn move can be useful to activate a bishop and create immediate threats against the opponent's plans.
plans: Black should aim for ...Qc7, ...Bd6, and ...Nf6, with the option of ...Bb4 if White plays Bf4.

explains: In this Caro-Kann Classical structure, if White chooses Bf4 instead of Bd2, Black must be ready to meet it with Bb4, which requires having played e6 earlier. This move disrupts White's queenside plans and prevents an easy long castle.
teaches: When your opponent's bishop move creates a threat or supports a plan, look for a resource that challenges their setup before they consolidate. Here, Bb4 exploits the pin on the c3 pawn and forces White to either take or play c3, both of which are concessions.
plans: After Bb4, if White retreats the bishop, Black can proceed with the standard setup: ...Qc7, ...Nf6, and ...Be7, aiming for a sound structure. If White plays c3, Black has achieved the goal of disrupting White's queenside castling plans.

explains: In the Bd2 line, Black has a choice: castle kingside or play Qc7 early. Castling kingside is engine-approved but practically dangerous because White can launch a pawn storm with g4, supported by pieces on e4 and f5. Black's position becomes hard to defend for humans.
teaches: Engine evaluations do not always reflect practical difficulties. When facing a kingside attack, consider whether your king will be safe and whether you have active counterplay; sometimes it's better to avoid the sharpest lines if they are hard to handle.
plans: If Black castles kingside, they must be ready to meet White's g4 advance with precise moves like ...Qd5 to force queen trades and reach an endgame, though White retains a slight edge. Alternatively, Black can avoid this by playing ...Qc7 early and preparing queenside castling.

explains: After Bd2, Black's recommended plan is to play ...Qc7 early, then ...Nf6, and castle queenside. This avoids the dangerous kingside attack and keeps the position more manageable, even if the engine might prefer other moves.
teaches: Choosing a plan that sidesteps your opponent's attacking ideas is often more important than following the engine's top choice. Early queen moves can be useful to prepare castling and avoid tactical complications.
plans: Black will continue with ...Nf6, ...Be7, and ...O-O-O, aiming for a solid structure with counterplay on the queenside. White may try to create play in the center or on the kingside, but Black's king is safer on the queenside.

explains: After the early queen to c7, black aims to break with c5 and often castles queenside. The engine slightly prefers kingside castling, but the difference is negligible in practice, and white's kingside attacking potential is neutralized.
teaches: Choosing a plan based on practical chances rather than tiny engine preferences is often better in human play.
plans: Black will continue with c5, developing pieces and preparing queenside castling.

explains: In the line with bishop c3, the g7 pawn can become a weakness, especially if white can plant a knight on f5. Black must address this by blocking with knight f6 and preventing knight b5 with a6.
teaches: When a pawn becomes a target, proactively block the entry squares and prevent piece invasions.
plans: Black will play cxd4, then a6 to stop Nb5, and later address the f5 square.

explains: If white plays d5 instead, black gets a favorable structure: a 3-to-2 queenside majority while white's d5 pawn is blockaded and its outposts are covered by b7 and f7. The main issue remains the f5 square and pressure on g7.
teaches: A pawn majority is valuable if the opponent's passed pawn is blockaded and cannot create outposts.
plans: Black will develop, aim to liquidate on d5, and use the queenside majority while watching f5.

explains: When white can force a knight to f5, black may have to resort to tactical resources like rook e5 and a theoretical sacrifice to avoid being worse. This is the downside of the queen c7 plan.
teaches: Sometimes you must accept dynamic compensation or tactical tricks to counter a strong outpost.
plans: Black will play rook e5, then after f4, take on h5, and later use tactical shots to maintain balance.

explains: If white avoids the main lines and plays a safe setup like bishop d3, black can simply develop normally with e6, since the c8 bishop is already outside the pawn chain. This leads to a standard Caro-Kann structure with no strategic problems.
teaches: When the opponent plays passively, just develop and play the typical pawn structure; there is no need to force complications.
plans: Black will castle, develop knights and bishop, and play c4, reaching a common Caro-Kann middlegame.

explains: In this Caro-Kann structure with pawns on e6 and c6 against d4 and c4, the light-squared bishop is outside the pawn chain, so there are no immediate strategic threats from White's safe setups.
teaches: When your bishop is outside the pawn chain, you can develop naturally without fear of being trapped or facing immediate pressure.
plans: Develop pieces normally: castle kingside, play Nf6, Be7, and prepare to challenge the center.

explains: Against Bc4, White prepares Ne2 to reroute the knight to f4, similar to the Fantasy Variation. Black should play Bd6 to control f4 and be ready to capture the knight if it comes.
teaches: When the opponent reroutes a knight to an outpost like f4, you need a piece that can challenge or capture it; placing a bishop on the adjacent diagonal is often the right response.
plans: Play e6, then Bd6, and if White plays h4 and Nf4, capture the knight with Bxf4.

explains: After the bishop trade on f4, Black has given up the bishop pair but has no structural weaknesses. Castling kingside is preferable to queenside, which is almost unplayable here.
teaches: Trading off pieces can reduce the opponent's attacking potential, especially when they have a kingside pawn storm in mind.
plans: Castle kingside, develop the bishop to h7, and prepare to trade rooks on the e-file.

explains: If White plays Ne2 early, Black can choose between the solid e6 setup or the more ambitious e5 break. The e5 break is a modern equalizer: after Nf4, Black plays e5, and if White captures, Qa5+ regains the pawn.
teaches: When facing a knight maneuver, a central pawn break can be a strong counter, especially if it comes with tempo on the queen.
plans: If White plays Ne2, consider playing Nf6 and then e5 when the knight goes to f4, aiming for quick central activity.

explains: In the Fantasy Variation, White aims for Nf4, and Black must be ready to eliminate that knight. The bishop on d6 is crucial to avoid being trapped or losing material.
teaches: When the opponent has a clear plan to place a knight on a strong square, you must have a concrete defensive resource, such as a bishop that can capture it.
plans: Play Bd6 to meet h4 and Nf4 with Bxf4, keeping the position solid.

explains: After the exchange on f6, Black's pawn structure is doubled on the f-file, but the position is balanced. White can try to exploit the weakened kingside dark squares, but Black has active piece play.
teaches: In the Classical Caro-Kann, the doubled f-pawns are not a weakness if Black can develop harmoniously and target the center.
plans: Black should continue development with e6, Be7, O-O, and prepare to challenge the center with c5 or f6.

explains: The 'floor' variation (a line where White plays Nf4) and the Nge2 variation often transpose to the same type of position. After White's knight goes to f4, Black can respond with ...Bd6, challenging the knight and preparing to eliminate it if necessary.
teaches: Recognizing transpositions between similar lines reduces the amount of theory you need to memorize. The key idea is to neutralize White's knight on f4 before it becomes a powerful attacking piece.
plans: Black should play ...e6, ...Bd6, and be ready to meet h4 with ...Bxf4, eliminating the knight and blunting White's attack.

explains: Against the 'floor' setup, Black can also consider ...Qc7 as a sideline. If White plays h4, Black can then play ...Bd6, forcing White to take on d6 because the knight is hanging.
teaches: Flexibility in move order can create additional options. Sometimes a queen move can be useful before committing the bishop, as it may force favorable trades.
plans: If White plays h4, Black plays ...Bd6, and if White takes, Black recaptures with the queen, maintaining a solid structure.

explains: The theory of the Classical Caro-Kann with ...Bf5 can be reduced to three main types of positions: those with the typical h4 plan, the 'floor' type with Nf4, and slow positional lines where White plays Nf3, Bd3, and castles.
teaches: Organizing opening theory into thematic groups helps you understand the underlying plans rather than memorizing endless variations.
plans: For the h4 lines, choose between castling kingside (with more theory) or queenside (with a slightly worse but playable position). For the Nf4 lines, remember to eliminate the knight with ...Bd6. For the slow lines, just develop normally.

explains: The best way to learn an opening is to study games of strong players who play it, rather than relying solely on books or videos.
teaches: Analyzing master games gives you insight into typical middlegame plans and helps you understand the opening on a deeper level.
plans: Find games in the Classical Caro-Kann and study them, noting how both sides handle the typical plans and tactics.

explains: After the Benko Gambit is accepted, White is down a pawn but has development and central control. Black must prioritize castling with Be7 before White can create threats.
teaches: In gambit lines, development and king safety matter more than material. Black should castle quickly to avoid being punished.
plans: White will continue developing, aiming to exploit Black's lag in development and the weak queenside pawns.

explains: In the main line, Black plays ...Bb7, and White can choose a setup with Qc2, allowing the pawn sacrifice. The resulting position features White giving up a rook for two pieces, with material technically equal but White having a significant advantage.
teaches: Material equality can be misleading; two pieces for a rook and a pawn can be favorable if the pieces are active and the king is safe.
plans: White will coordinate the two pieces against Black's rook and pawns, aiming for central breaks and pressure.

explains: If Black plays ...Nc6 instead of ...Be7, it is already losing due to tactical resources like Qe4 and Nd7, with the knight heading to d5.
teaches: In sharp openings, one inaccuracy can be fatal. Always check for tactical refutations before deviating from known theory.
plans: White will exploit the weakened squares and coordinate pieces to deliver a decisive attack.

explains: When Black plays ...bc4 instead of the main line, White can recapture on c4, leading to a structure similar to the main line but with Black's pawn still on a7. This gives Black the option to play ...Ba6 to trade light-squared bishops, which is a subtle difference.
teaches: The placement of pawns on the queenside affects piece activity. A pawn on a7 allows Black to use the a6 square for a bishop trade, which can ease defense.
plans: White will proceed with development, aiming for e4-e5 break, and be aware of the bishop trade possibility.

explains: In the line with ...g6, White should play h3 to restrict ...Ng4 and ...Nd5, and then prepare e4-e5. The plan is straightforward: develop pieces to f4 and d1, and push e5.
teaches: Prophylactic moves like h3 can prevent annoying knight jumps, allowing you to proceed with your own central plan.
plans: White will play Be2, Bf4, Rfd1, and then e4-e5, aiming for a central breakthrough.

explains: Black's idea of ...Nh5 to trade on e5 doesn't work because White can simply take on h5, leaving Black's knight misplaced.
teaches: When your opponent tries to trade off a key defender, check if you can simply capture back and leave their piece out of play.
plans: White will continue with the e5 break, ignoring the temporary knight maneuver.

explains: If Black plays ...b4 instead of ...bc4, White should immediately play a3 to undermine Black's pawn chain. If Black takes on a3, White gets a nearly winning advantage due to access to c3 and weak a7 pawn.
teaches: When your opponent has a pawn chain, attacking its base can create weaknesses and open lines for your pieces.
plans: White will play a3, and if Black doesn't take, continue with development and the e5 break.

explains: After a3, Black has two main replies: ...Na6 or ...g6. In both cases, White can develop normally and aim for the same e5 break, with the closed a-file and semi-open b-file helping White.
teaches: In the Benko, White's plan is often to ignore the queenside and focus on the center, using the closed files to limit Black's counterplay.
plans: White will play Nc3, Be2, O-O, Bf4, and then prepare e5 with rooks on e1 and d1.

explains: After d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 b5 cxb5 a6 bxa6 Bxa6, White has a strong position. The key is that White can play Nc3, attacking the weak a7 pawn, and the rook will come to a1. Black's bishop on a6 is misplaced and Black's counterplay is limited.
teaches: In the Benko Gambit declined, White can aim for a solid setup with Nc3, controlling the center and preparing to exploit the weak a7 pawn. The a-file being closed and the b-file semi-open can reduce Black's usual counterplay.
plans: White plans to develop with Nc3, then e4, Be2, 0-0, and Be3 or Bf4, followed by Rfe1 and pushing e5. The rook on a1 will support the a-file pressure.

explains: If Black plays …Na6, White can simply take on b4 with the knight and then play Nc3. The knight on b4 looks active but White can play e4 without worry. After Be2, Bg7, 0-0, 0-0, and Bf4, White follows the same plan of Rfe1 and e5. The closed a-file and semi-open b-file (due to Black's knight on b4) help prevent typical Benko counterplay.
teaches: When Black tries to hold the b4 pawn with ...Na6, White can ignore it and build a strong center with e4. The knight on b4 is not dangerous because White can challenge it with a3 or simply continue development.
plans: White develops with Be2, castles, plays Bf4, then Rfe1 and e5, maintaining central pressure and keeping the a-file closed.

explains: The Benko Gambit declined offers White a more positional and subtle game compared to accepting the gambit. The ideas are not about immediate attack on the b-file but about defending b5 and b6 and slowly outplaying Black.
teaches: Declining the Benko can be a great practical weapon because many players are unfamiliar with the positional ideas. White can aim for a solid center and exploit Black's weaknesses without giving up the pawn.

explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3, Black can immediately play …Bb4, pinning the knight on c3. White must respond precisely, and the only good move is Nxc6, forcing Black to recapture. If Black recaptures with the b-pawn, White can later play f3 to solidify the center, and despite doubled c-pawns, White's bishop pair and safer king give a slight edge.
teaches: When facing a pin on the knight in the Sicilian, exchanging the knight on c6 can be a precise defensive resource, especially when it leads to a favorable pawn structure or relieves pressure.
plans: After Nxc6, White should be ready to meet recaptures and then play f3 to support e4, aiming to keep the center solid and exploit the bishop pair.

explains: If Black recaptures with the d-pawn (…dxc6), White can exchange queens and then play Bd2 to prevent Black from doubling the pawns. If Black takes on c3, White recaptures and can later take on g7, so White is not worse. Black should then play e5 to restrain White's pieces and prevent f4 breaks.
teaches: After queen exchanges, developing pieces while preventing pawn weaknesses is key. A move like Bd2 can stop the opponent from doubling your pawns.
plans: White should aim to castle quickly and then use the open files and bishop pair to maintain pressure, while Black should play e5 to limit White's piece activity.

explains: In the line with ...dxc6, after Black castles, White has a tactical idea: if Black tries to grab a pawn, White can use checks and tactics to gain an edge. For example, after ...Bc5, White can play Nb5+ and then capture on c7, leading to a position where White has a better bishop, a weakness on e6, and a tempo up.
teaches: Tactical motifs like discovered attacks and checks can turn a seemingly quiet position into an advantage. Always look for intermediate checks that force the king to move.
plans: White should pursue the tactical sequence to win a pawn or gain a positional edge, targeting the e6 weakness and keeping the initiative.

explains: For Black, recapturing with the b-pawn (…bxc6) is better because it captures toward the center and prepares the d5 break. White must play Bd3 to defend e4, accepting doubled c-pawns, because the alternative f3 fails to a tactic: ...Nxe4, fxe4, Qh4+.
teaches: When recapturing, prefer capturing toward the center to support pawn breaks. Also, be aware of tactical refutations to natural-looking moves like f3.
plans: White should play Bd3, then be ready to meet ...d5 with exd5, opening the e-file for a check. Black should aim for ...d5 to challenge the center.

explains: After Bd3, Black can play …d5. White should capture with exd5, opening the e-file for a check. After ...cxd5, White castles, unpinning the knight and threatening attacks on the e-file. Black must play ...dxc4, and White can either recapture or play Qe2+ to avoid queen trade and keep pressure. If Black defends with the bishop, White is better because Black is undeveloped.
teaches: Opening a file for a check can gain time and create attacking chances. Sometimes declining a queen trade is better to maintain pressure on the opponent's king.
plans: White should continue with Qe2+, then Rook to e1 as an intermezzo, and then capture on e4, aiming to keep the initiative and exploit Black's pinned pieces.

explains: In the Accelerated Dragon, after Nc3, White aims to build a setup similar to the Yugoslav Attack against the Dragon, with f3, Be3, Qd2, and long castling, while Black develops with Bg7, Nf6, O-O, Qc7, d6, Bd7, and Rc8, preparing a queenside attack along the c-file.
teaches: The side that attacks faster usually wins in the Accelerated Dragon; every move must count because there is little time for maneuvering.
plans: White should proceed with the standard Yugoslav setup: f3, Be3, Qd2, and O-O-O, while Black should develop harmoniously and prepare ...b5 and ...a5 to attack on the queenside.

explains: After Nc3, Black's most common move is …a5, which is aggressive and aims to chase the bishop on b3 and attack the e4 pawn, but it has drawbacks: it trades a flank pawn for a central pawn and activates White's pieces.
teaches: Flank pawn advances like ...a5 can be double-edged; they may gain space but can also weaken your structure and give the opponent targets.
plans: If Black plays ...a5, White should respond with a move like Nb5 or f3, maintaining pressure and exploiting the slightly loose queenside.

explains: The move …d6 is more solid than ...a5, as it avoids overextending on the queenside and keeps the position more flexible, though it is slightly passive.
teaches: In sharp openings, sometimes the more solid move is better than the flashy one, especially if the flashy move has hidden drawbacks.
plans: After ...d6, White should play f3 to solidify the e4 pawn, and Black can continue with ...Bd7 and ...Rc8, preparing the standard queenside play.

explains: In the line with ...d6, after White plays f3 and Black plays ...Bd7, Black has a choice; the best move is ...Rc8, preparing to attack along the c-file.
teaches: Rooks belong on open or semi-open files; in the Accelerated Dragon, the c-file is Black's main avenue of counterplay.
plans: Black should aim for ...Rc8, ...b5, and ...a5 to create threats against White's queenside, while White continues with Be3, Qd2, and long castling.

explains: In the O'Kelly Sicilian, after e4 c5 Nf3 a6, the tempting d4 is actually bad because …d5 refutes it: the pawn on d4 is undefended and the knight on f3 is also loose, so White cannot recapture properly. The engine evaluation is around -0.7 for Black, meaning White is clearly worse.
teaches: Before playing a central pawn break, check whether the pawn and supporting pieces are adequately defended. A move that leaves both a pawn and a knight en prise can be immediately punished by a central pawn push.
plans: Discard d4 entirely in this position. Instead, consider moves that maintain a healthy pawn structure and piece coordination.

explains: After Nc3, Black can transpose to the Najdorf or Kan Sicilian, which are solid and well-known for Black. Since White wants to punish Black's early a6, allowing a normal Sicilian is not ambitious enough.
teaches: When your opponent plays a slightly committal move like a6 early, you should aim for a line that exploits that move rather than allowing a comfortable transposition to a main line.
plans: Avoid Nc3 if you want to punish a6. Look for a move that gives White a more specific advantage, such as c3.

explains: The move c3 is a solid choice, leading to the c3-Sicilian. It is safe and slightly better for White, but it does not give as much advantage as other tries. If Black responds with …e6, the game can transpose to a French Defense structure after d4 d5 e5, which is the Advance French.
teaches: Knowing multiple openings can be useful when your opponent accidentally transposes into a different defense. If you are prepared for the French, you can exploit your opponent's unfamiliarity.
plans: After c3, if Black plays …e6, aim for the French structure with d4 and e5, developing pieces to natural squares like Bd3 and Nge7 for Black.

explains: In this Sicilian position, White has a slight edge because the king is already developed and Black's knight on f6 is pinned by the bishop on g5. Material is equal, and Black could double White's pawns to reach a symmetrical position, but White's development advantage and the pin give a persistent plus.
teaches: A lead in development and a pin can justify a small edge even when material is equal and pawn structure is symmetrical. Prefer positions where you have active pieces and the opponent has a weakness to exploit.
plans: White should aim to maintain pressure, possibly by exchanging bishops to isolate Black's a-pawn, and then target the weak pawns in the endgame.

explains: Black should play ...Rd8 preparing ...Kf8, and White can use the opportunity to exchange bishops with Be6, isolating Black's a-pawn. After Bf6? (or similar), White can play Bd2, preventing Black from doubling pawns on the c-file.
teaches: When your opponent has a pinned piece, use tactics to force favorable exchanges or create permanent weaknesses. Exchanging pieces can turn a dynamic advantage into a static one.
plans: White should continue developing, aiming to keep the bishop pair and target Black's isolated pawns, especially in the endgame.

explains: In a position with White's rook on c1, the move Bc3 is less active than Rc1, which defends the b-pawn and places the rook on an open file. The position is better for White because of the active rook and the pressure on Black's position.
teaches: Choose the most active square for your pieces. A rook on an open file often outweighs a bishop exchange that doesn't improve your position.
plans: White should keep the tension, maintain the rook on c1, and look for ways to increase pressure on Black's queenside.

explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6, Black should play ...Nc6; if not, White's d4 becomes stronger. White can choose between Nc3 and d4, with d4 being more aggressive and Nc3 leading to a positional grind.
teaches: In the Open Sicilian, ...Nc6 is a key move for Black to challenge White's center. White's choice between Nc3 and d4 depends on the opponent's strength: d4 for aggressive play, Nc3 for a slow grind.
plans: If White plays d4, the game enters sharp main lines; if Nc3, White aims for a long-term positional squeeze.

explains: In the Kramnik Variation, after ...Bb4, White can play Nxc6, and Black recaptures with the b-pawn, which is better than the d-pawn. White develops with Bd3, and Black has options like castling or ...d5. The move ...d5 resolves the central tension, while ...e5 keeps it.
teaches: When recapturing, consider which pawn recapture gives you a better pawn structure. Resolving central tension with ...d5 can simplify, while ...e5 keeps the game complex.
plans: Both sides should castle quickly and then fight for the center. White may target the d5 square if Black plays ...Na4.

explains: In the game, Black played ...Na4, which weakens the d5 square, allowing White to play d5. After a series of trades, White has a slight edge due to the bishop pair and a queenside majority, while Black's bishops eye White's kingside.
teaches: A knight on the rim can leave key central squares weak. Use such weaknesses to open the position and create targets.
plans: White should aim to utilize the queenside majority and the bishop pair, while being mindful of Black's attacking chances on the kingside.

explains: In the resulting middlegame, White's passed pawn on the queenside becomes a strong asset. It ties down Black's pieces to block it, while White's king can participate in the attack on the other side.
teaches: A passed pawn can be a decisive advantage if it is far advanced and supported, as it forces the opponent to allocate resources to stop it, leaving the rest of the position vulnerable.
plans: White should push the passed pawn to create threats, while using the king and pieces to attack Black's king, since Black must defend the pawn's advance.

explains: The Kramnik Variation is not commonly known among Black players, which gives White a practical advantage. It leads to unbalanced positions where both sides have chances, but White's plan is clear.
teaches: Choosing a less common but sound opening line can be a practical weapon, as opponents may be unfamiliar with the resulting positions and the typical plans.
plans: White should aim to reach the typical middlegame with a queenside passed pawn and then play actively, using the initiative.

explains: With the knight already on c3, the Maroczy Bind is no longer available, so Black's main options are either to aim for a win with ...e5 or to set up a small center. The light-squared bishop is less useful against the e5 pawn chain, so queenside castling without playing Bc4-b3 leaves it misplaced.
teaches: In the Sicilian, the choice of setup depends on whether the c3 knight has been played; if so, the Maroczy is off the table, and the placement of the light-squared bishop should be coordinated with the castling plan.
plans: Black can choose between a small center with ...e5 or a more dynamic setup; if White castles queenside, the bishop should be developed to a useful square like b3 or c4.

explains: After Bc4, White's setup is very committal: he intends to castle kingside, play f4-f5, Qd3, and bring a rook to the e-file to break open the e6 pawn. If White does not follow through with f4-f5, the bishop on c4 becomes misplaced, especially if he castles queenside in a Yugoslav/English attack style.
teaches: A move like Bc4 in the Sicilian is only good if it fits a specific attacking plan; otherwise it can be a waste of time and leave the bishop poorly placed.
plans: White should commit to the kingside attack with f4-f5 and rook to e1, while Black should be ready to counter on the queenside.

explains: In the main line, after Nf6, Nb3, and castling, Black plays ...a6 to prevent Nb5 and prepare ...b5. White plays f4, and Black responds with ...Qc7, defending the knight and preparing ...e5 to undermine White's attack. The exchange on d4 gives Black pressure on the c-file.
teaches: In the Taimanov/Paulsen Sicilian, Black's ...a6 and ...b5 is a standard queenside expansion, while ...Qc7 both defends and prepares ...e5, a key break against White's kingside attack.
plans: Black continues with ...b5 and ...Bb7, while White builds up on the kingside with f5 and Qf3.

explains: After fxe6, White always recaptures with the f-pawn to keep the option of playing e5, which is very useful for opening the position. White's pieces are well placed: bishops active, rook on the e-file, queen ready to go to h3. Black has weaknesses on e4, c2, and the a8-h1 diagonal, but White's attack is strong.
teaches: When recapturing on e6, using the f-pawn preserves the possibility of e5, a key pawn break to open lines against the enemy king.
plans: White plays Qh3 to pressure e6, then Qg3, while Black defends and prepares ...e5 as a positional counter.

explains: Black's ...e5 is a strong positional move if White does not play it himself, as it fixes the weak pawns on e4 and c2 and gives Black a very comfortable position. White correctly plays e5 himself, forcing ...d5 and then Qxe5, after which Black must move the knight, and White's bishops and rook become very dangerous.
teaches: In sharp Sicilian positions, the player who plays ...e5 first often gains a positional edge; White must be proactive with e5 to avoid being worse.
plans: After Qxe5, Black moves the knight (e.g., to h5 or elsewhere), and White continues with Rfe1 and tries to bring the knight into the attack via e5.

explains: Black plays ...Qc6, connecting rooks and preparing ...Bd6, which would improve his pieces significantly. White must respond with Qg5 to anticipate ...Bd6, and then Black gains a tempo with ...h6.
teaches: Connecting rooks and preparing a bishop move like ...Bd6 can be a strong regrouping; White must be alert to such ideas and prevent them with timely queen moves.
plans: White continues to build the attack, while Black seeks counterplay with ...Bd6 and ...h6 to gain tempi on the queen.

explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 e5, White's last move c3 signals the c3 Sicilian. Black has two main setups: Nc6 (entering the mainline complications) or a6 (a forcing alternative). The position is roughly equal, with White's central pawns loose and Black's knights also loose.
teaches: Recognize the opponent's opening intentions early. When facing the c3 Sicilian, you have a choice between entering the mainline or choosing a sideline; both can be viable, but you must be prepared for the specific plans.
plans: Black should decide between Nc6 and a6. Nc6 leads to the mainline where Black can equalize easily; a6 leads to a different, forcing variation.

explains: In the line after d4 cxd4 cxd4 d6 Bc4, White puts pressure on the loose knight on f7. This resembles a reversed Caro-Kann. After …Bb4+, White has more space and piece activity, but Black is completely equal according to engines.
teaches: In the Sicilian, Black often accepts a slight space disadvantage in exchange for dynamic counterplay and solid equality. Don't panic if White has more space; the position can still be balanced.
plans: Black should continue developing and aim to complete kingside castling, while White will try to exploit the space advantage and piece activity.

explains: After …Nc6, White can also choose Bc4 instead of the immediate d4. This leads to a different type of Sicilian, often called the 'Closed Sicilian' or 'developing' approach. Black can respond with …d6, …e6, or …Nf6, each leading to distinct plans.
teaches: In the Open Sicilian, White doesn't always have to play d4 immediately. Delaying d4 can transpose to other systems, and Black must be flexible in responding to different move orders.
plans: Black should choose a setup that fights for control of d4 and d5, such as ...d6 or ...e6, and be ready for White's eventual d4 break.

explains: In the mainline after d4 cxd4 Qxd4, White's queen is active. Black plays …Nf6 to protect the knight on c6, and after Bc4 Nc6 Qe4, White maintains pressure on the knight. Black must respond with …d6 to break the central bind, leading to a forced sequence that results in a balanced position.
teaches: When the opponent's queen becomes active, you must often force a reaction to break the bind. In these sharp lines, memorizing the key forced moves is essential to reach a playable middlegame.
plans: Black should play …d6, then continue with ...e6, ...Nf6, ...Be7, and castle, aiming for a normal development. White will develop the knight to c3 and prepare to castle.

explains: Black's bishop on d6 is a strong piece, and White must address the threat it poses. The queen on g5 is a response to the bishop's pressure, but it can be harassed by h6, gaining a tempo.
teaches: When your opponent develops a bishop to a strong diagonal, consider how to neutralize it or use your queen to create counterplay, but be aware of tempo-gaining pawn moves against your queen.
plans: White should consider maintaining pressure on the diagonal while dealing with the queen's safety, possibly by repositioning the bishop or preparing an attack.

explains: The diagonal a7-g1 (or a2-g8 for Black) becomes critical when the f-pawn has moved. With a knight on f6, there are tactical motifs involving knight jumps to g4 or e4, attacking f2 and h2.
teaches: Always check for tactics along the long diagonal when the opponent's f-pawn has moved. A knight on f6 can leap to g4 or e4, creating threats against the king's position.
plans: White must keep a piece on the diagonal to prevent these tactics, possibly by playing Ba7 or Bf2, and consider solidifying the position to avoid immediate threats.

explains: Black's move taking on e5 is a mistake because it allows a tactical sequence. The knight on g4 is a strong move, attacking the rook and threatening Nf2, which would be decisive if the queen can join via b6 or c5.
teaches: When you have a lead in development or a tactical opportunity, look for forcing moves like knight forks that target the king and rook simultaneously. The combination of a knight on g4 and queen on the b6-c5 diagonal can be lethal.
plans: Black should execute the tactic: Ng4, then if the rook moves, Nf2+ and queen to c5 or b6, winning material. If White exchanges rooks, the king is forced to h1, and the knight continues to cause damage.

explains: After the tactical sequence, Black has infiltrated the second rank with the rook. This rook is extremely powerful, and White's best chance is to exchange it, even at the cost of material, because it restricts the king and attacks pawns.
teaches: In the middlegame, a rook on the opponent's second rank is often worth more than a pawn or even a piece. Keep it there to create threats, and if the opponent offers to trade, consider whether the rook's activity justifies keeping it.
plans: Black should maintain the rook on the second rank, using it to attack the king and pawns, while converting the material advantage in the endgame.

explains: After infiltrating the opponent's second rank with a rook, the rook is extremely powerful. Even if it seems technically unsound to keep it there, the opponent's best option is often to trade it off because its activity outweighs material considerations.
teaches: When you have a rook on the opponent's second rank, prioritize keeping it active; forcing the opponent to trade it off is often a win.
plans: Maintain the rook on the second rank, using it to create threats and tie down the opponent's pieces.

explains: In an endgame or late middlegame where you are up the exchange and the opponent still has one rook, trading off that rook is very favorable for you. It simplifies to a position where your extra material is more decisive.
teaches: When you are up the exchange, actively seek to trade the opponent's remaining rook to convert your advantage.
plans: Look for opportunities to exchange rooks, even if it requires a tactical sequence.

explains: When you are up material, avoid rushing to win immediately. Instead, consolidate and deny the opponent any counterplay. In the game, a careless pawn move allowed the opponent to create passed pawns and counterplay.
teaches: When ahead in material, prioritize safety and prophylaxis over immediate aggression; don't give the opponent unnecessary chances.
plans: Solidify your position, trade pieces, and only then proceed with a slow, methodical win.

explains: After the opponent has moved kingside pawns and weakened the second rank, be alert to counterplay. In the game, the opponent had many pieces ready to attack the king, so prophylactic moves were necessary to avoid mate threats.
teaches: When your own king is exposed, play prophylactic moves to prevent mating threats, even if it means giving up some activity. It's better to win later than to risk a counterattack.
plans: Move the rook to f8 to guard against back-rank mates and also to prepare attacking the opponent's knight from e8.

explains: In this Sicilian setup, White has many pieces aimed at the black king, so Black must be pragmatic and play prophylactically, aiming to win later rather than immediately.
teaches: When facing a dangerous attacking setup, prioritize safety and prophylaxis over active play; it's okay to make defensive moves that also prepare counterplay.
plans: Play Rf8 to avoid back-rank mate threats and prepare to challenge the center with Re8, attacking the knight on e4.

explains: Rf8 serves two purposes: it prevents immediate mating threats (even if the rook is given up, the king can escape), and it prepares Re8 to attack the knight on e4, potentially winning it if White is careless.
teaches: A single move can serve multiple defensive and offensive purposes; look for moves that both neutralize threats and create threats of your own.
plans: After Rf8, follow up with Re8 to pressure the knight, forcing White to defend accurately or lose material.

explains: The move Kg7 was a mistake because it allowed Rc7+ Kf8, cutting off the black king and forcing it to the back rank, which is undesirable. White could have played Rb7 instead, preparing to attack the pawn, leading to a drawish rook vs minor piece endgame despite Black being up an exchange.
teaches: Keep your king off the back rank and avoid moves that allow your opponent to cut off your king or force it to a passive square. In rook endgames, activity matters more than material.
plans: If given the chance, Black should have kept the king active and avoided the check that cut it off. In the resulting rook vs minor piece position, accurate defense can hold a draw.

explains: In the rook endgame, Black's king approaches the passed pawn, which is good, but White missed a chance to play Rb7, stopping the pawn. After Bxb3, White loses a piece, which was the final blunder in a complex and double-edged position.
teaches: In rook endgames, the king's activity and the ability to stop passed pawns are crucial. Always check if your opponent's last move leaves a piece hanging or a pawn unstoppable.
plans: Black should capitalize on the blunder by winning the knight, then converting the material advantage to win the game.

explains: After d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 e6, if Black plays an early ...Bf5, White can expand with e4. The engine evaluates the position as equal, but White gets a free tempo and a space advantage.
teaches: When Black commits the bishop to f5 before developing the knight, White should immediately challenge it with e4, gaining time and central space.
plans: Follow up with h4 to harass the bishop, and later develop the bishop to d3 to create pressure on the h7-e4 diagonal.

explains: After e4, Black's bishop must move. If Black plays ...h6, White can continue with g4 and g5, opening lines against Black's king, making castling kingside unsafe.
teaches: When the opponent weakens their kingside with pawn moves like ...h6, use pawn storms (g4-g5) to open lines and prevent castling.
plans: If ...h6, play g4 and g5 to undermine the bishop and create attacking chances.

explains: If Black plays ...h5 instead, White can play Bg5, forcing the queen to move. Then White develops the bishop to d3, creating threats on the diagonal. Black should exchange in the center, but if they take on e4, White can play Nf3, and ...exf4 is not possible due to Bb5+ winning the queen.
teaches: When the opponent's queen is misplaced, use pins and checks to win material or gain time.
plans: After ...h5, play Bg5, then develop the bishop to d3, and if Black takes on e4, play Nf3 to save the pawn while maintaining threats.

explains: In the line with ...f6 to chase the bishop, White can play d5, gaining a tempo on the queen. After exchanges, White can castle queenside and Black's knight is trapped, leading to a huge advantage (engine +4).
teaches: When the opponent weakens their kingside with ...f6, use central pawn breaks (d5) to open the position and exploit the exposed king.
plans: Play d5, then after exchanges, castle queenside and target the trapped knight on a7 or the weak pawns.

explains: Against the more common ...Nf6 on move two, after d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 Bf5 f3 e6 g4 Bg6 h4, Black has a tricky third option: ...c5. If White takes the bishop, Black gets a much better position with a ruined pawn structure. So White should play e3 first, preventing ...cxd4 and keeping the bishop.
teaches: When the opponent offers a piece for a pawn, evaluate the resulting pawn structure and piece activity; sometimes declining the capture is best.
plans: Against ...c5, play e3 to solidify the center, then continue with the standard plan of h5 and Bg5, or Nb5 ideas.

explains: After d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 e6, if Black plays ...c5, White should respond with e3 to prevent ...cxd4 and ...Qb6 ideas. This also keeps the option of Nb5, pressuring a7.
teaches: In the Jobava London, meeting ...c5 with e3 is a flexible way to maintain central control and keep tactical threats like Nb5 alive.
plans: If Black does nothing, play Nb5, and if ...Qa5, then c3, forcing ...Na6 and maintaining pressure on a7.

explains: Black often plays ...h5 or ...h6. Against ...h6, White has more flexibility because g5 is possible, and the pawn structure is less committed. After ...h5, g5 only attacks the knight and reduces White's options.
teaches: When choosing between similar pawn moves, prefer the one that leaves your own pawn structure more flexible and gives you more attacking options.
plans: After ...h6, prepare e4 and castling queenside, keeping the king safe before starting a kingside pawn storm.

explains: If White wants a safe game, they can play e3, Bd3, and trade bishops, leading to an equal position. But for a win, White should aim for a more aggressive setup with f3 and a kingside pawn storm.
teaches: In sharp openings, you can choose between solid equality and a double-edged attacking game; the choice depends on your style and risk tolerance.
plans: If choosing the aggressive path, focus on preparing e4 and castling queenside before committing to kingside pawn moves.

explains: In the Jobava London, when Black plays ...Bf5 and then ...Bd6, White can trade bishops and then open the center with d4xc5 or e4, even if it looks risky. The key is that if Black has castled kingside, White's g5 and h6 breaks become decisive.
teaches: Trading off the light-squared bishops can be good because it removes a defender of the kingside and allows White to proceed with a pawn storm. If Black castles kingside, the g5-h6 pawn push can be overwhelming.
plans: After trading bishops, White should aim to open the center with e4 and continue the kingside attack, while being aware of Black's queenside counterplay with c4 and b5.

explains: Against the resilient ...a6 setup, White plays Bd3, and Black often trades bishops. Taking back with the queen is better than with the pawn because White will get e4 in anyway. If Black plays ...c5, White can either take on c5 or castle queenside; taking gives Black a tempo to develop the bishop, so not taking is more optimal but riskier.
teaches: When deciding whether to capture a pawn that opens the center, consider the tempo cost. Sometimes declining the capture to maintain development is better, even if it leads to a more complicated game.
plans: If White declines ...c5, castle queenside and prepare e4, while Black will try to gain space on the queenside with c4 and b5.

explains: In the h6 setup, Black's plan is to attack on the queenside with c4, b5, and possibly queen a5. White's plan is to expand in the center with e4 and create complications before Black's queenside attack becomes meaningful. If Black plays b5, White can play g5 to force the knight away, then e4.
teaches: When both sides attack on opposite wings, speed is crucial. White must create central threats to distract Black from the queenside pawn storm.
plans: White should continue with g5 and e4, while Black tries to open lines on the queenside. If Black plays b4, White can block with b3 and knight a4.

explains: In the double-edged positions arising from the h6 setup, both kings are potentially exposed. White's king is often safer, but Black can create threats with rook lifts and knight maneuvers. For example, if Black can trade off the light-squared bishop, a knight on a7 could be dangerous.
teaches: In sharp positions, king safety is relative. Even if your king is safer, you must respect your opponent's counterplay and avoid allowing tactical motifs like knight forks or rook invasions.
plans: White should aim to open the center and get the rook to e1, while Black tries to exploit the semi-open files and create threats against the white king.

explains: The second option for Black is ...h5, which forces White to play g5 to prevent ...hxg4 and ...fxg4, which would stop e4. Black can then play ...Ng8 and ...Ne7-f5, aiming for a strong knight outpost. White must be careful not to allow ...Bxf4 and ...exf4, which would give Black a good game.
teaches: When your opponent plays a pawn move to stop your central break, you must find a way to maintain the tension. Sometimes you have to allow a piece to retreat but then redeploy it to a better square.
plans: White should play g5 and then prepare e4, while Black maneuvers the knight to f5. White must decide whether to allow the bishop trade or keep the tension.

explains: In the Jobava London, after d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 e6, Black may try to develop the knight to f5 via ...Ne7, but White can keep the option of playing e4 to chase the knight away, making that plan risky.
teaches: When the opponent posts a knight on f5, keep the option of e4 to challenge it; don't commit to a move that allows it to settle.
plans: White should aim for e3 and Bd3, maintaining flexibility to play e4 later.

explains: Black's best response is ...a6 to prevent Nb5 ideas, and if Black plays ...c5, White can use Nb5 and c3 to handle it. After ...Bxd3 and cxd3, White gets a solid but double-edged position where Black scores well because White must balance offense and defense.
teaches: In this structure, White's plans matter more than memorized theory; recognize the typical plans and complications.
plans: White should look for the g6 pawn move to weaken Black's kingside and prepare a queenside castle.

explains: White's key early idea is to play g6, provoking ...f6, which creates a permanent weakness on Black's kingside and discourages castling there. Black's best reply is ...f6, but that weakens the e6 pawn and the g6 square.
teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, create weaknesses in their castling zone to restrict their options.
plans: After g6, White can continue with Nge2, castle queenside, and prepare e4 to expand in the center.

explains: Black will typically play ...c5 and then launch a queenside attack with ...c4, ...b5, ...Qa5, ...b4, aiming to checkmate White's king after White castles queenside. White's counter is to play in the center with e4 whenever Black attacks on the wing.
teaches: When the opponent attacks on the wing, counter in the center; e4 is often the correct response to ...b5.
plans: White should continue with e4, trying to open the center and exploit Black's king's exposure.

explains: In the example game, White delayed g6 and castled queenside, allowing Black to start a direct attack with ...Qa5. This shows that g6 is more precise and should be played as soon as possible.
teaches: Timing is critical: play the weakening move g6 before committing to castling, to avoid giving Black free attacking tempo.
plans: White should prioritize g6, then Nge2, castle queenside, and prepare e4.

explains: In this line, Black's early ...Bf5 setup invites White to start a pawn storm with g4 and h4. If Black delays the thematic ...g6, White's attack gains speed and Black's counterplay arrives too late, leaving Black worse.
teaches: When facing a flank pawn storm, do not delay the standard defensive move ...g6; it is often the critical resource to blunt the attack and keep the position balanced.
plans: Black should aim to play ...g6 early, then castle queenside, and follow with ...c5 and ...Qa5 to generate counterplay.

explains: In the game, White's attack was too slow because ...g6 was not played in time. Black's counterattack with ...b5 and ...e4 was strong, but White's king was exposed and Black missed the most accurate continuations, allowing White to survive and eventually win.
teaches: Timing is crucial in opposite-side castling races: every tempo matters, and a single defensive move like ...g6 can be the difference between a winning attack and a lost position.
plans: When attacking on the flank, keep the king safe and do not allow the opponent's counterplay to outpace your own threats.

explains: In the final phase, Black missed the only winning move ...f5, which would have prevented White's rook from invading on d6. Instead, ...c3 allowed White to equalize and later convert the extra pawn.
teaches: In sharp positions, look for prophylactic moves that stop the opponent's key ideas, even if they are not immediately obvious. A move like ...f5 can be the only way to keep the advantage.
plans: Black should have played ...f5 to control the d6 square and keep the rook out, then consolidate the material advantage.

explains: The recommended approach against the Bf5 setup is to play ...g6 early, then castle queenside, and if White plays c4, respond with ...Qa5 and immediately break in the center with ...e4. This gives Black active counterplay and avoids the risk of being overrun on the kingside.
teaches: Against a kingside pawn storm, a timely central break can be more effective than passive defense. Combining ...g6 with a quick ...e4 creates imbalances and practical chances.
plans: Black should aim for the setup: ...g6, ...f6, ...Qa5, ...e4, and then castle queenside, keeping the position complicated and fighting for the initiative.

explains: After d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 e6, Black's ...c5 is a critical test. If White continues with Nc3 and tries to maintain the Jobava setup, Black can capture on d4 and follow with ...Nc6, leaving White with a worse version. The only move that preserves an advantage is d5, entering the Old Benoni.
teaches: When facing ...c5, the principled response is to push d4-d5, transposing into the Old Benoni, rather than allowing a transposition to an inferior line. Recognize that certain moves force you out of your intended setup.
plans: If Black plays ...c5, White should play d5 and study the Old Benoni structures, focusing on space advantage and piece activity.

explains: Against ...f5 (Dutch), continuing with Nc3 leads to the Raphael Variation. If White insists on Bf4, the position is equal but not better. Black can choose setups like ...d6, ...e6, ...g6, and the game becomes a normal Dutch where White has no opening advantage.
teaches: In the Dutch, the Jobava setup with Bf4 is playable but yields equality. To fight for an advantage, you need to know the specific main lines of the Dutch, such as the Raphael Variation with Bg5.
plans: If facing the Dutch, consider playing Bg5 instead of Bf4 to maintain more tension, or accept equality with Bf4 and play a sound positional game.

explains: Against ...g6 or ...d6 (Modern or Old Indian setups), the best move is e4, transposing into the Modern Defense or Old Indian. Playing Bf4 is slightly inferior, as Black can quickly break the center with ...c5, forcing d5 and leading to messy positions.
teaches: When Black avoids the main lines and plays flexible setups like ...g6 or ...d6, the principled response is to seize the center with e4. Trying to maintain the Jobava with Bf4 allows Black to undermine your center.
plans: If Black plays ...g6 or ...d6, White should play e4 and enter the Modern or Old Indian main lines, aiming for a central advantage.

explains: The most irritating transposition is when Black plays ...e6 after d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6, threatening to enter the French Defense if White plays e4. If White plays Bf4 instead, Black can play ...Bd6, and the position is equal. White has no advantage.
teaches: When Black plays ...e6, you must decide whether to enter the French with e4 or accept equality with Bf4. If you play the Tarrasch against the French (Nd2), you may prefer Bf4, but you must be ready for ...Bd6 equalizing.
plans: If Black plays ...e6, White can choose between e4 (French) or Bf4 (equal). If opting for Bf4, be prepared for ...Bd6 and a balanced game.

explains: In the Jobava London, after d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 e6, if White plays e4, the game transposes to the French Defense, which Black may know well. Since White's knight is on c3, this is not the Tarrasch French (where the knight goes to d2), so White might be less comfortable.
teaches: Be aware of transpositions when choosing an opening. If you play a system like the Jobava London, you must be ready for the resulting structures, including the French, Caro-Kann, and others.
plans: If you want to avoid the French, you can play e3, keeping the game in Jobava London territory.

explains: If White delays Nb5 and plays Nf3 instead, Black cannot safely develop the knight to c6. If Black plays ...Nc6, White plays Nb5, and since Black cannot play ...Ne6 (the knight is already on c6), White threatens Nc7+ winning the rook.
teaches: In this structure, the knight on b5 is a powerful fork threat. Always consider such tactical resources when developing.
plans: If Black plays ...Nh5, White can respond with Bc7, attacking the queen and setting up tactics.

explains: In this sharp line, Black's early ...Nh5 is met by Bc7, which is more precise than grabbing material. After Qe7, Bd6 attacks the queen, and the ensuing tactics with Nc7+ and g5 lead to a fork or checkmate, giving White a winning position.
teaches: When the opponent tries to harass your bishop with a knight, look for a precise retreat that maintains the initiative and creates tactical threats, rather than just grabbing material.
plans: Continue the attack with g5 and c4, exploiting Black's exposed king and undeveloped pieces.

explains: In the main line after d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 c5 e3 a6, Black's a6 prevents Nb5. White should exchange on c5 first, then develop normally. Black has two main setups: ...Bg4 or ...Nc6.
teaches: In the Jobava London, White should be ready to meet Black's ...c5 by exchanging and then choosing a plan based on Black's setup. The position remains balanced but White has no worse.
plans: Against ...Bg4, play h3 and then expand with g4-g5, while the king is already safe. Against ...Nc6, consider g5 to provoke weaknesses, or prepare a minority attack with Na4-c5.

explains: When Black plays ...Bf5, White has a specific pawn expansion with f3 and then g4 (or e4 if Black hasn't played ...Nf6). This gains space and challenges the bishop. If Black retreats to g6, White can play h4 to further harass.
teaches: In the Jobava London, the f3-g4 expansion is a key idea to gain space and create attacking chances, but it is double-edged and requires precise handling.
plans: After ...Bg6, continue with h4 and consider trading the bishop with Bd3, then recapture with the c-pawn or queen, and develop the knight to g2 or h3.

explains: After d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 e6, Black's light-squared bishop is attacked by the pawn on d4. Black must save it, and the two main options are h6 and h5. h6 is less forcing because White can simply continue with e3, preparing to develop the bishop to d3 and trade off Black's good bishop.
teaches: When your opponent's bishop is attacked, consider which retreat square gives you the most flexibility and least commitment. A retreat that doesn't force your opponent's hand can be less dangerous.
plans: If Black plays h6, White should play e3, then Bf1-d3, aiming to exchange the bishops. After the trade, Black can recapture with the c-pawn or the queen, but must be careful about the threat of g5.

explains: If Black instead plays h5, White is practically forced to play g5, chasing the bishop back to d7. This gains space on the kingside and continues White's plan of development and pressure.
teaches: A pawn advance like g5 can be used to gain space and drive back a developed piece, even if it creates weaknesses. The resulting position can be rich in strategic ideas.
plans: After g5 and ...Nd7, White continues with the same setup: e3, Bd3, and possibly Nge2, preparing to castle and expand.

explains: Black's best response to White's setup is to close the center with c4 and then push b5, aiming for a queenside attack. This is a typical plan for Black in these structures, and it leads to sharp play.
teaches: When facing a kingside space advantage, it's often good to counter on the opposite wing. Closing the center can reduce the opponent's attacking potential and allow you to start your own pawn storm.
plans: Black should play c4, then b5, and try to attack on the queenside. White must be alert to the threat of g5 and find ways to break through the center.

explains: The position after Black saves the bishop is rich with strategic questions: what to do if Black plays Bd6, whether to allow doubled pawns, whether to play Nh3-f4, whether to expand with e4, and how Black should respond with f6 or c5. These are the main themes to study.
teaches: In complex opening positions, it's important to identify the key strategic questions and patterns. This helps you navigate the middlegame with a plan.
plans: Study the two main setups for Black (with and without Bf5) and the various plans for both sides. This will prepare you for the detailed videos to come.

explains: After d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 e6, White aims for a flexible setup with e3 and Nf3, keeping options open. Black's choices include the Stonewall (with c6) or c5, but the bishop on f4 is well-placed against the Stonewall.
teaches: In the Jobava London, White's setup is normal and flexible; the bishop on f4 is a good piece against the Stonewall, so White should not fear it.
plans: Develop with e3 and Nf3, then choose a plan based on Black's setup.

explains: If Black plays ...Bd6, White should not trade bishops but play Bd3, keeping the bishop and controlling e5. If Black plays ...Be7, White follows the same plan with Bd3 and later c4.
teaches: Avoid trading the light-squared bishop for Black's dark-squared bishop; instead, place it on d3 to support central and kingside play.
plans: After Bd3, castle, then play c4 to break in the center, and prepare kingside attacks with moves like Ne2, g4, and Nh5.

explains: A key maneuver is Ne2, preparing c4 and supporting kingside expansion. If Black plays ...Bd7 and ...Be8, White can play c4, and if Black plays ...c6, White has the annoying Qb3.
teaches: The knight maneuver to e2 is important in this system to support c4 and kingside play.
plans: Play c4 to break the center, and if Black plays ...c6, use Qb3 to create pressure.

explains: Against ...d6, if White plays Bf4, Black can enter a Benko-like gambit with ...b5, giving up a pawn for activity. This is tricky for White, so it's better to avoid Bf4 and instead play e4 to transpose into mainline Pirc/Modern lines.
teaches: In the Jobava London, if Black plays ...d6, it's often better to transpose to mainline Pirc/Modern with e4 rather than stick to the London setup, to avoid tricky gambits.
plans: If Black plays ...d6, consider e4 to enter mainline Pirc/Modern, where White can be comfortable.

explains: If Black plays ...c6, White can play e4, transposing into the Classical Caro-Kann. This is a normal and good option.
teaches: The Jobava London can transpose into the Caro-Kann if Black plays ...c6, and White should be ready to play the Classical variation.
plans: After ...c6, play e4 and proceed with normal Caro-Kann plans.

explains: After d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4, if Black plays …c6, they are inviting the Caro-Kann. If White continues with e4, the game transposes to the Classical Caro-Kann, which is a well-known main line. However, c6 is a useful move for Black because it prevents Nb5 ideas in the Jobava London setup.
teaches: Recognize transpositions to other openings and be prepared to play your normal system even if the opponent tries to steer into familiar territory. The move c6 is not a waste of time; it has a specific purpose against the Jobava London.
plans: If Black plays c6, White can either accept the Caro-Kann with e4 or continue with the Jobava London setup (e3, then f3, g4, h4 if Black plays Bf5).

explains: If Black plays …e6, they are inviting the French Defense. If White plays e4, the game goes into the main lines of the French, which may not be desirable if White is not a French player. Instead, White can play e3 to keep the Jobava London setup, but Black has the annoying option of Bb4 or Bd6 immediately, which can lead to equality.
teaches: When facing an invitation to another opening, you have a choice: either accept the transposition if you are comfortable, or stick to your own system. Be aware of the downsides of your setup, such as the bishop being exposed to early attacks.
plans: If Black plays e6 and then Bd6, White should consider taking on d6 to simplify, accepting a roughly equal position, and then play on from there.

explains: The trickiest move for Black is …c5, which can lead to the Albin Counter Gambit with a tempo up for White if White plays e4. However, this results in a messy position. Alternatively, White can play d5 to transpose into a favorable version of the Albin Counter Gambit, where White has a lead in development and Black's king is stuck in the center.
teaches: When facing an early c5, you have a choice between a sharp gambit line or a more solid approach. The move d5 can be strong because it opens the position while Black's king is still vulnerable.
plans: If Black plays c5, White can either play e4 (Irish Gambit) or d5. After d5, if Black takes, White recaptures with the queen, and after queens are exchanged, White can develop quickly and put pressure on Black's uncastled king.

explains: After d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 e6, White can simply play the normal Jobava London setup. If Black tries …c5, White can avoid sharp gambits and play Bf4, keeping a calm position. If Black takes on d4, White recaptures with the queen, and Black must waste time dealing with the attack on e6, so there is no tempo gain.
teaches: In the Jobava London, when Black plays an early c5, White does not need to enter sharp lines; a solid setup with Bf4 and e3 is sufficient, as Black's pawn on e6 remains a target.
plans: Develop naturally with e3, Nf3, Bd3, and castle, aiming for a comfortable position with a slight edge.

explains: If Black plays …c5 and White chooses Bf4, Black can transpose to main lines with Nf6 and e3, which is fine for White. Alternatively, if Black plays Nc6, White plays e3, and after cxd4 exd4, Black's bishop on f5 is not easy to use for a pawn storm; White can simply play Bd3 and get a good Carlsbad structure.
teaches: In the Jobava London, White can often force a Carlsbad structure where Black's pieces are less active, and White's bishop pair or better-placed pieces give a slight edge.
plans: Play Bd3, trade bishops if possible, then develop Nf3, Ne2, and castle, aiming for a slow buildup with a slight advantage.

explains: Against …g6 (a fianchetto setup), White can deviate from the normal system and play e4, using the knight on c3 to support the center break. After d4xe4, Nxe4, Bg7, Nf3, Nf6, White can recapture and then play c3, with ideas of Bc4, Qb3, and kingside pressure. This is comfortable for White because Black's development is awkward, and any Bg4 is met by Qb3.
teaches: When Black fianchettoes against the Jobava London, White can seize the center with e4, leveraging the knight on c3, and then build up a kingside attack.
plans: Play c3, Bc4, Qb3, castle kingside, and prepare Rfe1, Ng5, or Ne5 to pressure Black's position.

explains: If Black plays …Nc6 (symmetrical setup) and then …Bf5, White should play e4! This is not a gambit because White will win the pawn back. If Black takes on e4, White plays d5, and if Black's knight goes to b4, White can play a3 and Qd4, winning the pawn and getting a great position. If Black retreats the knight to b8, White can still play Qd4 and regain the pawn.
teaches: In the Jobava London, an early e4 break can be strong even when Black tries to copy, as it opens the position and White's development advantage becomes significant.
plans: After e4, if Black takes, play d5 and then Qd4 to win back the pawn, with a clear advantage and attacking chances.

explains: After d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 e6, if Black plays ...exd4, White can recapture with the queen on d4, winning back the pawn while maintaining pressure. The position is comfortable for White, with options to castle queenside and enjoy a spatial advantage.
