teaches: When facing a pawn capture on d4, recapturing with the queen is often a safe and active way to regain material while keeping the initiative.
plans: Develop naturally, castle queenside, and use the central pawn majority to gain space.

explains: If Black instead captures with the bishop on d4, White can recapture, then play d5, securing the bishop pair and central space. The resulting position is very pleasant for White, with all pieces defended and clear plans.
teaches: After a bishop capture on d4, recapturing and then advancing d5 can secure a lasting space advantage and the bishop pair.
plans: Maintain the central pawn duo, develop the pieces, and exploit the bishop pair in the middlegame.

explains: In the line with ...Nf6 and ...e6, if Black plays ...Nbd7, White should avoid an immediate queen d4 because it would lose the queen. Instead, simple moves like c4 keep everything defended and maintain a great position.
teaches: Always check for tactical refutations before centralizing the queen; sometimes a quiet developing move is stronger.
plans: Play c4 to support the center and continue development.

explains: The excerpt concludes that the Jobava London player must be prepared for specific defenses: the Old Benoni, the Dutch with ...f5, and the Pirc/Modern with ...d6. Against the Dutch, ...f5 leads to the Raphael Variation, where Bf4 is inferior. Against ...d6, the Pirc setup is recommended, and if Bf4 is chosen, one must be ready for Benko/Benoni-like positions.
teaches: A complete opening repertoire requires specific preparation against the most critical defenses, not just general principles.
plans: Study the recommended lines against the Old Benoni, Dutch (Raphael), and Pirc/Modern setups.

explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 f5 Nxe5 Nf6, taking the pawn on e4 with Nxe4? is risky; Black gets active play and White often ends up worse. Similarly, d4 gives Black what he wants, leading to a normal position where White has no advantage.
teaches: In sharp gambit lines, avoid grabbing material or playing central moves that allow the opponent to dictate the pace. Look for the most principled move that maintains control.
plans: White should play g4, a move that challenges Black's setup and offers White a slight edge if both sides play accurately.

explains: If Black plays …d6 immediately (after g4 Nxe4 Nxe5), White must avoid the natural Nc4? because Black gets a much better position, almost winning. Instead, White should play Ng4, which leads to a normal game.
teaches: In sharp lines, a knight move that is common in other openings can be a mistake here. Always check if the opponent can exploit the knight's placement.
plans: After Ng4, Black plays ...Be7, ...Nf6, ...Bf6, and both sides castle, with White slightly better.

explains: After g4 Nxe4 Nxe5, if Black plays …Nc6, White wins with Qh5+! If …g6, then Nxg6 wins. If …Kd7, there is a forced mate: Qf7+ Kd6 Nc4+ Kc5 Qd5+ Kb4 a3+ Ka4 b3#.
teaches: When the opponent makes a natural developing move, look for immediate tactical blows. A queen check can exploit the weakened kingside and lead to a decisive attack.
plans: White should play Qh5+ and follow the forcing line to win.

explains: If Black plays …Nf6 (guarding h5), White plays Bc4, creating threats on f7. Black must play …Qe7, and White can continue with d4. If Black plays …Nc6, White castles, and if …Nxe5, then dxe5 Qxe5 exf5 leaves White with powerful bishops and a winning initiative.
teaches: When the opponent defends against one threat, look for a central pawn push to open lines for your pieces. A lead in development and active pieces can outweigh material equality.
plans: White should play d4, castle, and maintain the initiative, with the bishops becoming monsters.

explains: After …Nf6 Bc4 Qe7 d4, Black's best move is …Qf6, reaching a critical position. White must play d4 (defending the knight and opening the bishop), not Qh5? because Black plays …Qg6, preventing the queen from staying and winning the knight.
teaches: In critical positions, the only move may be a quiet one that defends and opens lines. Avoid rushing with the queen if it can be driven away.
plans: After d4, Black has two losing moves: …fxe4? Bc4 wins, and …Nc6? Nc3! (the knight is immune due to Nd5) is overwhelming. Black's only move is …d6, chasing the knight away.

explains: After d4 d6, White should play Nc4, not Ng4, because Black still has the f5 pawn. Black then takes on e4, and after Nc3, Black must play the counter-intuitive …Qg6, defending the e4 pawn. If Black plays …Nc6, White plays d5 and wins.
teaches: When a pawn is attacked, sometimes the best defense is a queen move that also maintains pressure. Look for counter-intuitive moves that are forced.
plans: White should continue developing and maintain the initiative, with the position offering White a clear advantage.

explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 f5 Nxe5 Qe7, White's knight on e5 is attacked, so the forcing sequence continues with d4, forcing Black to play …d6, chasing the knight away. White then retreats to c4, where the knight attacks the f7 pawn and the e5 square, while Black recaptures the pawn on e4. This is all forced if both sides know the theory.
teaches: In sharp gambit lines, recognize forced sequences and keep pieces active while the opponent is tied down to defending their extra pawn.
plans: After Nc4, White will develop the knight to c3, preparing to control the center and target Black's weaknesses.

explains: After Nc4, Black's best move is the counter-intuitive …Qg6, defending the e4 pawn and preventing White's bishop from developing to c4. If Black plays …Nc6, White plays d5, winning; if …Ne7, White plays Ne3, making development hard for Black; if …Bb7, White plays Nd5, creating threats.
teaches: When your opponent has a strong knight on c4, look for moves that both defend your material and restrict the opponent's development, even if they seem unnatural.
plans: White will play Bf4, preparing to castle queenside and build pressure against Black's position.

explains: After Bf4, Black has two main setups: either …Ne7 or …Be7, which often transpose. White has two good plans: one is Ne3, guarding the g2 pawn, and then playing h4-h5 to attack Black's king stuck in the center; the other is Qd2, preparing queenside castling and then playing f3 to challenge the e4 pawn.
teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, use pawn storms (h4-h5) to open lines, or prepare a safe castling and then undermine the center with f3.
plans: If White chooses Qd2, after castling queenside and Black castling kingside, White plays f3, aiming to open the f-file and activate the rook.

explains: In the key position after f3, if Black plays exf3, White recaptures with gxf3, opening the g-file. White then plays Ne3 to control the d5 square, threatening the c7 pawn and supporting the bishop. Black's pieces are worse, and White's pieces come into play with tempo.
teaches: After opening a file, use it to bring rooks into the attack, and control key central squares like d5 to restrict the opponent's pieces.
plans: White will continue developing with moves like Bc4+, Rg1, and Bg5 to trade off Black's defender, leading to an overwhelming attack.

explains: If Black tries …b5 to gain counterplay, White can take it with Nxb5, and after …Nd5, White's bishop retreats, but White should still be winning because of the extra pawn and better piece activity, despite Black having the open b-file.
teaches: When the opponent sacrifices a pawn for activity, you can accept it if you can consolidate and maintain your advantage, even if they get some counterplay.
plans: White will aim to complete development and use the extra pawn to convert the advantage, while neutralizing Black's activity.

explains: After the gambit pawn is taken, the position can transpose into a setup where White has a comfortable edge. The recommended setup involves developing the queen to d2, castling queenside, and then playing f3 to break in the center.
teaches: When facing an aggressive gambit, a solid setup with queenside castling and a central pawn break can neutralize the initiative.
plans: Develop the pieces to their natural squares, castle queenside, and prepare f3 to challenge the center.

explains: If Black plays exf3, White can recapture with the g-pawn. Black may then try b5 to gain activity, sacrificing a pawn to get a knight to d5 and open the b-file. However, White's activity along the g-file and diagonals is stronger than Black's play on the b-file.
teaches: In dynamic positions, compare the quality of activity on open files and diagonals; a lead in development and safer king can outweigh a pawn sacrifice.
plans: Maintain the initiative by exploiting the g-file and diagonal pressure, while keeping the king safe on the queenside.

explains: The recommended move order is: take the pawn, play d4, develop the knight to c4 (likely a typo for c3), develop the bishop to f4, and after Nf6, play Qd2, castle queenside, and then f3.
teaches: A clear development plan with rapid castling and a central break is a reliable method against gambit lines.
plans: Follow the standard development: d4, Nc3, Bf4, Qd2, O-O-O, and f3.

explains: In the Queen's Indian, after White plays b2-d2, the threat of e4 becomes real. If Black plays c5 prematurely, White can respond with e4, leading to sharp play. The move Bb7-a6 is a way to undermine White's control of key central squares, specifically preparing against the d4-d5 break.
teaches: A bishop on a6 can be used to fight for light squares and prevent White from playing d5, which is a common central expansion in the Queen's Indian.
plans: Black aims to play ...Bb4 or ...c5, while White may consider Nc3 and d5 if Black is not careful.

explains: The choice of where to place the d-pawn (d5 or d6) determines the nature of the position. With d5, White can quickly play Ne5, a strong central outpost. With d6, Black protects e5 and leaves more options, but it is less ambitious.
teaches: The d-pawn's placement in the Queen's Indian dictates the strategic direction: d5 leads to more dynamic play, d6 to more solid but passive setups.
plans: If Black plays d5, White should consider Ne5. If Black plays d6, Black can later aim for ...e5 or ...c5 breaks.

explains: An isolated queen's pawn (IQP) can also arise from the same position if Black recaptures on c5 with the bishop instead of the pawn. This is a more static but still aggressive structure, requiring active piece play.
teaches: The IQP position demands active piece placement and attacking chances; passive play will allow White to blockade and win the pawn.
plans: Black should aim for piece pressure against White's king and use the d4 square for a knight. White should try to blockade the pawn and trade pieces.

explains: After d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2, White has not committed the bishop to f4, so e3 is a natural developing move that doesn't block the bishop. Black's bishop on b7 is already developed, so ...Ba6 makes little sense.
teaches: In the Queen's Indian, White often plays e3 to support d4 and prepare development, without worrying about the c1-bishop. Black's light-squared bishop is already active on b7, so ...Ba6 is usually a waste of time.
plans: White will continue with 0-0, Nbd2 or Nc3, and possibly Re1, aiming for a solid center and harmonious development.

explains: Black's main options after e3 are ...Be7 (solid, main line) and ...Bb4 (fighting for light squares with tempo). ...Bb4 forces White to defend the check, but White can do so with Nbd2 or Nfd2, keeping the position sound.
teaches: When facing a check, choose the defense that best fits your plans. Here, Nbd2 is common because it keeps the b1-knight's route to c3 open, where it controls d5 and e4.
plans: If White plays Nbd2, the setup resembles a London system with pawns on c3 and d4. If Black plays ...Be7, White can continue with Nc3 and develop normally.

explains: With ...Be7, Black prepares to castle and threatens ...Nh5 to win the bishop if it is on f4. White can meet ...Nh5 with Bg5, forcing an exchange, or play h3 to save the bishop, or ignore it with Nc3.
teaches: When your bishop is attacked by a knight on the rim, you have several options: trade it, retreat it, or ignore it if the attack is not real. Here, ignoring with Nc3 is often best, as ...Nxg3 can be met with hxg3, giving White pressure on the h-file.
plans: White can combine Nc3 with Qc2 and long castling for an aggressive setup, or play h3 to preserve the bishop pair and keep the position safer.

explains: Black's sidelines like ...g6 or ...c5 are possible but not common. ...g6 creates dark-square weaknesses and White can just play normal moves like Nc3, Bg7, Be2 (since Bd3 would bite on granite against ...g6). ...c5 leads to a Benoni-type structure, but White should not fear it.
teaches: When facing unusual moves, rely on sound principles: develop, control the center, and don't overreact. Against ...g6, avoid placing the bishop on d3 if it will be blocked by ...g6; instead, choose a flexible square like e2.
plans: Against ...c5, White plays d5, and if Black captures on c4, White can use the tactical trick Nb5, threatening Nc7, to disrupt Black's development.

explains: Another important structure is the Hedgehog, which arises when White has a pawn on e4 and Black plays c5, leading to an exchange on d4. Black then plays a6 to prevent Nb5, and sets up with Bb7, Qa8, and Rc8 to pressure the diagonal.
teaches: The Hedgehog is a flexible setup where Black accepts a cramped but solid position, aiming to strike later. Key moves are a6, Bb7, Qa8, and Rc8 to create pressure.
plans: Develop the queen to a8, rook to c8, and prepare to break with b5 or d5 when the time is right.

explains: A third structure involves an open b-file, where after an exchange on c5, Black recaptures with the b-pawn. Black then plays d6 to solidify the center and uses the b-file for pressure with Qb6 and Qb8.
teaches: When you have an open b-file, use it to pressure White's queenside. Solidify the center first with d6 to avoid weaknesses.
plans: Play d6, then maneuver the queen to b6 or b8 to double on the b-file and create threats.

explains: In the main line after d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 c5 d5, Black has a choice. Instead of capturing on d5, Black can play Bb4+ to provoke a weakness. White's best response is Bd2, but then the bishop on d2 is misplaced, blocking the queen and not participating in the game.
teaches: The check Bb4+ is a thematic idea in the Queen's Indian and similar openings (Catalan, Bogo-Indian) to force White into a slightly awkward move, gaining time and improving Black's piece placement.
plans: After Bb4+ and Bd2, retreat the bishop to e7, then develop normally. White's bishop on d2 is passive, giving Black comfortable equality.

explains: After Bg2, Black's best move is c6, preparing d5. White has weakened the d5 square because the bishop on d2 blocks the queen, leaving only one pawn defending d5. Black can play d5 with no fear, and White cannot prevent it.
teaches: When your opponent's piece placement blocks their queen, central pawn breaks become more effective. Look for such weaknesses to challenge the center.
plans: Play c6, then d5, reaching a balanced middlegame. Black's only weakness is the e5 square, but overall the position is equal and easy to play.

explains: After the moves d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 c5 d5, Black has just played d5, striking at the center. White cannot play d5 himself without giving up pawns, so the position is fine for Black.
teaches: In the Queen's Indian, Black's plan is to challenge the center with c5 and d5, aiming for equality. The e5 square is a potential weakness for Black, but otherwise Black has no issues.
plans: Black will develop naturally, castle, and prepare to challenge White's center. The main concern is to avoid losing the c6 pawn, so Black may play Nbd7 to support it.

explains: After White plays e4, the position resembles a Semi-Slav with b6 and Ba6, which is slightly unusual. White's e4 is supported, and this is a critical point where Black must choose a plan.
teaches: When facing a central break like e4, Black must decide between breaking the center (c5) or playing on the flank (b5). The choice should be based on which move best challenges White's center.
plans: Black can play c5 to break the center, leading to a symmetrical pawn structure and simplified position, which often results in a draw. Alternatively, b5 is more popular but also leads to balanced play.

explains: After the central tension is released (e4xd5, exd5, dxc5, dxc4), the position becomes simpler with symmetrical pawns and reduced material. Both sides have two bishops and a knight, so winning chances are minimal.
teaches: When the center is resolved and the pawn structure becomes symmetrical, the game often heads toward a draw. Understanding this helps in evaluating the position and choosing moves.
plans: Black can continue with c6, and if White takes on b3, Black can recapture with the rook, maintaining balance. The position is interesting but likely drawn.

explains: After Nb1-d2 meets Ba6, the c4-pawn is defended, and Black has several options. Returning the bishop to b7 is the most principled because it keeps the bishop on the best diagonal and indirectly challenges White's control of d5.
teaches: When your bishop has provoked a concession (like Nb1-d2), it is often best to return it to its most active diagonal rather than committing to a risky pawn break.
plans: Black should play Bb7, then after Bg2, develop with Be7 and castle, aiming for a slow setup with d5 later.

explains: If Black plays c5 too early after Nb1-d2, White can play e4, and after cxd4, White castles, leading to a Hedgehog-type structure that is not the best for Black. The early c5 allows White to seize space with e4.
teaches: Avoid premature pawn breaks when the opponent has a central pawn majority; the concession of Nb1-d2 is meaningful because it enables e4, so Black should not open the position too soon.
plans: Instead of c5, Black should play Be7 and castle, preparing d5 to challenge the center.

explains: Against Qb3, Black should play Nc6, forcing Nb1-d2 to defend the c4-pawn. After Na5, the queen must move again, and after Qc3, Black plays c5, reaching a pleasant Sicilian-type structure with pressure on the b-file and a strong d4 outpost.
teaches: When the opponent plays a provocative queen move, use it to gain time and force concessions; here, Black's main priority is to get a knight to d4, weakening White's control of that square.
plans: Black should aim for ...e5, trade knights on e4, and then play ...Nc6 to ...Nd4, while preparing ...Rb8 to pressure the b-file.

explains: After d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 c5 d5, Black has a Sicilian-like pawn structure with a pawn on c5 and a half-open c-file. This is a very pleasant position for Black, as it resembles a Sicilian where Black is doing well.
teaches: Recognize when the pawn structure resembles another opening (like the Sicilian) and use the associated plans. In such structures, Black often has good counterplay.
plans: Black will aim to play ...exd5 and ...Nxd5, winning a pawn, while White gets activity as compensation.

explains: Against Qc2, Black plays …cxd4, forcing White to play d5, which is a pawn sacrifice. After …exd5 cxd5 Bb7, the pawn on d5 is undefended, and Black can win it with ...Nxd5. White gets active piece play, but Black has an extra pawn and can aim to consolidate.
teaches: Sometimes it is worth giving up a pawn for long-term material gain, especially if the opponent's compensation is not clear. Black should be willing to accept a pawn and then defend accurately.
plans: Black should aim to castle quickly, but if that is difficult, be prepared to give up castling rights and use the extra pawn to counterattack. A key idea is to play ...d4 to create a passed pawn and simplify.

explains: Against Qa4, Black again plays …cxd4, and after Nxd4 (or similar), the inclusion of Qa4 and ...cxd4 does not clearly help either side. Black's bishop on b7 is pinned (if White plays Bg5), but that is not a big deal as long as Black has a pawn.
teaches: In many openings, a pin on the b7-bishop is not a serious weakness if you have other assets. Do not overreact to pins; focus on the overall position.
plans: Black should continue development, castle, and prepare to put pressure on the b-file, especially with ...Qb6.

explains: In the line with …cxd4 Nxd4 Bxg2 Kxg2 (or similar), Black recaptures with the b-pawn (bxc5) when the pawn is not on d5 yet. This is not a concession; it is a pawn moving toward the center and can be defended. The resulting structure has a semi-open b-file, and Black should put pressure on b2 with ...Qb6.
teaches: When recapturing on c5, prefer the b-pawn if it helps central control and can be defended. Use the semi-open b-file to create pressure on the opponent's queenside.
plans: Play ...Qb6 to defend the bishop and attack b2. If White plays Bf4, be careful about ...Qxb2 due to tactics, but the pressure is still useful.

explains: In the resulting hedgehog-like structure with a pawn on d6, Black should reinforce e5 and prepare a kingside expansion with ...h6, ...g5, ...g4, ...h5. This is a typical plan in the Queen's Indian when the b-file is open and White doubles rooks on the d-file.
teaches: Even in seemingly defensive openings, you must play actively. The Queen's Indian is versatile and can lead to many pawn structures, so understanding the typical plans is crucial.
plans: Black's plan is to expand on the kingside with ...g5-g4 and ...h5, creating an attack. This shows that the defense is not passive but dynamic.

explains: d6 setups are often more positional but can be aggressive by keeping the center closed and enabling f5 for a kingside attack.
teaches: Closed centers can allow flank attacks; don't assume d6 is passive.
plans: Consider f5 and kingside play when the center is closed.

explains: Hedgehog positions can arise from the Queen's Indian if Black plays c5 after d6, with White achieving e4 and a Maroczy bind.
teaches: Knowledge of Sicilian hedgehog structures helps in these Queen's Indian lines.
plans: Play flexibly against the bind, aiming for timely breaks.

explains: Some Queen's Indian lines lead to symmetrical pawn structures with no center, which are very drawish.
teaches: Against lower-rated opponents, avoid simplifying central exchanges that lead to dead equal positions.
plans: If facing a weaker player, choose lines that keep imbalance and winning chances.

explains: After d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 c5 d5, Black can choose between …Bb4+ (Capablanca variation) and …Be7 (main line).
teaches: The bishop on e7 is useful and should not be traded off; Bb4+ aims to misplace pieces or double pawns in Bogo-Indian fashion.
plans: In the main line, develop normally and prepare to challenge the center.

explains: Against Nbd2, Black can take the knight, play d5, or other moves. Taking the knight avoids allowing White to play e4.
teaches: Prevent White from achieving e4 in the Queen's Indian; the knight on d2 supports e4.
plans: After …Bxd2+ Qxd2, play d6 and develop with ...Nbd7, ...Qe7, aiming for e5.

explains: If Black plays d5, White can play Ne5, and after ...Nbd7, Qa4 attacks the bishop, leading to trades and a position with few winning chances for Black.
teaches: Playing d5 in the Queen's Indian commits to specific pawn structures and can give White the e5 square.
plans: Avoid d5 if it leads to a passive or drawish position; prefer ...d6 and play for e5.

explains: After d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6 g3 Bb7 Bg2 c5 d5, Black faces a central space disadvantage. The d5 pawn is strong, and Black must avoid creating pawn weaknesses. Defending d5 with c6 allows Rc1, which is annoying. The position is tense, and one side could easily blunder a piece along the long diagonal.
teaches: In the Queen's Indian, when White plays d5, Black must be careful not to create weaknesses. The tension on the diagonal means both sides must watch for tactical shots.
plans: Black should aim to undermine the white center, often by playing ...d6 and ...e5, or by preparing ...f5 for a kingside attack.

explains: After …Bb4+ Nbd2 is rare; Bd2 is the main move. Black can retreat the bishop, play ...d5, ...Na6, or even ...c5, but taking on d2 is the most principled. After …Bxd2+ Qxd2, Black can play ...d6, ...Nbd7, ...Bb2, ...Qe7, and aim for ...e5. The bishop on d2 is not misplaced; it's still a tempo move.
teaches: When a bishop is developed with check, taking it can be principled if it gives the opponent a misplaced piece, but here the bishop on d2 is fine, so Black should not fear the trade.
plans: Develop normally with ...d6, ...Nbd7, ...Qe7, and prepare ...e5 to undermine White's center.

explains: After ...Bxd2+ and ...Qxd2, Black castles and White plays Nc3. Black must be alert: as soon as Nc3 is played, White threatens e4. Black can play ...Ne4 to challenge the knight and prevent e4. This is not a draw offer; it's about starting a kingside attack and opening lines. This setup resembles the Classical Dutch, where ...f5 and the long-diagonal bishop support a strong attack.
teaches: In the Queen's Indian, ...Ne4 is a common resource to blunt White's e4 break. It's a thematic move that also prepares ...f5 for a kingside attack.
plans: After ...Ne4, Black can continue with ...f5, ...d6, and develop the knight to d7, aiming for a Dutch-like attack.

explains: In the d6-f5 setup, Black has a very thematic pawn structure. After ...f5, White often plays Ng5, and after Bxg5, fxg5, and Kxg5, Black plays ...Qe7, preparing ...e5. This is a pattern: with pieces traded and a pawn on f5, ...Nd7 and ...e5 is a common way to start an attack. Black can even consider ...h6, ...g5, and ...f4, a straightforward attacking plan.
teaches: The d6-f5 structure in the Queen's Indian is a schematic setup. Remember the pattern ...Qe7 preparing ...e5, and the possibility of a pawn storm with ...h6, ...g5, and ...f4.
plans: Play ...Qe7, ...Nd7, and ...e5 to open the position. If White plays d5, Black can respond with ...e5, and the knight on e6 becomes strong.

explains: In the Queen's Indian, when Black has not played d5, White's thematic central break is d5, even if it allows e5. The concrete point is that after Qh4 and h6, the knight can go to e6, where it is very strong, supporting the center.
teaches: Recognize the central break d5 as a key resource in the Queen's Indian when Black delays d5. Understand that allowing e5 can be fine if it leads to a strong knight outpost on e6.
plans: If White plays d5 and Black responds with e5, White should aim for Qh4, h6, and Ne6, establishing a powerful knight in the center.

explains: Black's pawn structure is better in this line, and if given time, Black can improve with moves like Rf6, Nd7, and Nf8, leading to a very pleasant position. White's c4 break is never happening, so Black can close the position with a5 and then proceed with g5, f4, and doubling rooks on the f-file.
teaches: When you have a better pawn structure, avoid unnecessary trades and aim to close the position to limit your opponent's counterplay. Use pawn breaks like f4 to generate a kingside attack.
plans: Black should play a5 to prevent c4, then continue with g5, f4, and double rooks on the f-file to build a kingside initiative.

explains: After Bb7 and White's Nc3, Black should almost always play Ne4 to prevent e4. The options are d5 or g4, with g4 being more common and better. After g4, White's Bd2 is a main position, and Black has several moves: Bf6, f5, d5, Nxc3, and others, all with similar ideas of increasing control over e4 or switching to dark-squared control.
teaches: When facing Nc3 in the Queen's Indian, Ne4 is a key move to stop e4. Recognize the main plans: increasing light-squared control with d5, f5, or Nxc3, or switching to dark-squared play with Bf6.
plans: Black should choose between f5 (most aggressive) or Bf6 (for a Benoni-type structure), depending on preference for a kingside attack or a more strategic game.

explains: After Bf6, both sides castle, and Black aims for c5 and d5 to play a reversed d4-c4 structure. White should play d5 himself to prevent that. After trades, Black switches to dark-squared control with g6, Bg7, Nd7, Qe7, and Re8, aiming to occupy e5. The position becomes more like a Benoni than a Queen's Indian.
teaches: When you switch to a dark-squared setup, the nature of the position changes. Recognize when a Queen's Indian transforms into a Benoni-like structure and adjust your plans accordingly.
plans: Black should play g6, Bg7, Nd7, Qe7, and Re8 to control e5, while White should play f4 to fight for that square.

explains: When Black plays f5, White should strike in the center with d5. Black cannot play e5, so he must react with Bf6, which makes it harder for White to play Ne4 because of tactics involving the b2 pawn. After Qd1, Na6 is thematic, and Black can choose between Nd6, c6, d6, or c5, with Nd6 being most principled.
teaches: When your opponent plays a flank pawn move like f5, the correct response is often a central break. Be aware of tactical resources that prevent your opponent's intended moves.
plans: Black should play Nd6 to defend the pawn and then consider a kingside expansion with h6, g5, or castle for safety. White should aim for central play with d5.

explains: After the moves leading to this Queen's Indian position, Black has several options: c6, d6, or c5, but the most principled is Nbd7, moving the knight away from the attack on the pawn and maintaining a normal Queen's Indian setup.
teaches: When a pawn is attacked, the most principled response is often to move the attacked piece to a useful square rather than defending passively.
plans: Black can choose between sharp setups with h6 and g5, or safer castling followed by standard development.

explains: After both sides castle and White plays Nc3, Black's typical plan is to play Ne4, followed by g4 and f5, aiming for a Dutch-like attack. This is a standard approach in the Queen's Indian.
teaches: In the Queen's Indian, Black often seeks counterplay on the kingside with f5 and g4, creating a sharp structure.
plans: Black should aim for Ne4, then g4 and f5 to gain space and attack on the kingside.

explains: White has several options after Black's Ne4: Bf4, Qc2, or taking on e4. Taking on e4 leads to a symmetrical pawn structure and a very drawish position, which is a good practical choice for White if they want a quiet game.
teaches: When facing a sharp opening, White can choose to simplify into a symmetrical structure to reduce losing chances, even if it means a drawish game.
plans: If White wants to play for a win, they should avoid the exchange on e4 and instead choose Qc2 or Bf4 to maintain tension.

explains: After Qc2, Black should take on c3 to avoid doubled pawns, and then play c5, f5, or d6. The choice determines the nature of the position: c5 leads to structures similar to the Sicilian, while f5 leads to a Dutch-like setup.
teaches: When given a choice of pawn breaks, consider the resulting pawn structure and how it fits your style. c5 creates a hedgehog-like structure, while f5 gives a kingside attacking setup.
plans: If Black chooses f5, they should follow up with Bf6, d6, Nbd7, and Qe7, aiming for e5. If c5, White should play Rd1 and Black can develop with d6 and Bf6.

explains: The main line after Ne4 is Bf4, and Black has several options: f5, Bf6, d5, d6, or Nxc3. The recommended move is f5, which is aggressive and consistent with Black's plans.
teaches: In the Queen's Indian, Black should often play f5 to gain space and prepare a kingside attack, even if it weakens the e6 pawn, because it gives active play.
plans: After f5, if White plays d5, Black can continue with Bf6, d6, Nbd7, and Qe7, with rooks placed flexibly. If White delays d5, Black's next moves are still Bf6, d6, Nbd7, and Qe7.

explains: In this Queen's Indian structure with pawns on d5 and e6, Black's next moves are flexible and always good: d6, Nbd7, Qe7, and Bf6. The rooks' placement depends on White's setup, but these moves are solid regardless.
teaches: When facing a closed center, develop with flexible moves that keep options open for your rooks and pieces.
plans: Play d6, Nbd7, Qe7, and Bf6, then decide rook placement based on White's next move.

explains: After White plays d5, Black has a weakness on e6, but the bishop on b7 becomes very strong. White may try to trade pieces, but Black's bishop remains good.
teaches: Accept structural weaknesses if they are compensated by active piece play.
plans: Keep the bishop on b7 active and be ready to recapture on c3 with tempo if White plays Qc2.

explains: The main line continues with White playing b4, Black plays Nxc3, Bxc3, then Ne4, centralizing another knight. After Bxf6 and Qxf6, Black's pieces are aimed at White's king, so White often trades queens to reduce the attack.
teaches: In the Queen's Indian, Black can generate a kingside attack by centralizing knights and trading off the dark-squared bishop to open lines.
plans: Aim for Ne4 and prepare a kingside attack; if White offers queen trades, consider whether to accept or keep the queens for attacking chances.

explains: The position after the main line is complicated and balanced. Black can try aggressive moves like g5-g4 to create quick attacks, as White often doesn't know how to respond. Alternatively, Black can aim to break open the center and win the d5 pawn, or play e5 to solidify the pawn structure.
teaches: In rich, unbalanced positions, both sides have chances; choose a plan that suits your style, whether it's a direct attack or a slow squeeze.
plans: Consider g5-g4 for a quick attack, or prepare e5 and f4 to break open the position and target d5.

explains: The Queen's Indian with Bb7 leads to thematic pawn structures and rich plans. Studying grandmaster games from this position is valuable because there are many examples to learn from.
teaches: To master an opening, study model games and understand the typical plans and structures that arise.
plans: Review games by strong players from this position to learn typical plans and tactical motifs.

explains: In the Najdorf, Black's king is almost always going to castle kingside because queenside castling is impractical without the c-pawn. The semi-open c-file is Black's main counterplay, aimed at White's queenside. Therefore, White's attacking plans, like the English Attack, are justified because Black's king will likely end up on g8.
teaches: When evaluating opening plans, consider where the opponent's king will likely castle and whether your attack targets that area.
plans: White can prepare a kingside attack, while Black will use the c-file for counterplay.

explains: Black has two main pawn structures in the Najdorf: the 'Knight of' with e5, and the 'Scheveningen' with e6. The move Nb3 is played before Black commits to e5, so it avoids giving Black the 'Najdorf tempo' (where e5 attacks the knight on f5 or b3).
teaches: In the Open Sicilian, the move Nb3 is often a prophylaxis against ...e5, preventing Black from gaining a tempo on the knight and steering the game into a Scheveningen structure.
plans: White aims to keep the knight on b3, ready to support a central or kingside initiative without being kicked back by ...e5.

explains: In the main line with Bg5, Black cannot play ...e5 because White would play Nf5, and after ...exf5, Bxf6 and Qxf6, White has N d5, winning material. This is why Black avoids ...e5 against Bg5. In the English Attack (Be3), ...e5 is possible because Nf5 would be met by ...d5, breaking the pin on the f5 knight.
teaches: The viability of ...e5 in the Najdorf depends on whether White can exploit the f5 square and the pin on the f6 knight. If the bishop is on g5, ...e5 is often bad; if on e3, it may be playable.
plans: White should consider the specific bishop placement when deciding whether to allow ...e5.

explains: The move Nb3 is a flexible waiting move that discourages ...e5 and invites Black to choose among e6, g6, Nc6, or Nbd7. Black's best responses are e6 (Scheveningen) or g6 (Dragon setup), while Nc6 is not great.
teaches: A move like Nb3 can be a useful 'waiting move' that forces Black to commit to a pawn structure before White decides on the most effective setup.
plans: White will adapt to Black's choice: against e6, play a Scheveningen setup; against g6, a Dragon setup; against Nc6, exploit the lack of central control.

explains: After the moves Nbd7, Be2, Be6, Be3, and both sides castle, White's most sensible move is Nd5, reinforcing the d5-square and preventing Black's d5 break. Black should capture on d5, and after exd5, Black can play Ba5 or other moves. White then plays Qd2, and Black should play h6 to create a retreat square for the bishop, anticipating g4.
teaches: In the Najdorf, controlling the d5-square is crucial; if White can play Nd5, Black should trade knights to avoid a permanent knight on d5. Black must also prepare against White's g4 push by creating luft for the bishop.
plans: Black can continue with h6, then possibly Bg5 to trade bishops, preventing White's f4 push. Alternatively, Black can play Qb6 and Nc5 to reinforce the position and pressure the c-pawn.

explains: In the line after Nd5, Nxd5, exd5, Ba5, Qd2, h6, Black can offer the trade of bishops with Bg5. This trade is useful for Black because it removes a defender and prevents White from playing f4, reducing White's attacking potential.
teaches: Trading bishops in the Najdorf can be a strategic tool to blunt White's kingside attack, especially when it stops the f4 push that would support a pawn storm.
plans: After the bishop trade, Black can play f6 to solidify the e-pawn, though it's not always necessary. Black can also aim for Qb6 and Nc5 to pressure the c-pawn and resolve the weak d6-pawn if White captures.

explains: In the English Attack (Be3), Black's best response is e5, forcing the knight back to b3. Other moves like a6 or Ng4 are possible, but Ng4 is considered worse for Black. After Ng4, White can play Bc1, which is popular but not best, or Bg5, which is more challenging.
teaches: Against the English Attack, Black should aim to challenge the center with e5, forcing the knight to a less active square. If Black plays Ng4, White should respond with Bg5 to maintain pressure, not retreat with Bc1.
plans: After e5 and Nb3, Black can develop normally with Be7, castle, and then play Be6, keeping the d6-pawn defended. White may play h3 to prevent Ng4, and Black can continue with Nc6 or Nbd7.

explains: In the line after Ng4, Bg5, Nf6, Be2, e5, Nb3, Be7, O-O, Be3, Be6, White should play h3 to prevent the knight from coming back to g4. Black should play Nc6 rather than Nbd7 to keep defending the d6-pawn, and then consider f3 and Nd7.
teaches: In the Najdorf, when White has not played f3, Black can often develop with Nc6 to maintain control over d4 and support the d6-pawn. White must be careful about Ng4 tricks and often plays h3 to prevent them.
plans: Black can aim for Qd2, then possibly f5 (though engines may not favor it) or Nb6 to pressure the bishop pair. White may play Bg5 to trade light-squared bishops, but Black can handle it.

explains: After Nb3 in the Najdorf, Black's typical ...e5 is discouraged because White can meet it with Bg5, pinning and attacking the knight on f6, and then play for the d5 square. This gives Black a slightly worse position if they insist on ...e5.
teaches: When a knight retreats to b3, it often aims to control d4 and e5, making ...e5 a positional concession. Recognize such moves as a way to steer the opponent away from their ideal setup.
plans: White should be ready to punish ...e5 with Bg5, followed by pressure on the d5 square.

explains: Against …Nbd7, White can immediately start a kingside attack with g4, because the knight on d7 blocks the bishop on c8, making it harder for Black to defend the kingside. If Black delays with ...e6, White plays g5, forcing the knight back and gaining a huge space advantage.
teaches: When the opponent's piece placement blocks their own development, a quick pawn storm can be very effective. The move g4 is a typical attacking resource when the bishop on c8 is blocked.
plans: White should play g4, and if Black tries ...e6, continue with g5 to drive the knight back. After ...h6, White can develop harmoniously, often with a4 to prevent ...b5.

explains: Against …Nc6, White should continue with Be3. If Black plays ...Ng4, the knight is not a real threat because it can be taken or the bishop can retreat to d2 or g5, maintaining an edge. White's position remains harmonious and natural.
teaches: When a knight attacks a bishop, it's not always a threat if the bishop has safe retreats that keep the position solid. Sometimes the best response is to develop naturally and let the opponent waste time.
plans: White can play Be3, and if ...Ng4, retreat the bishop to g5 or d2, then continue with Qd2 and maintain a small but stable advantage.

explains: The move …e6 is the most solid and best response to Nb3. It avoids giving up the d5 square and transposes to a Hedgehog-like setup with a safe position and the semi-open c-file for counterplay.
teaches: In the Najdorf, ...e6 is often a flexible and solid choice, especially when White's knight has retreated to b3. It keeps the position flexible and avoids immediate weaknesses.
plans: Black aims for a Hedgehog structure, with pieces developing behind the pawns, and will use the c-file for counterplay.

explains: After Nb3, White voluntarily retreats the knight without having induced the ...d5 weakness, so Black should not feel compelled to punish it with ...Nc6. The position remains balanced, and Black can choose between ...g6 and ...e6.
teaches: Don't react to a retreating piece just because it feels like it should be punished; choose the move that fits your setup and keeps the position sound.
plans: Consider ...g6 or ...e6; ...e6 is the more solid choice, preparing development without conceding the d5 square.

explains: The main move is ...e6. It is best because it does not give away the d5 square, prepares development, and leads to an equal position without problems. White's main tries are a4 and g4.
teaches: In the Najdorf, ...e6 is a flexible and solid choice that keeps the d5 pawn break available and avoids the weaknesses of ...g6.
plans: After ...e6, be ready for White's a4 or g4 plans; against a4, develop with ...Nc6; against g4, play ...b5.

explains: The move a4 by White is a key strategic idea: it prevents ...b5 (which would hang the a8 rook) and prepares a5, N a4, and Nb6 (or Bb6) to pressure the queenside. Against a4, Black can simply play ...Nc6, and after f4, Be7, Be2, b6, Be3, O-O, a standard Sicilian position arises where d6 is the main weakness until ...d5 is played.
teaches: In the Sicilian, a4 is a typical prophylactic move that both stops ...b5 and creates a plan of a5, Na4, and Nb6 to attack the queenside. Black must be aware of this and develop harmoniously.
plans: After a4, develop with ...Nc6, ...Be7, ...b6, ...O-O, and aim for the ...d5 break to neutralize the d6 weakness.

explains: When White plays g4 after ...e6, it is an improved English Attack because White has already blocked in the bishop, so the pawn storm can start without preparatory moves. Black must ignore the kingside threat and play ...b5 to stay equal. If White continues g5, Black can play ...b4, and if White takes on g7, it is a mistake due to ...Qf6.
teaches: Against a kingside pawn storm, sometimes the best defense is a counterattack on the queenside. The ...b5 break is a standard resource in the Najdorf to create counterplay.
plans: After g4, play ...b5, and if g5, continue with ...b4, attacking the knight and preparing ...Qf6 if White grabs on g7.

explains: After White plays g4, Black should not react to the kingside pawn thrust. The d6 pawn is defended, and the knight can retreat to d7, so g5 is not scary. Black can play b5, starting queenside play and ignoring White's demonstration.
teaches: In sharp Sicilian lines, when the opponent attacks on one side, counterplay on the other side is often the correct response. Do not be distracted by pawn moves that do not create real threats.
plans: After b5, if White plays g5, Black can continue with b4, attacking the knight on c3. If White takes on c3, Black recaptures with the queen, and if White takes on g7, the knight on c3 is hanging.

explains: If White instead plays Bg2 after g4, Black must be careful because White threatens e5, which would win a pawn after Nd5 and Bxd5. Black can defend with Nfd7 or better, Bb7, which also develops a piece.
teaches: When the opponent threatens a central break, you must either prevent it or be ready to meet it. Developing a piece while defending is often the most efficient solution.
plans: After Bb7, White is practically forced to play g5. Black can then play Nfd7, keeping b4 in reserve for later. This prepares to meet White's further attacks.

explains: If White castles after the g4-g5 push, Black can breathe and play normal developing moves like Be7, Nc6, O-O, and Rc8. The immediate mating threats are gone, and Black has a sound position.
teaches: Recognize when the opponent's attack has fizzled out. If they castle, it often signals that they are no longer pursuing the direct attack, and you can revert to standard development.
plans: Develop harmoniously: Be7, Nc6, castle kingside, and prepare Rc8. Black's structure is solid, and the game becomes a normal middlegame.

explains: If White continues attacking with f4 and Be3, Black faces a crossroads. The engine prefers castling, but as a human, castling into the attack is unappealing. Instead, Black can play b4, a practical move that creates counterplay.
teaches: Sometimes the engine's top move is not the most human choice. It is acceptable to choose a move that is easier to handle over-the-board, even if it is not objectively best.
plans: After b4, if White plays Nbd2, Black can play a5, waiting for White to commit. Black has many waiting moves like Nc5 or Rc8, and White's attack is not scary because Black's king is safe.

explains: The move e6 is flexible, but it allows g4 because it undefends the f5 square. However, Black should not be afraid of this, as the position remains fine. Nb3 is a rare and not problematic line for Black.
teaches: In the Najdorf, moves that are flexible and keep options open are often good, even if they allow some pawn pushes. Do not fear rare lines; they are usually less dangerous than main lines.
plans: Black should continue with the standard Najdorf setup, developing pieces and preparing queenside play. White's Nb3 does not pose serious threats.

explains: In this London System setup against a Queen's Indian-style setup, the choice between c3 and c4 is significant. Playing c3 is a sensible move that keeps the center solid and avoids the typical Queen's Indian central tension.
teaches: When facing a Queen's Indian setup, c3 can be a useful move to maintain a strong center without allowing black to pressure the c4 square.
plans: Develop naturally with h3, Nbd2, and Bd3, preparing for central breaks or kingside play.

explains: Black has several options: Nc6, d6, d5, or taking on d4. The choice between d6 and d5 is crucial. d5 fights for the center directly, making it harder for white to play e4, but it weakens the dark-squared bishop's prospects if the center remains closed. d6 keeps the center flexible and allows white to play e4, but gives up the e5 outpost for a knight.
teaches: When facing a London System, black's central pawn break choice (d5 vs d6) determines the nature of the position: d5 leads to a more closed, Queen's Indian-like struggle, while d6 allows white to play e4 and opens up attacking chances.
plans: If black plays d5, white can aim for the e5 outpost for a knight. If black plays d6, white can prepare e4 with moves like Qd3 and c3.

explains: If black plays d6 and white plays e4, black's most principled response is a5, which stops white's play on the e-file and locks the position, giving black counterplay. This pattern is familiar from Semi-Slav and other Queen's pawn defenses.
teaches: The move a5 against e4 is a typical resource to halt white's central expansion and create a static structure where black can maneuver.
plans: After a5, white should avoid opening the center too much; instead, maintain tension and prepare piece play, possibly with Bf4-h2 and Rfe1.

explains: If black takes on d4 immediately, white can recapture with either the e-pawn or c-pawn. Taking with the e-pawn is more promising because it blocks black's counterplay on the c-file, preventing pressure on c2 or c1. Taking with the c-pawn gives black more options.
teaches: When recapturing in the center, consider which pawn recapture limits the opponent's counterplay. Here, exd4 is preferable to cxd4 because it closes the c-file.
plans: After exd4, black often plays d6, leading to a Scheveningen-like pawn structure. White should then focus on piece play and possible kingside attack.

explains: The resulting pawn structure after black plays d6 resembles the Scheveningen Sicilian, characterized by pawns on d6 and e6. This leads to a Hedgehog-type position where black has a solid but passive setup.
teaches: Recognizing pawn structures from other openings helps in understanding the plans. Here, the Scheveningen structure indicates that black will play a Hedgehog defense, and white should aim for a gradual buildup.
plans: White should develop harmoniously, possibly with h3, Nbd2, and Bd3, and prepare central breaks or kingside expansion.

explains: In the London System against the Queen's Indian, white's move order matters. Starting with h3 is recommended to avoid giving black early counterplay. The moves h3, Nbd2, and Bd3 are all useful regardless of black's setup, but the order can be adjusted.
teaches: In flexible openings, choose move orders that minimize black's options and keep your own plans flexible. h3 is a useful prophylactic move that prevents ...Bg4 and prepares a later g4 or kingside expansion.
plans: Proceed with Nbd2 and Bd3, then decide on central breaks based on black's setup.

explains: In this London System setup against the Queen's Indian, the bishop on f4 is already developed, and White has several reasonable moves: h3, Nbd2, or Bd3. The move Be2 is passive and not recommended because it doesn't contribute to White's main plans.
teaches: When facing the Queen's Indian setup, prioritize flexible developing moves that support your central breaks and piece activity. Avoid passive moves that don't help your plans.
plans: Start with h3 to prevent ...Nh5, then develop the bishop to d3 and the knight to d2, regardless of Black's setup.

explains: After both sides castle, Black typically plays ...c5 to gain counterplay, and White responds with c3. The key decision is whether Black plays ...d5 or ...d6. If ...d5, White aims to occupy e5, while Black tries to occupy e4. The move Qe1 is useful to support e4 and prevent ...Ne4.
teaches: In these structures, the fight for the central squares e4 and e5 is crucial. A queen move to e1 can support the e4 break and stop a knight landing on e4.
plans: White continues with Nbd2, and if Black plays ...d5, White prepares e4 with Qe1, while Black may play ...Nbd7 to control e5.

explains: If White plays a4 to break up Black's queenside structure, Black should respond with ...a6 to prevent ...a5. If Black gets a knight to e4, it can be very annoying, especially if followed by ...f5, creating a strong attacking setup. White must be careful not to allow this.
teaches: When you have a space advantage on the queenside, use pawn breaks like a4 to create weaknesses, but be aware of the opponent's counterplay in the center. A well-placed knight on e4 can be a precursor to a kingside attack.
plans: If Black plays ...Ne4, White should consider exchanging it or preventing ...f5. Otherwise, Black's attack can become dangerous.

explains: If Black plays ...d6 instead of ...d5, the position is different: Black controls d5, preventing White's e4 break easily. White continues with Nbd2, and if Black plays ...c5, White plays c3. Black may play ...Qc7 to support ...e5, and White should meet ...e5 with ...e5 (likely a typo for e5) to counter. If White can play e5 supported by a pawn, the bishop on d3 can become very dangerous on the h7 diagonal.
teaches: In the ...d6 setup, Black's ...e5 is a key move to challenge the center. White must be ready to meet it with e5, but only if it can be supported. The bishop on d3 can be a powerful attacking piece if the center opens.
plans: White aims to play e5 when possible, supported by a pawn, to open the diagonal for the bishop. If Black plays ...exd5, White recaptures and the bishop on d3 becomes active.

explains: After the exchange on e5, the position is roughly equal, but White has a slight edge due to the more active bishop. The white bishop can go to c4 and pressure f7, while the black bishop is less active. White also has a bit more space on the queenside.
teaches: In these equal-looking positions, small advantages like a more active bishop and extra space can be the basis for a long-term plan. There are no quick attacks; you must build pressure gradually.
plans: White should play a4 to gain space, then develop the bishop to c4, double rooks on the d-file, and slowly increase pressure. Black's setup is solid, so patience is required.

explains: Against the Queen's Indian setup (with ...b6 and ...Bb7), White's usual London System ideas are blunted: there is no target on g6 for h4-h5, the bishop on b7 makes it hard to play e4, and ...b6 has already secured the b7 pawn against Qb3. White has a bit more space on the queenside and a more active bishop, but no quick attack.
teaches: When facing a Queen's Indian setup, don't expect a direct attack; the position is solid for Black, so aim for a slow, positional edge rather than forcing tactics.
plans: Develop normally, keep the bishop active, and consider queenside expansion or central play without rushing.

explains: In a London System game where Black plays ...c5 and White recaptures on d4 with the c-pawn, the resulting symmetrical pawn structure is fine for White. The key benefit is that White can then play Nc3, which is more active than Nd2, controlling d5 and d4.
teaches: When recapturing on d4 with the c-pawn, the follow-up Nc3 is a major advantage because it develops the knight to a more active square, fighting for central control.
plans: Continue development with Bd3, Qe2, and castle, aiming for a solid center and potential play on the c-file or kingside.

explains: In a Hedgehog setup (Black's pawns on a6, b6, d6, e6), Black's position is very solid and hard to break through. White's kingside attack with g4-g5 and h4-h5 is not as powerful because there are few pieces left and Black's defensive resources are sufficient.
teaches: Against the Hedgehog, don't overcommit to a kingside attack; the pawn structure is resilient, and you need to find a way to create weaknesses or trade into a favorable endgame.
plans: Consider central breaks or piece exchanges to exploit the pawn majority on the queenside, rather than a direct assault.

explains: In a position where White has a doubled pawn and Black has a solid defense, even a material advantage (like a pawn up) may not be enough to win. The attacking pieces are not coordinated, and Black's pieces are well placed to defend.
teaches: Material advantages are not always decisive if the opponent's position is solid and your own pawn structure is compromised; focus on improving piece activity and creating real weaknesses.
plans: Look for ways to trade queens or simplify into a favorable endgame, rather than forcing an attack that may fizzle.

explains: In a game where Black plays ...d5 against the London, White's g4-g5 plan becomes weaker and e4 is harder to achieve. A good move is Bxd6, recapturing with the a-pawn to create a strong outpost on e5 for the knight.
teaches: When Black plays ...d5, consider exchanging on d6 and recapturing with the a-pawn to gain a central outpost, even if it gives Black a queenside pawn majority.
plans: After Bxd6 and ...cxd6, White can aim to control e5 and use the queenside pawn majority as a long-term asset.

explains: After d4 Nf6 Nf3 g6 Bf4 Bg7 e3 d6 Be2 O-O, Black's setup with ...d6 and ...g6 leaves the e5 square weak. White aims to control e5 and later place a knight there, which becomes a long-term strategic asset.
teaches: In structures where Black has pawns on d6 and g6 (like the King's Indian or Queen's Indian), the e5 square is a key outpost. White should try to weaken it and occupy it with a knight.
plans: Develop harmoniously, keep pressure on e5, and be ready to exchange pieces to facilitate a knight landing on e5.

explains: When Black played ...g5 to challenge the knight on e5, White responded with f4, not allowing further pawn advances and forcing Black to take. This keeps the knight strong and creates weaknesses in Black's kingside.
teaches: When your opponent tries to kick your well-placed knight with a pawn, you can often support it with a pawn advance of your own, maintaining the outpost and creating weaknesses.
plans: After ...gxf4, recapture with the rook to keep the knight on e5 and prepare an attack on the kingside.

explains: White sacrificed a pawn to activate the rook and maintain the initiative. Black wisely declined the pawn, retreating the knight to exchange the main attacker. This shows the importance of activity over material.
teaches: Sometimes a pawn sacrifice is justified to open lines and improve piece activity. Conversely, when your opponent offers a pawn, consider whether taking it allows them to seize the initiative.
plans: Continue to press with active pieces, using the lead in development to create threats.

explains: After a series of exchanges, White transposed into a favorable endgame with a better minor piece (knight vs. bishop) and no pawn weaknesses, while Black had multiple targets. This proved decisive.
teaches: In endgames, a knight can be superior to a bishop when the position is closed or when there are weaknesses to attack. Having a better minor piece and no weaknesses is a winning advantage.
plans: Use the knight to target Black's weak pawns and restrict the bishop's activity.

explains: Against ...d5 setups, White should aim to weaken the e5 square and place a knight there. Against ...d6 setups, an early f4 (the 'London' setup) can be effective. This game illustrates the importance of knowing how to handle different Black setups.
teaches: In the London System, the plan against ...d5 is to control e5, while against ...d6, an early f4 can create attacking chances and prevent Black's typical pawn breaks.
plans: Study typical plans against various Black setups to be prepared for different structures.

explains: After d4 Nf6 Nf3 g6 Bf4 Bg7 e3 d6 Be2 O-O, White's plan is to build a strong center with c3 and e4, then launch a kingside attack. Black's bishop on g7 is a standard fianchetto, but White can target it with Bh6, forcing Black to either trade or retreat.
teaches: In the London System, when Black fianchettoes the kingside bishop, White can often play Bh6 to exchange it, weakening Black's kingside defenses and gaining space.
plans: White should aim to play c3, e4, and then Bh6, followed by Qd2, O-O-O, and h4-h5 to start a kingside pawn storm.

explains: If Black plays ...b5 to avoid the bishop trade, White can respond with f3 to support the e4 pawn and prepare g4. The move f3 also prevents ...Ng4 and keeps the center solid.
teaches: Supporting the center with f3 is a key idea in the London System when Black tries to counterattack on the queenside; it also prepares a kingside pawn advance.
plans: After f3, White can continue with g4, h4, and a kingside pawn storm, while Black may try to open the center with ...e5 or ...c5.

explains: In the resulting sharp positions, Black often tries to open the center with ...e5 or ...c5 to undermine White's center and create counterplay. White must be careful not to overextend on the kingside while Black has central breaks.
teaches: When one side attacks on the wing, the other should seek counterplay in the center. Black's ...e5 or ...c5 breaks are typical ways to challenge White's space advantage.
plans: White should continue with g4 and h4, but be ready to meet central breaks with accurate play, possibly sacrificing material for a kingside attack.

explains: After Black plays ...d5 instead of ...Bg7, White has a choice between Qd2 and e3. The move e3 is safer, supporting the center and avoiding early bishop exchanges, while Qd2 aims for a quick queenside castling and bishop trade.
teaches: In the London System, when Black plays ...d5, White should prioritize a solid center (e3) over a quick bishop exchange (Qd2), as the latter can give Black counterplay.
plans: White should develop naturally, castle kingside or queenside, and prepare a kingside attack with h4-h5 and g4, while keeping the center stable.

explains: The key takeaway is that when White has both e4 and d4 pawns, White has a space advantage and easier kingside play. Black's counterplay is often slower, so White should not fear Black's setup but proceed with a consistent plan.
teaches: In positions with a big center, the side with more space should attack on the flank, while the opponent must seek counterplay in the center. Do not waste moves; execute your plan efficiently.
plans: White should aim for h4-h5, g4, and a kingside attack, while being ready to meet central breaks with accurate play.

explains: After Black plays d5, White should avoid the common Qd2 plan and instead play e4, supporting the center and avoiding early bishop exchanges. This keeps the position solid and prepares for development and a kingside attack.
teaches: In the London System, when Black sets up with d5, supporting the center with e4 is safer than committing to Qd2 and the typical plan. Prioritize central control and flexible development.
plans: Develop the bishop to g7, then play h4 to provoke weaknesses, aiming for a kingside attack.

explains: After White plays h4, Black's best response is h5 to prevent White from playing h5 themselves. If Black castles instead, White can continue with h5, and Black's best try is c5 for counterplay, but White gets a strong attack.
teaches: When a pawn move like h4 creates a threat, the defender must often make a prophylactic move like h5 to stop it. Ignoring the threat can lead to a dangerous attack.
plans: If Black castles, White plays h5, then builds up with Bg4, Bf3, Qf3/Qh3, and aims for checkmate. If Black plays h5, White switches to Nb5 to target c7.

explains: After h5, White's best move is Nb5, attacking c7. Black must play Na6 to defend, and then White plays Be2, supporting a future g4 push. The alternative Nf3 is less effective because it allows Black to castle and play c5, and h4 becomes a weakness.
teaches: In sharp positions, a direct move like Nb5 can be stronger than a developing move like Nf3, especially when it creates concrete threats. Also, a pawn move like h4 can be a weakness if it doesn't lead to an attack, so it's important to follow up energetically.
plans: After Nb5 Na6 Be2, White prepares g4 to storm Black's kingside, keeping the king in the center for now.

explains: In this London System setup against the King's Indian, the bishop on e2 supports an early g4, which is a key attacking idea. Playing f3 immediately is risky and engine-unfavored, but it can be venomous if analyzed deeply.
teaches: The bishop on e2 is a flexible move that prepares a kingside pawn storm with g4. Be cautious with f3; it may be unsound but can pose practical problems.
plans: Develop the knight to f3 or consider the aggressive f3-g4 plan, but be aware of the king's safety in the center.

explains: After certain moves, black must play h5 to prevent g4, and the position becomes a normal London with the knight on c3. Black's knight on d5 is provocative and can be offside, requiring time to redeploy.
teaches: In the London, provoking weaknesses like h5 can be beneficial. A knight on d5 may look active but can be a target if it cannot stay.
plans: Continue with normal development, possibly aiming to exploit the offside knight.

explains: When the knight is on c3, black's c5 break is crucial because white lacks the light-squared bishop's consistency. If white takes on d4, black can play e5, gaining a broad center.
teaches: In London structures, black should strike at the center with c5 when the knight is on c3, as it challenges white's pawn center.
plans: After c5, if white takes, play e5 to establish a strong center.

explains: In the main line with knight c3, white's g4 is the critical move. Black must take, and then white opens the g-file, which becomes dangerous with the knight on e5. Black must defend precisely.
teaches: When you have a knight on e5, opening the g-file can be decisive. Even if the pawn is defended, the open file can lead to a strong attack.
plans: Play g4, and if black takes, recapture and aim to open the g-file with h5, targeting the king.

explains: An alternative to knight c3 is e3, which is a solid setup. Black should remember to play h5 to prevent g4, but even then survival is not easy.
teaches: The London can be played flexibly; e3 is a more restrained option. Black must be precise to avoid being overrun.
plans: If white plays e3, continue with normal development and consider h5 to stop g4.

explains: After d4 Nf6 Nf3 g6 Bf4 Bg7 e3 d6 Be2 O-O, White has a choice between Nc3 and c3. Nc3 is aggressive and double-edged, but c3 leads to a more solid London setup.
teaches: In the London System, the move c3 supports the center and prepares to develop the bishop to e2, avoiding sharp lines that can arise after Nc3.
plans: White can choose between Nc3 for active play or c3 for a solid setup. With c3, White will develop the bishop to e2 and maintain a strong center.

explains: In the line with d6, the main move is h3 to prevent ...Bg4 and to preserve the dark-squared bishop. If White plays Be2 instead, Black can force the bishop pair with ...Nh5, leading to a sharp theoretical line.
teaches: The London bishop is a valuable piece; h3 is a prophylactic move that keeps it safe and avoids forcing lines where Black wins the bishop pair.
plans: White should play h3 before Be2 to maintain the bishop and avoid complications. If Black plays ...Nh5, White must know the precise response to keep the balance.

explains: In the sharp line after ...Nh5, White plays Bg5, and if Black plays ...h6, White retreats to h4. Then ...g5 attacks the bishop, but White can play Nfd2, attacking the knight on h5. If Black takes the bishop, White gets pressure on the f7 pawn.
teaches: In sharp tactical lines, precise move order is crucial. White can use the attack on the knight to maintain pressure even if the bishop is captured.
plans: White should aim to create pressure on f7 and the diagonal, while Black must be careful not to allow White's pieces to become active.

explains: After ...Nf4, White must deal with the threats to g2 and the bishop. The line continues with g3, ...Nxg3, ...hxg3, and then c3, c5, dxc5, Na3, and O-O. The position is very tricky and double-edged.
teaches: In sharp positions, both sides must be precise. White can choose to sacrifice material for activity, but the position is not easy for either side.
plans: White should be aware of this forcing line and decide whether to enter it or avoid it with h3. If entering, White must know the follow-up moves to maintain the initiative.

explains: In the position after ...O-O, White can play h3 and then Be2, transposing to a normal London setup. Black's main counterplay is ...c5, which opens the center and activates the bishop on g7. White should avoid taking on c5 and instead play c3 to support the center.
teaches: Against the King's Indian setup, ...c5 is a typical break. White should maintain the center with c3 rather than allowing Black to open the position favorably.
plans: White plays h3, Be2, and c3 to solidify the center. Black can choose between ...c5, ...b6, or ...Nbd7 with ...e5, each leading to different plans.

explains: In this London System setup, Black has several alternatives to the main c5 break, including Nb7 or b6, leading to a double fianchetto or a King's Indian setup with Nd7 and e5. The move Nd7 prepares e5, which is a common plan, and White must be ready to meet it.
teaches: When facing a King's Indian setup, be aware that Black may delay c5 in favor of e5, so White should consider prophylactic moves like Bh2 to keep the center flexible.
plans: White can choose between c4, which gives the knight a great square on c3, or retreating the bishop to h2 to maintain the center. Black aims for e5 and central play.

explains: If White plays c4, Black's c5 break becomes less effective because the knight can go to c3, and e5 becomes the more scary move. Alternatively, White can retreat the bishop to h2, which is a normal move against kingside fianchetto setups.
teaches: In these positions, the bishop on h2 can be better than on g5 because it keeps the center closed and supports a future d5 push.
plans: White should decide between c4 and Bh2 based on whether they want to allow e5 or keep the center closed. Black should be ready to play e5 if White doesn't address it.

explains: After Nd2 and Nxd2, Qxd2, the position resembles a reversed Queen's Indian, with White's pawn on h2 instead of b2. The bishop is on h2, and one could argue it's better on b2, but the position is still okay for White.
teaches: Recognizing reversed openings can help you understand the plans and piece placements. Here, the bishop on h2 is slightly passive compared to b2, but the structure is solid.
plans: White should aim to develop and connect rooks, while Black can try to exploit the bishop's placement.

explains: In the mainline, after Nd7, White plays Bh2 in anticipation of e5. Black plays Re8 reinforcing d5, and White plays c3. If Black plays e5, White is not afraid because the bishop is already on h2, and the center is solid.
teaches: Prophylactic moves like Bh2 can prevent the opponent's freeing breaks from being effective. Here, it blunts the impact of e5.
plans: White continues with centralization and connecting rooks, while Black can choose between b6 and Qb6, with Qb6 being more active, targeting the b2 pawn.

explains: In the line with d5, Black castles, and both sides develop normally. When Black plays Nd7, White should consider Bh2 in anticipation of e5. Black plays Qc7, and White starts a counterattack with a4, gaining space. Black must play a6 to be able to meet a5 with b5.
teaches: In these London structures, a4 is a common space-gaining move, but Black must be ready with a6 to prevent further queenside expansion.
plans: White continues with Nb3, aiming for a solid central pawn structure. Black should maintain flexibility and consider active moves like Qb6.

explains: The final setup is fine for both sides, but White may prefer it because of the very solid central pawn structure. White's bad bishop is outside the pawn chain, while Black's light-squared bishop is good. The King's Indian positions have an advantage over normal d5 lines because the pawn on d6 means there is no f4 break, making it hard to attack.
teaches: In these structures, the placement of pawns determines which pieces are good or bad. White's solid center gives a slight edge, but Black's flexibility can compensate.
plans: White should aim to maintain the center and possibly expand on the queenside. Black should look for active piece play and potential breaks.

explains: In this King's Indian setup, Black's pawn is on d6 rather than d5, so the typical London System plan of c4 to challenge the center is less effective. The light-squared bishop on f4 is well placed, but Black can target the b2 pawn with Qb6, a common weakness in the London.
teaches: Recognize when the opponent's pawn structure changes your standard plans. With Black's pawn on d6, the usual c4 break is not as strong, and you must be alert to pressure on b2.
plans: Consider Qb3 to meet Qb6, or allow the exchange of queens if it leads to a favorable endgame. Keep the b2 pawn protected and avoid creating light-square weaknesses.

explains: Black may play ...Bg4 to pin the knight, or ...Nc6, ...Nd7, ...Na5 to target the light squares, which are weak because White's pawns are on dark squares. White still has pieces to defend these squares, so the position remains balanced.
teaches: When your pawns occupy dark squares, your light squares can become weak. Use your pieces to control those squares and be wary of maneuvers like ...Na5 to exploit them.
plans: Maintain piece coordination to defend the light squares. If Black plays ...Bg4, consider h3 and g4 to gain space, or simply castle and keep the position solid.

explains: After the queens are traded, White has a slight edge due to a healthy pawn structure and two good bishops, especially the dark-squared bishop, which is better than Black's. Black cannot easily attack, so White can play for a positional grind.
teaches: In queenless middlegames, small structural advantages and better minor pieces become more significant. Aim for a slow squeeze rather than a direct attack.
plans: Improve piece placement, target Black's weak pawns, and prepare to transition into a favorable endgame. Avoid unnecessary risks since the position is already slightly better.

explains: Against King's Indian setups, White has a choice between Nc3 and e3. Nc3 leads to a more tactical game, while e3 gives a positional game with queens likely traded. Both are viable, and the choice depends on style.
teaches: Understand the character of different setups: Nc3 invites more dynamic play, while e3 leads to a quieter, more strategic struggle. Knowing both allows you to adapt to your opponent's preferences.
plans: If you prefer tactical chances, play Nc3; if you prefer a slow positional game, play e3. Study both to be flexible.

explains: After d4 Nf6 Nf3 g6 Bf4 Bg7 e3 d6 Be2 O-O, White can delay developing the knight and bishop to play h4 immediately. If Black does nothing, White can reinforce the h5 push with Be2, keeping the f3 square free for the knight to go to e5.
teaches: In the Jobava London, the knight often belongs on e5, so avoid blocking the f3 square with a knight on d2. Use h4 to start a kingside attack, and if Black ignores it, continue with Be2 and h5.
plans: If Black plays c6 or Nbd7, White can play Be2, then h5, and later open the position. The knight can go to e5, and White can castle queenside and attack.

explains: Black often responds to h4 with h5 to stop the pawn advance. If Black instead plays Qb6, attacking b2, White has a typical antidote: Na4, which attacks the queen and forces it to move. After Qa5+ c3, White can expand with b4 and put the knight on c5, gaining control over e5.
teaches: When the queen comes to b6 in these setups, Na4 is a strong resource. It chases the queen and prepares b4, placing the knight on c5 where it supports e5 and queenside play.
plans: After Na4, if Black plays Qa5+, White blocks with c3, then plays b4 and Nc5. If Black pushes b6, the knight retreats to a good square, maintaining control over e5.

explains: If Black castles immediately after h4, White can continue with h5. If Black takes on h5, White recaptures with the rook, reaching a dream position. The engine gives +1.6, but in practice it's even better because White has a strong attack.
teaches: When the opponent castles into an attack, don't hesitate to open the kingside. The rook lift after Nxh5 is a classic pattern that gives White a powerful initiative.
plans: After Rxh5, White can play c6, Bd3, f5, and Nf3-g4, creating a mating attack. Black's early castling is risky and often leads to a quick defeat.

explains: Black's best responses to h4 are h5 or h6. If Black plays h6, White can continue with Nf3, and after Black castles, White can choose between Nb5, Ne5, Qd2, or Be2. Ne5 is a simple plan, preparing g4 to blast open the position.
teaches: When Black plays h6, it's less dangerous than h5. White can calmly develop and prepare g4, often sacrificing material to open lines against the king.
plans: After h6, White can play Nf3, and if Black castles, play Ne5, then g4. If Black plays h5, White should prevent g4 and instead focus on queenside play or other breaks.

explains: Black's king is already castled and all kingside pieces are developed, so there are no immediate threats on c7. This means a premature Nb5 by White is not dangerous and can be met by ...dxc4, opening the position and preparing ...e5, which would be a strong threat.
teaches: Do not play a knight to b5 for tactical threats if the opponent's king is safe and the c7 square is not weak; the move may just lose time or allow the opponent to seize the initiative.
plans: If White plays Nb5 and Black takes on d4, White must recapture; otherwise, Black gets a decisive attack. Avoid this line and instead play c3 to maintain the center.

explains: After h4, Black can simply play h5 to prevent g4, and then meet c5 with ...dxc5, reaching a position where White lacks the typical attacking chances. The knight on f3 is not yet on e5, and Black has pressure with ideas like ...e5, ...d4, or ...Bf5.
teaches: The most aggressive-looking move (h4) is not always the best if the opponent can easily neutralize it and force a transposition to a less favorable setup. Sometimes delaying the attack is more effective.
plans: Instead of h4, develop with Be2 and Nf3, then later play Ne5 and g4, having the knight already on f3 to support the attack.

explains: In this position, White has already played Nf3 and Be2, and Black has castled. White's next move is Ne5, which is strong because it prevents Black from playing ...Nc6 and supports the g4 advance.
teaches: Developing the knight to f3 early allows a quick jump to e5 before Black can challenge it with ...Nc6, and it reinforces the g4 pawn break.
plans: After Ne5, White can proceed with g4, and if Black plays ...Bg4, White can play g5, forcing the trade and then castling queenside with a strong attack.

explains: After d4 Nf6 Nf3 g6 Bf4 Bg7 e3 d6 Be2 O-O, Black's most challenging move is …c5, aiming to trade on d4 and free the queen. Other moves like ...Bg4 or ...c6 allow White to proceed with h4 and g4, building a kingside attack with castling long.
teaches: In the Jobava London, when Black delays ...c5, White can seize the initiative with h4 and g4, preparing a direct attack. The move ...c5 is Black's most principled try to counter White's setup.
plans: White should be ready to meet ...c5 with either g4 or castling, both leading to similar positions. Against ...Bg4, White plays h3, forcing the trade, then can castle queenside and continue with g4.

explains: If Black plays ...Bg4, it is not very good because White can force the trade with h3, and after Qxg4, White is ready to castle queenside. The bishop trade removes Black's good piece and White's pawn on h4 supports g4, creating attacking chances.
teaches: Trading off a fianchettoed bishop early can leave Black's kingside weakened, especially when White can quickly build a pawn storm with h4 and g4.
plans: White should aim to castle queenside and then play g4, h5, and possibly trade off the remaining bishop, leading to a dream attacking position.

explains: Against ...c6 setups where Black tries ...Nfd7 to trade pieces, White can simply continue with h4 and g4, or play Qd2 and castle queenside. Black's ...f6 is very committal and weakens the kingside, giving White a clear plan.
