plans: White can play Bf1, c6, Bg2, and then develop the queen and bishop, deciding castling later. Black should aim for ...Qc7 and ...Bd6 to consolidate.

explains: The alternative with O-O is safer for White. After a6, h3, Bh5, Nc6, White should retreat the bishop to e2 in anticipation of b5. Black's a6 pawn is useful to support b5 and gain space.
teaches: When the opponent pins your knight, sometimes it's better to retreat the bishop voluntarily to avoid being kicked later, especially if you have castled.
plans: White can play Be2, Bd6, b3, Bb2, and then castle, creating a solid but less ambitious setup. Black can continue with ...Qc7 and ...Rd8.

explains: The move Qb3 after the bishop has moved is tempting but bad. Black can play Bxf3, gxf3, and then Nd7, giving White doubled f-pawns and a ruined structure. If White grabs the b7 pawn, Black gets huge compensation with ...c5 and active pieces.
teaches: Do not chase pawns at the cost of time and structure when the opponent has dynamic compensation. A lead in development and a better pawn structure can outweigh a pawn.
plans: Black should continue with ...c5, ...Nc6, and ...Qb6, targeting the weak pawns. White's position is unpleasant despite the extra pawn.

explains: After …a6, the move ...e6 is the most principled, transposing to main lines. The alternative ...b5 is not recommended because it allows the bishop to retreat to a good square and gives Black too many different setups to study.
teaches: When you have a choice between a flexible move that transposes to known lines and a committal move that creates many variations, often the flexible move is more practical.
plans: Black should play ...e6, and after Bxc4, continue with ...c5, ...Nf6, and ...Be7, reaching a standard QGA structure.

explains: In the main line after …e6, White takes on c4. Black can choose between ...a6 and ...c5. The ...c5 move leads to two typical pawn structures: either the c-pawns are traded off, leading to a symmetrical drawish position, or White allows ...cxd4 and recaptures with the e-pawn, creating an isolated queen's pawn (IQP) position that is sharper.
teaches: Understanding the resulting pawn structures is crucial: symmetrical pawn structures tend to be drawish, while IQP positions offer dynamic chances for both sides.
plans: If White takes on c5, Black should aim for piece play and potential draws. If White allows an IQP, Black should target the isolated pawn and use the open files.

explains: In this Queen's Gambit Accepted position, the central tension after ...c5 is the key: if White takes on d5, the central pawns are traded off, leading to a symmetrical structure that often ends in a draw. If White allows Black to take on d4 and recaptures with the e-pawn, White gets an isolated queen's pawn (IQP), which is sharper and requires aggressive play.
teaches: The decision to take or allow the trade of central pawns defines the character of the game: symmetrical structures are drawish, while IQP positions demand active piece play from the side with the isolani.
plans: White should decide whether to aim for a quiet equality by taking on d5 or to enter the more complex IQP middlegame by recapturing with the e-pawn.

explains: After …a6, Black prepares ...c5 anyway. White has several options, including a4, which is a move that tries to prevent ...b5 but has a specific drawback: Black can later use ...Nb4 to attack the c2 bishop and blockade on d5.
teaches: When choosing a move, consider the long-term resources it gives the opponent. The move a4 weakens control over b4, allowing Black a handy square for a knight.
plans: If White plays a4, Black should aim for ...Nc6, ...Nb4, and ...Nd5 to blockade the IQP and trade off attacking pieces.

explains: If White takes on d5 immediately (after ...cxd4), the position becomes symmetrical and equal. Black can develop harmoniously with ...b5, ...Bb7, ...Nc6, ...Rc8, and ...Rd8, and the game is balanced.
teaches: In symmetrical pawn structures, piece placement and activity matter more than theory; both sides have equal chances.
plans: Black should develop naturally and aim for piece activity; White should avoid taking on d5 if he wants to play for a win.

explains: The main line is Bb3, when Black plays ...Nc6 and then ...cxd4. White must recapture with the pawn to keep the IQP, but if White recaptures with the queen or allows a queen trade, the IQP becomes weak without attacking chances. After exd4, Black can play ...Be7, ...O-O, ...Na5, ...b5, and ...Bb7, aiming for ...Nd5 to blockade.
teaches: When playing with an IQP, it's crucial to keep pieces on the board to generate attacking chances; trading queens or minor pieces favors the defender.
plans: White should keep pieces and attack; Black should harass the bishop with ...Na5, play ...b5, and prepare ...Nd5.

explains: In the IQP position after Black trades off the queen and knights, the defender is comfortable because the attacking potential of the isolated pawn is reduced. Black can proceed with b5, Bb7, Rd8, and Nd5, securing a positional edge.
teaches: When facing an isolated queen pawn, the side defending against it should aim to trade off the minor pieces and queen to neutralize the attacking chances, then blockade the pawn on d5.
plans: Black will play b5, Bb7, Rd8, and Nd5 to blockade the pawn and dominate the position.

explains: In the Queen's Gambit Accepted main line after d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4 c5, White's main move is O-O. Black can transpose to the a6 line with …a6, but the recommended move is …cxd4, forcing exd4, and then playing …Be7 without committing to Nc6 or a6.
teaches: In the QGA, Black can choose between transposing to known lines or playing the immediate cxd4 to reach a solid setup with Be7, avoiding early commitment of the b8 knight.
plans: After …Be7, White may play Nc3, Re1, Qe2, Bg5, or a3. Black will continue with Nbd7, Nb6, and Nd5, achieving a harmonious blockade.

explains: After d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4 c5 O-O cxd4 exd4 Be7 Nc3 O-O Re1, Black's best is …Nbd7, preparing Nb6 and Nd5. This setup blocks the d5 square and prevents any tactical threats against the king.
teaches: Black's plan in this QGA line is to reroute the knight to d5 via b6, creating a solid blockade and avoiding any weaknesses. This simple plan is hard for White to counter.
plans: Black will play Nb6, then Nd5, and if White doesn't trade, follow up with b6 and Bb7, completing a harmonious development.

explains: In the Queen's Gambit Accepted, White often ends up with an isolated queen's pawn (IQP) after ...cxd4 and exd4. The side with the IQP wants to attack, while the defender wants to blockade the pawn and trade it off.
teaches: In IQP positions, the player with the isolated pawn should seek active piece play and kingside attacking chances, while the opponent should aim to blockade the pawn on d5 and simplify to a favorable endgame.
plans: White can play moves like Re1, Qb3, Bg5, and Ne5 to build pressure. Black should aim for ...Nbd7, ...Re8, and ...Nf8 to defend and prepare ...d5 to dissolve the pawn.

explains: After d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4 c5, White often castles and Black can choose between ...a6, ...Nc6, ...Qc7, or immediately ...cxd4. If Black plays ...cxd4, White should recapture with the e-pawn, not the knight, because ...Nxd4 would decentralize the knight and lose central control.
teaches: When recapturing in the center, prefer the pawn move that maintains central pawn mass and piece activity over a knight recapture that leaves the center weak.
plans: After ...cxd4, White plays exd4, reaching the typical IQP structure. Then both sides develop with Nc3, Nc6, and castling, leading to standard IQP play.

explains: White can also play e3 without an early Nf3, which gives Black extra options. Black can play ...e5, leading to an IQP after ...exd4 and exd4, but with differences: Black can play ...Bd6 instead of ...Be7, and White hasn't castled yet, making it harder for White to dissolve the pawn.
teaches: The move order matters: delaying Nf3 gives Black additional resources, such as ...e5, which can lead to a more favorable IQP for Black because White's king is still in the center and there is no pawn on e6 to attack.
plans: In the ...e5 line, Black develops with ...Nf6, ...Bd6, and castles, while White must handle the central tension carefully. White may need to play d5 to dissolve the pawn, but it's less effective without the e6 pawn target.

explains: White can also play e4, the most straightforward attempt to get the pawn back and claim central control. Black has several replies, including ...e5 and ...Nf6. ...Nf6 leads to Alekhine-like positions where the knight goes to b6 after ...e5, ...Nd5, and ...Nxb6, which can be uncomfortable for Black.
teaches: When White plays e4 in the QGA, White is playing for compensation and central control, not just material. Black must be precise to avoid falling behind in development and center.
plans: Against ...Nf6, White plays e5, then Bxc4, and after ...Nb6, White's knight goes to b3. Black should avoid this line if uncomfortable with the resulting pawn structure. Against ...e5, White can play Nf3 and after ...exd4, Bxc4, with pressure on f7 and the center.

explains: After d4 d5 c4 dxc4 Nf3 Nf6 e3 e6 Bxc4 c5 Qe2 a6 dxc5 Bxc5 O-O Nc6 e4, White has a central pawn duo and aims to dominate the center. Black's immediate …e5 challenges the center directly, but it is not the best; instead, …c5 is a strong move that questions White's setup.
teaches: In the Queen's Gambit Accepted, Black can counter White's central expansion with a timely ...c5, undermining the center and creating dynamic play.
plans: Black should aim to play ...c5, followed by ...Nf6 and ...b5, creating a queenside pawn majority and pressure against White's center.

explains: After …c5, White cannot easily take on c5 because Black would recapture with the bishop, and the pawn on e4 becomes vulnerable. Instead, White often plays d5, after which Black can play …Nf6, attacking the center immediately. White defends with Nc3, and then Black plays …b5, creating a 4-to-2 pawn majority on the queenside.
teaches: A queenside pawn majority can be a long-term advantage, especially if White is not careful. Black should use it to create passed pawns and pressure on the queenside.
plans: After ...b5, Black should aim to expand further with ...a5 and ...b4, while keeping the center stable. White cannot easily take on b5 due to tactical tricks like ...Qa5+ and ...Nxe4.

explains: If White plays e5 instead of d5, Black can respond with …Nc6, and after d5 Ne5 Qd4+ Bd3, the position is complicated. Alternatively, Black can play …Nf3 Bg4 d5, which should be okay for Black, though not the most comfortable.
teaches: When facing a central pawn push, Black should look for active piece play and counterattacks rather than passive defense. Moves like ...Nc6 and ...Bg4 can create tactical chances.
plans: Black should choose the line that offers the most active piece play, such as ...Nc6 followed by ...Ne5, or ...Nf3 and ...Bg4, depending on the position.

explains: The Queen's Gambit Accepted offers Black a solid and dynamic repertoire. Against setups with e3 and Nf3, Black can either dissolve the isolated queen's pawn and reach equality, or force an IQP position where Black is better.
teaches: The QGA is a reliable opening for Black because it provides multiple ways to handle White's setups, often leading to positions where Black has active pieces and good long-term chances.
plans: Black should be familiar with the main plans: either exchanging the IQP for equality or maintaining pressure on it to gain an advantage.

explains: In the Chigorin structure with d5, White closes the center, and Black's knight on a5 is cut off from its natural square c6. The knight's most logical route is to b7, then c5, via c4 if possible.
teaches: When a knight is displaced from its best square, reroute it to a strong outpost, often via a circuitous path, to improve its activity and pressure on the opponent's position.
plans: Black aims for Nb7-c5, possibly through c4, to dominate the position. White can counter with b3 or Nd2-f1-e3 to prevent Nc4.

explains: In the closed Chigorin structure, Black's pawn is on c5, which limits undermining options compared to structures where the pawn is on c7. Black cannot attack the base of White's pawn chain with c6, and White cannot play c4 to transpose to a King's Indian setup.
teaches: The placement of a pawn on c5 vs c7 drastically changes the available pawn breaks and plans. With a pawn on c5, Black's main breaks are f5 and a5 (to undermine b4).
plans: Black often plays ...Re8, ...g6, ...Bf8, and sometimes ...Nh5-g7 to prepare f5. Alternatively, if White plays b4, Black can play ...a5 to undermine the queenside.

explains: In the more flexible Chigorin structure without d5, Black often exchanges on d4 to gain piece activity and prevent White from playing d5 under favorable circumstances. This also allows Black to develop the c8-bishop to d7, discouraging d5.
teaches: Exchanging central pawns can be beneficial when it opens lines for your pieces and restricts your opponent's central expansion.
plans: After ...cxd4, Black can play ...Rc8 to pressure the bishop on c2, and develop the bishop to d7 to control the e4-d5 squares.

explains: In the open Chigorin structure, the knight on a5 has a brighter future because it can access c4 and potentially e5. If White prevents Nc4 with b3, the knight can reroute to c6 or b7.
teaches: Knights on the rim can be repositioned to strong central squares if the opponent's pawn moves create weaknesses or if the knight has multiple routes.
plans: Black can aim for ...Nc4-e5, or if b3 is played, consider ...a5 to undermine the queenside and reroute the knight to c6 or b7.

explains: In the open Chigorin structure, Black's queen on c7 defends the e5 pawn, but when the c-file opens, a white rook may pressure the queen. Black often plays ...Re8 to defend e5 with the rook, freeing the queen from that duty.
teaches: When a piece has multiple defensive duties, consider using another piece to relieve it, allowing it to reposition or avoid harassment.
plans: Black should play ...Re8 to defend e5, allowing the queen to move if needed, and prepare for potential pressure on the c-file.

explains: In the closed Chigorin structure with a locked d5 pawn and black's pawn on c5, black's queen on c7 is placed to defend the e5 pawn, but the open c-file invites a white rook to c1, pressuring the queen. Black often responds with Re8 and Bf8 to keep the e5 pawn defended.
teaches: When a queen is tied to defending a key pawn, anticipate pressure along the open file and prepare to reinforce the pawn with pieces like a rook and bishop.
plans: Black should aim to play Re8 and Bf8 to solidify the e5 pawn, while white will look to exploit the queen's limited mobility by doubling rooks on the c-file.

explains: The knight on a5 is a central strategic element. Black often tries to reroute it to c5 via b7 and c4, but white can prevent this with b4. However, this creates a weakness on b4 that black can undermine with a5, potentially leaving black with a protected passed pawn on c4.
teaches: When a knight is misplaced, look for a route back into the game, but be aware that the opponent may prevent it with a pawn move that creates a new weakness to exploit.
plans: Black should consider undermining white's b4 pawn with a5 to create a passed pawn, while white must weigh the cost of preventing the knight's return.

explains: In the Chigorin, black plays Na5 to free the c-pawn for c5, challenging white's center. The downside is that the knight is misplaced and may struggle to re-enter the game. White responds with Bc2, which is not a loss of tempo because the bishop is well-placed on the b1-h7 diagonal, overprotecting e4.
teaches: A move that appears to lose a tempo can be justified if it improves the piece's long-term prospects; here, the bishop is better on c2 than b5.
plans: Black should aim to play c5 and challenge the center, while white will reinforce e4 and prepare to meet ...cxd4 with Bxd3.

explains: In the Chigorin, Black's first idea is c5, challenging White's center. If White makes a random move, Black can play c4, and after d4, cxd3, Bxd3, Be6, Black dominates the light squares and the knight on c5 becomes a key piece.
teaches: When you have a knight that can be posted on an advanced outpost, support it with pawn breaks and piece play to control key squares.
plans: Black should aim for c5-c4 to gain space and activate the bishop to e6, while the knight on c5 exerts pressure.

explains: After c5, White must play d4 to liberate the position, develop the c1-bishop, and attack the e5 pawn. Black's main move is Qc7, which defends e5 and is flexible. Sidelines like Nd7 (Caris) are inferior because White can play d5, and after Nb6, both knights control c4, but Black's play is difficult.
teaches: In closed openings, the player who can maintain central tension while improving pieces often gets a lasting advantage. Avoid passive piece placements that allow the opponent to seize the initiative.
plans: Black should prefer Qc7, keeping the position flexible and maintaining pressure on the center.

explains: In the main line after Qc7, White often plays Nbd2. Black can choose cxd4 or exd4. cxd4 leads to pressure on d4 with Nc6, but Black may struggle to consolidate the queenside. exd4 keeps a pawn mass and offers long-term prospects, even though White can play e5 later.
teaches: When choosing between recaptures, consider the resulting pawn structure and long-term piece activity, not just immediate tactics.
plans: Black should consider exd4 to maintain a solid queenside pawn structure and prepare piece play.

explains: After exd4, Black plays Nc6, and White should play d5. Black's knight should go to e5, but if White trades, f4 becomes strong, and Black's knight is driven back. Black should play f5 to block the center, but this allows White a protected passed pawn on e6, which is risky.
teaches: When a knight is on an outpost, be wary of pawn advances that can undermine it. Sometimes you must accept a compromised structure to avoid a worse fate.
plans: Black should consider f5 to challenge White's center, but must be prepared to handle the resulting passed pawn.

explains: Other sidelines like Bb7 are bad because White plays d5, and the bishop is misplaced. cxd4 can transpose to main lines with Qc7. The main move Qc7 is best because it defends e5 and keeps options open.
teaches: In the opening, moves that defend key central pawns while maintaining flexibility are often the most reliable.
plans: Black should focus on Qc7 as the main move, avoiding premature bishop placements.

explains: In this closed Spanish structure, developing the bishop to b7 is tempting but flawed: after d5 by White, the bishop becomes passive on b7, and Black often has to retreat it to c8, wasting time.
teaches: Avoid placing a bishop on a diagonal where a central pawn push can neutralize it; flexibility in development is more valuable than immediate pressure.
plans: Prefer queen c7, which defends e5 and keeps the queenside pieces flexible.

explains: Queen c7 is the main move because it defends e5 while maintaining flexibility for the queenside pieces, especially the bishop and knight.
teaches: When choosing a developing move, prioritize flexibility: a move that serves multiple purposes (defense and preparation) is often best.
plans: After queen c7, White may play d5 or knight bd2; Black should be ready for either.

explains: Black's knight on d7 ideally wants to reach c5, but immediate c4 is met by b4, keeping the c4 square under White's control. White can also play b3 to prevent c4 altogether.
teaches: When a piece has an ideal outpost, the opponent will try to control the squares leading to it; you must find alternative routes or wait for the right moment.
plans: Black may play knight b6 to prepare c4, or switch plans entirely.

explains: In the d5 structure, if Black cannot get a knight to c4 or c5, they can exploit the undefended rook on a1 with a5, creating a protected passed pawn on c4 after trades.
teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied up, look for tactical resources that exploit weaknesses (like an undefended rook) to create long-term compensation.
plans: Black should aim for a5 to gain counterplay on the queenside.

explains: After d5, bishop d7 is a popular alternative to knight d7. It supports the queenside and allows Black to switch to a kingside plan: after b3 and knight bd2, Black plays g6, rook e8, bishop g7, and prepares f5.
teaches: There are multiple ways to handle a structure; if one plan is blocked, a complete switch of plans (from queenside to kingside) can be effective.
plans: Black develops harmoniously and aims for a kingside attack with f5.

explains: After …Nd7 in the Chigorin, Black's knight on d7 supports queenside play and prepares to reroute to b7, then to g6 via ...Nb7 and ...g6, aiming for a kingside setup with ...Re8, ...Bf8, ...Bg7, and eventually ...Nh5 and ...f5.
teaches: When the center is closed, a knight can be repositioned from the queenside to the kingside to support a pawn break like ...f5, switching plans entirely.
plans: Black should continue with ...Nb7, ...g6, ...Re8, ...Bf8, ...Bg7, ...Nh5, and ...f5, creating kingside play.

explains: After …d5, Black's immediate ...Nc4 is possible but risky because White can play a4 or b3, forcing the knight back to b6, where it is poorly placed. Black must play energetically to avoid passivity, as passively defending the rook with ...Bd7 allows ...a5 and leaves the knight with no good squares, eventually going to c8.
teaches: In closed positions, a knight on the rim can be driven back with pawns; it's often better to keep the knight flexible rather than commit to a square that can be undermined.
plans: Black should prefer ...Nd7 over ...Nc4, keeping the knight active and avoiding a passive setup.

explains: After …d5, White can instead play Nbd2, the main move, keeping the tension. Black's best response is …cxd4, clarifying the pawn structure and gaining permanent pressure on the c-file, which forces White to move the bishop from c2. Alternatives like ...Nc6 (Rubinstein) and ...Bd7 (Petrician) are playable but less common.
teaches: Clarifying the pawn structure early can be beneficial when it creates lasting pressure on a file, even if it means giving up the center tension.
plans: Black should play ...cxd4, then ...Nc6, ...a5, ...Bd7, and ...Rc8, pressuring the c-file and preparing ...Bf8 and ...Re8.

explains: In the line after ...cxd4, White's main move is ...Nc6, and Black should avoid playing d5 too early because ...Nb4 gives Black an advantage, allowing the knight to later go to c5. Instead, White plays Rc1, and Black can unpin with ...Qb7, then ...Re8, and slowly switch to a kingside plan with ...Bf8.
teaches: When the opponent has a knight on c6, playing d5 can be a positional mistake if it gives away the c5 square; it's often better to keep the tension and develop.
plans: Black should continue with ...Qb7, ...Re8, ...Bf8, and prepare ...Nd7 if White plays d5 later.

explains: After ...cxd4, Black can also play ...Bd7, which completely discourages d5 because it would release the tension and give away the c5 square while the queen is tied to defending e5. White then plays Nf1, heading to e3 to defend the c2 bishop, and Black plays Rc8, pressuring the bishop.
teaches: A bishop on d7 can be a prophylactic move that prevents a central pawn break, as the break would weaken key squares and leave the center unresolved.
plans: Black should play ...Rc8, and depending on White's defense of c2 (e.g., Ne3 or b3), continue with pressure on the c-file and prepare ...Bf8 and ...Re8.

explains: In this Chigorin setup, Black's knight on a5 eyes the c4 square, which is a key outpost. If White develops the bishop to b7, Black essentially gives up the c5 square, so White instead reroutes the knight to f1, heading to e3 or g3, with e3 being best.
teaches: When your opponent has a knight eyeing a strong square like c4, consider developing a piece that can both defend and cover that square, such as a knight to e3.
plans: White will play Ne3 to defend the c2 bishop and cover c4, preventing Black's knight from coming to c4.

explains: Black's next move is Rf8, which defends e5 and frees the queen, anticipating White's rook coming to c1. White plays b3 to prevent Nc4, and Black responds with Nc6, returning the knight to the center. White then plays Bb2, pressuring e5, so Black defends with Bf8, and White plays Rc1, eyeing the queen. Black plays Qb7, which is precise because it avoids running into Nd5 after a future exchange on d5.
teaches: In closed positions, it's important to anticipate your opponent's pressure and make moves that both defend and maintain flexibility, such as placing the queen on a square that avoids tactical tricks.
plans: Black will aim to trade on d5 and then play Nb4, reaching a comfortable endgame with no problems.

explains: After the exchange on d5 and Nb4, Black reaches an equal endgame where the bishops may have greater long-term potential than White's knight on e5. This is a satisfactory outcome for Black.
teaches: In the Chigorin, the resulting endgame structures are often fine for Black, so don't fear simplification if it leads to a position with no weaknesses.
plans: Black will continue to develop harmoniously, aiming for the typical ideas of the Chigorin, such as playing ...c5 and ...d4 to open the center.

explains: The Chigorin is a rich opening with many possible move orders, but the underlying ideas remain consistent. Understanding these ideas is more important than memorizing theory, especially when facing non-book moves.
teaches: When studying an opening, focus on the strategic ideas and typical plans rather than trying to memorize every line. This will help you handle unfamiliar positions.
plans: Study games by strong players like Karpov and Kasparov to see how they handled the Chigorin, and play the opening yourself to gain practical experience.

explains: In the Scandinavian, despite its aggressive reputation, the first moves are calm and both sides develop without immediate conflict. Black's main options after Nf3 are Bf5 or c6, which usually transpose to the same setup.
teaches: Recognize that the opening phase can be quiet even in sharp openings; focus on achieving a solid setup rather than forcing early tactics.
plans: Black aims for the setup with Bf5, c6, e6, and Nd7, which is objectively best. White continues with Bd2 and Bc4, placing the bishop actively.

explains: The sideline Bg4 is not popular because after h3, Bh5, g4, Bg6, Ne5, Black is considered worse, with the engine giving White about +1.3. The bishop gets captured on g6, leaving Black with a disadvantage.
teaches: Some sidelines are rare because they are objectively worse; avoid them unless you have a specific surprise value.
plans: If White faces Bg4, play h3, then g4 to force the bishop to g6, and follow with Ne5 to gain an advantage.

explains: The sideline Nc6 is provocative because it prevents Black from playing c6 later, which is essential for the Scandinavian structure. White can play Bb5, Nd7, castles, a6, Bxc6, and Ne5, leaving Black with doubled pawns on c7 and c6 and a ruined pawn structure.
teaches: Avoid moves that compromise your pawn structure without clear compensation; in the Scandinavian, c6 is a key support pawn.
plans: If Black plays Nc6, White should play Bb5 to pin and eventually exchange, forcing doubled pawns and a structural weakness.

explains: The sideline Ne4 is forced and leads to a pawn win for Black after Nxc3, bxc3, and Qxc3+. However, White gets a huge initiative with two menacing bishops on d3 and c3, and the engine evaluates nearly +2 for White despite the pawn deficit.
teaches: Material is not everything; a lead in development and initiative can outweigh a pawn, especially against lower-rated players who may not exploit it.
plans: If Black takes the pawn, White should develop with tempo (Bf4, Qa3, castles, etc.) and aim for a Greek gift sacrifice or strong attacking play.

explains: If Black avoids Nf6 and plays ...Be7, ...Bb4, or ...a6, White's plan is to enter a Carlsbad structure and place the bishop on f4 instead of g5, since g5 is unavailable or less effective.
teaches: When the natural bishop development to g5 is prevented, f4 is a strong alternative square, keeping the bishop active and supporting the central and queenside plans.
plans: In these lines, play cxd5, then Bf4, followed by e3, Nc3, and Bd3, maintaining a harmonious setup and preparing a minority attack with a3-b4-b5.

explains: Against the Slav move ...Bf5, White can play the aggressive g4, chasing the bishop and gaining space on the kingside. This is a sharp but effective way to seize the initiative.
teaches: In the Carlsbad structure, a timely pawn thrust like g4 can disrupt Black's development and create attacking chances, but it requires precise handling.
plans: After ...Bf5, play g4, then h4, and if ...Bxh4, respond with Qb3, targeting the b7 pawn and maintaining pressure.

explains: In the line with ...Bb4 (the Ragozin-like setup), White can still enter a Carlsbad structure and play Bf4. The bishop on b4 is not a serious problem; in fact, it can become a target for a later a3-b4-b5 minority attack.
teaches: A bishop on b4 can be a liability for Black if White can gain time by attacking it with a3, so it's not a move to fear.
plans: Take on d5, then Bf4, e3, Nc3, and Bd3, with the option of a3 and b4 to start the minority attack.

explains: The ...a6 variation (Anovski) is not critical because if White simply takes on d5, Black's ...a6 is a wasted tempo. White can proceed with Bf4 and a normal Carlsbad setup.
teaches: Not every provocative move by Black deserves a reaction; sometimes the best response is to ignore it and continue with your own plan.
plans: After ...a6, play cxd5, then Bf4, e3, Nc3, and Bd3, with a slight edge due to Black's extra move being useless.

explains: In the Qe2 variation, both sides castle queenside. Black plays Bb4, and after a3, Bxc3 is best, giving up the dark-squared bishop. White gains the bishop pair, but Black's light-squared bishop has few targets, and the pawn structure is solid.
teaches: Giving up the bishop pair is acceptable if the remaining bishop is not very active and the pawn structure is sound. Here, Black's light-squared bishop is somewhat passive, so the exchange is not too costly.
plans: Black will continue development with Nbd7, and after Qc7, the position is balanced. White may try to use the bishop pair, but Black's structure is resilient.

explains: After the exchange of dark-squared bishops, White plays Ne5, and Black takes with the pawn (dxc5) rather than the knight, which is better. Then Nd5, Bd2, and both sides castle queenside. The position is equal, though Black may feel comfortable due to familiarity with the structure.
teaches: When recapturing, consider which piece should take. Taking with the pawn can maintain pawn structure and keep the knight for other duties.
plans: Both sides have castled queenside. White will look for aggressive breaks like g4 to attack Black's kingside, while Black will aim to counter on the queenside or in the center.

explains: In the resulting position, White often plays g4 to attack Black's kingside. Black responds with Bg6, and a sharp sequence follows: f4, h5, h3, Qb6, Rh2, f1, hxg4, hxg4, Qc5. Both sides battle for the h-file, with Black usually seizing it.
teaches: When both sides have castled on opposite wings, pawn storms are common. Control of open files becomes crucial, and every tempo matters.
plans: Black will try to use the h-file to attack White's king, while White will seek counterplay on the f-file and consider f5 as a break.

explains: Comparing Nd5 and Ne4: after Nd5, Black's queen only has d8, while after Ne4, Black can also use b6 or c7. This gives Black more options after Ne4, but the main line still leads to Qd8.
teaches: When choosing between similar moves, consider the opponent's possible replies. A move that restricts the opponent's options is often more forcing.
plans: After Nd5, the line is forced: Qd8. After Ne4, Black may choose Qc7 or Qb6, but the resulting positions are similar.

explains: After the knights are exchanged on f6, black's recapture choice matters: taking with the g-pawn ruins the kingside pawn structure, while taking with the queen leaves the queen exposed on f6, where it can be harassed by Bg5, forcing it to g6, a poor square.
teaches: When choosing between recaptures, weigh structural damage against piece activity and vulnerability. A ruined pawn structure can be a long-term weakness, but a misplaced queen can be a more immediate target.
plans: If black takes with the g-pawn, white can aim to exploit the open g-file and the weakened kingside. If black takes with the queen, white can develop with tempo by attacking the queen.

explains: In the main line after gxf6, white's bishop retreats to b3, a typical Sicilian-style maneuver to avoid harassment, while black develops with Nd7 and Qc7, preparing queenside castling. White castles queenside, and the position is balanced despite engine evaluations favoring white.
teaches: A space advantage from a central pawn does not guarantee an objective plus if the opponent has active counterplay. Engine evaluations can be misleading in dynamic positions.
plans: Black can aim for e5 to open the position, and if white captures, recapture with the h-pawn to open the h-file for the rook. White should maintain the space advantage and prepare kingside play.

explains: The difference between ...Ne4 and ...Nd5 is that after ...Ne4, black has access to b6 and c7 for the queen, whereas after ...Nd5, only Qd8 is viable. This gives black more flexibility in the ...Ne4 line.
teaches: Knight moves that create multiple queen retreat squares offer more flexibility and can avoid forced lines. Consider the queen's options when choosing which piece to exchange.
plans: In the ...Ne4 line, black can choose between Qc7, Qb6, or Qd8, each with different implications. White must be prepared for all three.

explains: After ...Ne4 and Qd8, white can decline the trade and play Ng3, gaining a tempo on the bishop and reinforcing the d4 pawn with c3 later. This sideline is particularly challenging for black.
teaches: Declining a trade can be a strong resource to improve piece placement and address weaknesses. A knight on g3 can support f4 and h4, and c3 solidifies the center.
plans: White aims to play c3 to reinforce d4, then develop calmly with a space advantage. Black must find active counterplay, often by trading the bishop for the knight on g3.

explains: In the ...Ne4 line, after white plays c3, the d4 weakness is gone, and white has a solid structure with a space advantage and a lead in development. Black's bishop on f5 is often traded off, leading to a position reminiscent of the Karpov-Korchnoi style with light-squared bishops off.
teaches: Reinforcing a central pawn can neutralize an opponent's counterplay, leaving you with a stable edge. Trading off the opponent's active pieces can simplify to a favorable structure.
plans: White should complete development and maintain the space advantage. Black should seek active piece play and try to create imbalances.

explains: After White plays c3, the center is solidified and White has a space advantage. White is also ahead in development, having completed development with four pieces out compared to Black's fewer.
teaches: In the Slav-style positions arising from this Scandinavian line, a solid center and a lead in development give White a comfortable edge. Recognizing when you have a space advantage and a development lead helps you decide to play actively.
plans: White can continue by finishing development, e.g., bringing the rook to d1, and then look to exploit the space advantage with pawn advances or piece pressure.

explains: After Black plays ...Nbd7, White plays h3 to chase the bishop. Black must take on f3, after which White recaptures with the queen. Black then places the bishop on d6, the most active square. The light-squared bishops are traded, and the position resembles a Karpov-Kokkan structure.
teaches: When the opponent's bishop is pinning or pressing on your king side, a timely h3 can force a favorable trade or gain a tempo. After the trade, recapturing with the queen can keep the king side flexible and maintain central control.
plans: Both sides castle kingside, and White places a rook on d1. Black is content to play on the first three ranks, accepting less space but having an active piece placement.

explains: In a game from the main line, after the moves ...Qc7, Nh4, Bg6, castles, and Re1, White played f4, but this was a mistake because the king is already castled queenside, so f4 does not support a kingside attack. Black responded with ...f5, a counterintuitive move that stops g4 and prepares ...Nf6, a great square for the knight eyeing e4. White's subsequent h3 and g4 were met by ...Bh5 and ...Nf3, leaving Black substantially better.
teaches: Pawn advances must be justified by the position. A move like f4 is only useful if it supports an attack or improves your structure; here it weakened White's position. Conversely, a move like ...f5 can be a strong defensive resource that also creates a strong outpost for a knight.
plans: Black's plan is to solidify the kingside and use the knight on f6 (or later e4) to pressure White's center. White's attempt to open the queenside with c3 and later Rg1 does not address the weaknesses created by f4.

explains: In the resulting position, Black's bishop on g6 is actually a good piece, staring at White's king on b1, while White's bishop is less active. The game concluded with a series of tactical blows: ...Ka7, Nxd6, Rxd6, Qf4, Bxc2, Bxc2, Re2+, and eventually Black's rook on b2 delivered the final blow, forcing resignation.
teaches: A bishop that is 'bad' in terms of pawn structure can still be a powerful attacking piece if it targets the enemy king. Activity and king safety often outweigh structural considerations. In sharp positions, precise calculation and tactical awareness are crucial.
plans: Black's plan is to maintain the initiative and keep the white king under pressure. The combination of rook lifts and bishop pressure creates mating threats that White cannot parry.

explains: The Scandinavian main line is a flexible and easy-to-learn opening. There are only three critical moves to study: Nd5, Ne4, and Qe2. Additionally, on move 5, Black can choose sidelines like ...Bg4 or ...Nc6 instead of ...c6 or ...Bf5.
teaches: An opening can be both sound and practical if you understand the key ideas and are willing to learn a few variations. The Scandinavian offers a wide range of positions with minimal memorization.
plans: Players can choose between the main lines and sidelines based on their preferences. The opening is suitable for players who want to avoid heavy theory while still getting playable positions.

explains: The main line of the Scandinavian Defense is a practical opening choice because it requires studying only a few key positions, making it easy to learn and flexible to play.
teaches: An opening can be effective without deep theoretical knowledge if you focus on the critical variations and understand the typical plans.
plans: Continue studying the main lines, especially the positions after …Nd5, …Ne4, and …Qe2, and be ready to enter sidelines if the opponent deviates.

explains: In the main line, Black has several viable setups, including the central knight moves and the queen move, each leading to different types of positions.
teaches: When learning an opening, identify the key branching points and understand the typical plans for each, rather than memorizing long forced lines.
plans: For White, be prepared to face Black's various setups and choose a plan that suits your style, whether it's active piece play or central control.

explains: On move five, Black can deviate from the main line with moves like Bg4 or Nc6, offering alternative paths that avoid the standard theory.
teaches: Having sidelines in your repertoire can be a useful way to steer the game into less familiar territory for your opponent.
plans: If you prefer to avoid the main line, consider these sidelines as part of your opening preparation.

explains: In this Gligorić System position, White's bishop on e3 is better than on c1, giving White an objective advantage due to improved piece placement and space. Black cannot continue with normal plans.
teaches: A bishop on e3 in the King's Indian can be more active than on c1, supporting central and kingside play.
plans: White aims to exploit the improved bishop and space advantage; Black must find challenging moves to counter.

explains: Black has several candidate moves here: Ng4, exd4, Na6, c6, and Nbd7. Ng4 is the main line, directly challenging the e3 bishop. If White castles, Black can take on e3, leaving White with a permanent weakness.
teaches: When a bishop is developed to e3, a knight on g4 can pressure it, potentially forcing weaknesses or trades.
plans: Black plays Ng4 to provoke a response; White must find a way to maintain the initiative.

explains: After Ng4, White's main reply is Bg5, gaining a tempo on the queen. Black responds with f6, forcing the bishop to h4. Black can then play g5, asking the bishop to retreat to g3, releasing the pin on the f6 pawn.
teaches: Using pawns to chase a bishop can gain time and release pins, but must be timed correctly.
plans: Black plays g5 to force the bishop back, then continues with Nh6 and central play.

explains: In the main line, after Bg3, Black can play Nh6, and if White takes on e5, Black recaptures with the d-pawn. If queens are exchanged, Black's dark-squared bishop can become active via f8, c5, b4, or d4, potentially outclassing White's bishop on g3.
teaches: In positions with opposite-colored bishops, the activity of the bishops is crucial; a seemingly passive bishop can be rerouted to a strong diagonal.
plans: Black aims to trade queens and activate the dark-squared bishop, while White tries to use the better pawn structure and king safety.

explains: White plays Qd2, and after Qd8, an exchange on d8 occurs. White then plays h4 to seek kingside activity. Black should respond with g4 to prevent the bishop from activating. White's idea is to play h5 and Bh4 to give the bishop a future.
teaches: When a bishop is misplaced, a plan to reroute it (e.g., h5 and Bh4) can improve its prospects; Black must prevent such activation.
plans: White plays h5 and Bh4 to activate the bishop; Black must counter with g4 to keep it passive.

explains: After White's g4, Black should respond with Ng4, attacking the bishop on e3 and forcing it to move. If White takes the knight, the bishop on g7 becomes active along the long diagonal, which is undesirable for White.
teaches: In the Gligorić System, Black's Ng4 is a key resource to challenge White's bishop and prevent it from settling on a strong diagonal.
plans: Black follows up with h5 and Bg4 to pressure the f6 pawn, while White must find a way to activate his light-squared bishop.

explains: Black's plan involves playing h5 and Bg4 to pressure f6, but White can respond by moving the bishop to h6 or f8 to challenge the diagonal, and then the king goes to g7 to defend f6, neutralizing Black's pressure.
teaches: When the opponent's bishop is pressuring a pawn, it's often useful to challenge the bishop's diagonal or defend the pawn with the king, reducing the bishop's effectiveness.
plans: Black should be prepared for White's bishop maneuver to h6 or f8, and then reposition the king to g7.

explains: With queens traded, Black's kingside pawn advances like g5 and g4 are less risky because there is no immediate attack on the king. Black can continue development with Be6, aiming for the best diagonal, while White plays Nb3 to challenge c5 and d5 squares.
teaches: In opposite-side castling positions, pawn advances on the side where the opponent's king is not castled are less dangerous if queens are off the board, as the attacking potential is reduced.
plans: Black should develop the bishop to e6 and consider central breaks like c5, aiming for the d4 square for a knight.

explains: Black's strategic goal is to get a knight to d4, which would be strategically winning. If the knight is traded for the bad bishop, Black gets a dangerous passed pawn on d4 and can open the c-file.
teaches: A knight firmly placed on a central outpost like d4 can be a decisive advantage, especially if it can be supported and traded for a less active piece.
plans: Black should aim to play c5 and Nb8-d7-f8-g6-e7-c6-d4, or similar maneuvers, to achieve the d4 outpost.

explains: After White plays h5 to prevent the bishop from coming to g4, Black can play Bh6, challenging the diagonal, and then Bg4 to the only active square, with the king on g7. This position is equal, but Black's better dark-squared bishop gives long-term chances.
teaches: In the Gligorić System, Black's dark-squared bishop can become a powerful piece if it can be activated, even if it has only one pawn target; its influence on the board matters more.
plans: White should try to create kingside pressure, while Black should focus on queenside play, possibly targeting the c4 pawn.

explains: In this Gligorić System position, White has played g4, a sharp and committal move that gives Black many options. This line has been played by top players, indicating it is a serious system for complicating the King's Indian.
teaches: When White chooses an aggressive setup like g4, Black should be aware that the game can become complex and that there are multiple viable plans to counter White's intentions.
plans: Black can consider standard King's Indian plans, but must be ready to adapt to White's specific setup.

explains: In the line with ...Nxd4, the central tension is released, leading to a simpler position than typical King's Indian structures. This is a key feature: White cannot aim for long-term kingside attack, but also avoids being attacked on the kingside.
teaches: When the center is simplified, the game becomes more about piece activity and pawn structure weaknesses. Black should be ready to play a more straightforward game, possibly with equal chances.
plans: Black can prepare ...d5 with ...c6 and ...Re8, then exchange central pawns to reach a comfortable position.

explains: Another line involves Black playing ...Na6 before ...Ng4. After White castles, Black plays ...Ng4, and the variation continues with ...Re8 and ...Qd8, accepting exchanges in the center. This leaves White with a Maroczy Bind setup and a weakness on d4.
teaches: Black's strategic goal is to exploit the d4 weakness by putting pressure on it, potentially placing a piece on d4. This is a common theme in Maroczy structures.
plans: Black should aim to weaken d4 further, support the e5 pawn, and try to occupy d4 with a knight or bishop.

explains: In a line where Black plays ...Ng4 and White retreats the bishop to d2, Black can develop with ...Qe7 and ...Nd7, preparing to connect rooks. White may play Nd5, but Black doesn't have to take; instead, ...Qd8 is a key move, making the e5 pawn immune because if White takes it, Black wins a piece.
teaches: Sometimes a retreating queen move can be strong, as it defends key pawns and maintains piece coordination. Recognizing tactical motifs like the immunity of a pawn due to a hanging piece is essential.
plans: Black should continue developing, possibly with ...b6 and ...c5, to challenge White's center and create counterplay.

explains: After the queen retreats to d8, the pawn on f6 is immune because if White captures it, the knight on d5 hangs and Black ends up a piece up. The main move is Nxf6, but after Qxf6 the pawn is defended again, and the position is roughly equal, though Black may have the better chances if play continues aggressively.
teaches: When a pawn seems undefended, check if capturing it leaves your own piece hanging. Sometimes a retreating move can make a pawn 'poisoned'.
plans: Black should aim to reinforce the queenside structure with b6 and c5, locking down the queenside and then rerouting the knight to d4 via b8-c6-d4.

explains: If Black gets to play b6 and c5, the queenside is locked and Black's structure is solid, making the d5 square forever protected. Then Black can plan Qc6 or maneuver the knight to d4, leading to a much better game. White must play c5 himself to prevent this and keep the game equal.
teaches: When your opponent threatens to lock the queenside with a pawn break, you must often play that break yourself to avoid being strategically worse. Seize the moment to play c5 if Black has the opportunity.
plans: White should play c5 to maintain equality, while Black, if allowed, will reinforce with b6 and then target d4 with the knight.

explains: The modern ...g6 setup combines ideas from ...g4 and ...Nb8-d7 lines: first ...Ng4 chases the bishop, then after Bg5, ...f6, and then ...c5 closes the queenside. This leads to a faster attack with ...a5 and ...h5, and if White plays h6, Black can respond with ...Nh6, which is a better idea than in other lines.
teaches: When combining plans, the order of moves matters: harass the bishop first to gain time, then close the queenside, and then launch the kingside pawn storm. This maximizes the speed of your attack.
plans: Black will play ...c5, then ...a5 and ...h5, with the knight going to h6 if needed, maintaining pressure on the kingside while the queenside is closed.

explains: After White plays d5, Black's plan is to close the queenside with c5, but first Ng4 chases the bishop. If White plays Bg5, then f6 forces the bishop back, combining ideas from lines with Be2 and Nd7.
teaches: In the King's Indian, when White closes the center with d5, Black should aim to fix the queenside with c5 and then develop a kingside attack, using piece play like Ng4 to provoke weaknesses.
plans: After c5, Black can quickly play a5 and g5, with the knight going to h6 and then f7 to support the g5 break.

explains: White's f3 prevents the knight from settling on g4, and Black has locked the queenside but the kingside attack is not clearly effective. The pieces are well placed for defense, and Black's practical chances are limited.
teaches: When the opponent's pieces are well coordinated for defense, a direct attack may not yield an advantage; it's important to assess whether the attack is real or just apparent.
plans: If the attack is not promising, consider alternative plans or a different move order to create more dynamic chances.

explains: After Be3, Black's main move is Nf4, which is the most aggressive and interesting. Alternatives like c6 or Nb7 are not dangerous enough. If Black wants a simpler game, exchanging on d4 releases central tension.
teaches: In the Gligorić System, the choice of move should be based on the type of game you want: main lines for complexity, exchanges for simplicity.
plans: With Nf4, Black can combine plans from the main line and later moves like Na6, aiming for a win. If choosing the exchange on d4, prepare for a simpler middlegame.

explains: The final position analyzed leads to a passed pawn, but experienced players will be prepared. It's advisable to have a sideline ready, such as c6 or taking on d4.
teaches: When a main line leads to a known or theoretical position, having a sideline can be a practical weapon to avoid prepared lines.
plans: Choose either g4 or g6 as your main weapon against the Gligorić, and prepare a sideline like c6 or exd4 for variety.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: In the Old Steinitz Defense, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 d6 c3 Bd7, White has a small edge because Black's bishop on d7 is passive and Black has not yet unpinned the knight on c6. The immediate threat is to take on e5, but White should maintain the tension.
teaches: When facing a passive setup, keep the tension and avoid premature captures; the pin on the knight is a valuable asset.
plans: White should develop with Nbd2 or Nc3, preparing d4, while keeping the pressure on e5.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: Black's only viable moves are ...Bd7 and ...exd4, which transpose to the same type of position. The nature of the game depends on White's choices. White's main plan is to develop with Nc3 or castles, then play d4, recapturing with the knight if Black takes.
teaches: In many openings, different move orders lead to the same position; understanding the transpositions helps in choosing the most flexible setup.
plans: White should develop with Nc3 or castles, then play d4, recapturing with the knight if Black takes.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: Black's attempts to pressure e4 are usually ineffective, making the Steinitz Defense slightly passive. White should not worry about facing it and need not be heavily prepared theoretically.
teaches: Recognize when an opening is passive and focus on sound development and central control rather than over-preparing against rare lines.
plans: White can choose between the main lines or the c3-d4 setup, both leading to a comfortable edge.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: An independent idea for White is to play c3 and then d4, recapturing with the pawn if Black takes. This leads to a different strategic structure compared to recapturing with the knight. The engine considers this a viable alternative.
teaches: Choosing to recapture with a pawn instead of a piece can change the pawn structure and strategic plans, offering different types of play.
plans: White can play c3, then d4, and if Black takes, recapture with the pawn, leading to a closed center and different plans.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: In the Old Steinitz Defense, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 d6 c3 Bd7 d4, White has a choice: play d4 immediately or first support it with c3. If White plays d4 without c3, Black can trade on d4 and force White to recapture with the knight, leading to main-line positions. If White plays c3 first, the position becomes independent and strategically different.
teaches: The move c3 in the Ruy Lopez prepares d4 and ensures that if Black captures on d4, White can recapture with the pawn, creating a central pawn duo. This is a key strategic distinction from the main lines where White recaptures with the knight.
plans: White aims to build a strong center with pawns on d4 and e4, while Black should avoid releasing the tension by taking on d4, as that would give White a mobile central pawn mass.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: After c3 and d4, Black often develops with Nf6 and Be7, and White must defend the e4 pawn before playing d4. A common sequence is Re1, Be7, and then d4. In this setup, Black should not take on d4 because White would recapture with the c-pawn, giving White a central pawn duo that controls many squares and can advance to d5 or e5.
teaches: When White has played c3, Black's capture on d4 is usually unfavorable because it trades a central pawn for a flank pawn and gives White a powerful pawn center. White's knight on b1 also gains a natural square on c3 or d2.
plans: White should aim to maintain the central pawns and develop pieces harmoniously, possibly with Nbd2 or Nc3, while Black should seek counterplay on the queenside with moves like a6-b5, but avoid releasing the central tension.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: In the line with c3 and d4, White must be careful of tactical tricks. For example, after Black castles, White might be tempted to play Nbd2, but this can allow Nxd4, a tactical trick. If White then takes on d7, Black recaptures with the knight, and the tactic fails. Instead, White can play Ba4 to defend the bishop and avoid the trick.
teaches: When playing with a central pawn duo, it's important to ensure that your pieces are defended and that you are not vulnerable to tactics on the d4 square. Defending key squares and pieces is crucial before advancing.
plans: White should continue developing and maintaining the center, possibly with moves like Ba4, Nbd2, or Nc3, while keeping an eye on tactical threats.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: In the main line of the Old Steinitz, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 d6 d4, Black can play exd4, and White recaptures with the knight. Alternatively, Black can play Bd7, transposing to main lines. A sideline for White is Qxd4, which is playable but gives Black extra options, such as Ne7, which can be awkward for White's development.
teaches: When recapturing on d4 with the queen, White must be prepared to trade on c6, which can lead to a less harmonious position. It's often better to recapture with the knight to maintain flexibility and avoid giving Black easy development.
plans: If White plays Qxd4, they may aim for quick castling queenside, but this is not the most critical. The main move is Nxd4, leading to standard main-line positions.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: A very interesting and engine-recommended move for White in the Old Steinitz is Nxc6, which might seem committal but gives White a structural advantage. By trading the knight on c6, White saddles Black with doubled pawns or a weak pawn structure, though it also releases the tension in the center.
teaches: Sometimes a move that appears to give up the center can be justified by a lasting structural advantage. It's important to evaluate positions based on pawn structure and long-term prospects, not just immediate activity.
plans: After Nxc6, White will aim to exploit Black's weakened pawn structure, possibly by targeting the d6 pawn or creating pressure on the queenside.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 d6 c3 Bd7 d4, White can choose between main lines with Nc3 or the sharp sideline Nxc6. The position is a Ruy Lopez, Old Steinitz Defense, where Black's pawn structure is slightly rigid.
teaches: In the Old Steinitz, White has a choice between solid development and a committal capture that changes the pawn structure. Understanding the trade-off between structure and piece activity is key.
plans: If White plays Nxc6, the plan is to target the c6 weakness and possibly play c3-c4 and Qa4. If White plays Nc3, the plan is to build a kingside attack, often with Be3, Qd2, and f3, resembling a Yugoslav Attack against the Sicilian.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: After …exd4, if White plays Nxd4, Black can play …Bd7, transposing to main lines. The move Nxc6 is a rare but interesting alternative that gives White a structural advantage: if Black recaptures with the bishop, White gains a tempo; if Black recaptures with the b-pawn, the c6 pawn becomes weak.
teaches: Capturing on c6 can be a way to unbalance the position and create long-term weaknesses, even if it seems committal. The resulting pawn structure (doubled c-pawns for Black) gives White targets.
plans: After Nxc6 and bxc6, White's bishop retreats to a4, and White plans to castle, develop, and pressure the c6 pawn. If Black plays ...c5 to defend, White gets d5 and targets c7.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: In the main line after Nxd4 Bd7, White often plays Nc3. Black can choose between ...g6 and ...Be7 setups, but both share ...Nf6. If Black plays ...g6, White can adopt a plan similar to the Yugoslav Attack against the Sicilian Dragon, with Be3, Qd2, and f3, castling queenside.
teaches: The Old Steinitz can transpose to a Sicilian-like structure, but with the c-file closed, which is favorable for White because Black loses the typical counterplay on the c-file.
plans: White aims for a kingside pawn storm with f3, g4, h4, while castling queenside. The closed c-file means White doesn't have to worry about ...Rc8 and ...Qc7 pressure.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: If White castles kingside instead of queenside, Black cannot play ...g6 immediately because of a tactical trick: after Bxc6, bxc6, Re1, if ...Bg7 then e5 breaks through. So Black must play ...Be7 first.
teaches: When choosing a setup, always check for tactical refutations. The move order matters: castling kingside changes the evaluation of Black's ...g6 plan.
plans: After ...Be7, White can choose between Nxc6, Bxc6, or Re1. A common plan is Bxc6, bxc6, then build up with b3, Bb2, f4, and Qf3, putting pressure on c6 and the kingside.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: In the Old Steinitz Defense, after d4, if White castles kingside, Black can meet Re1 with ...Be7, preventing the immediate ...exd4 and ...Nxd4 tricks. White's normal setup with Re1, Bg5, and Bf4 does not yield an advantage.
teaches: When facing the Old Steinitz, Black's key defensive resource is ...Be7 before castling, neutralizing White's pressure on e5. White should avoid routine development that allows Black to consolidate.
plans: White should consider alternative setups, such as f3 and Be3, to maintain pressure and avoid the simplified positions that arise from standard play.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: White can improve by playing Bxc6 immediately. If Black recaptures with the b-pawn, White castles kingside. If Black recaptures with the bishop, White prepares queenside castling with Qe2 (or Qd3/Qf3) and Be3, avoiding the problematic f3/Be3/queenside-castle setup.
teaches: Trading the bishop on c6 can be a useful move-order trick: it forces Black to choose a recapture that determines White's castling side, and it removes a piece that is often poorly placed.
plans: After Bxc6, if ...bxc6, castle kingside and proceed with standard play. If ...Bxc6, play Qe2, Be3, and prepare queenside castling, with ideas like Ne4 and Nf5 to exploit the weakened kingside.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: After Bxc6 and ...Bxc6, White can play Qe2 and Be3. The pawn on e4 is not hanging because if Black plays ...Bxe4, White has Ne4, and if ...Nxe4, then Nf5 creates threats against g7 and a discovered check.
teaches: Tactical resources like knight forks and discovered checks can protect central pawns and create counterplay. Recognizing these motifs allows White to play actively without fear of losing material.
plans: Continue with queenside castling, then build pressure with moves like f3 and possibly g4 or h4, targeting Black's weakened kingside.

opening: Ruy Lopez: Old Steinitz Defense, Semi-Duras Variation
explains: The recommended setup after Bxc6 and ...Bxc6 is Qe2, Be3, f3, and queenside castling. This is an original plan that has not been seen in master games, but it makes positional sense because Black's light-squared bishop is 'garbage' and the bishop pair is irrelevant.
teaches: Sometimes unconventional plans can be justified by the specific weaknesses in the opponent's position. Here, Black's bishop on c6 is passive, so White can ignore the bishop pair and focus on attacking the kingside.
plans: White castles queenside, then aims to launch a pawn storm with g4 and h4, while Black must defend against threats on the kingside.

explains: After Bc4, White has already castled kingside, and Black's most common reply is …Qd5, which threatens checks and allows ...Ba5 to trade off the light-squared bishops, giving Black initiative.
teaches: In sharp opening variations, using queen moves to provoke bishop trades can neutralize White's attacking piece and generate counterplay.
plans: Black can follow up with ...Ba5 to exchange bishops, aiming for a comfortable game.

explains: The engine evaluation shows White is better (+1), but this advantage is not meaningful until pieces are traded because the pawn structure (doubled f-pawns for Black) is not exploitable early.
teaches: Do not rely solely on engine evaluations in the opening; static weaknesses matter only in simplified positions.

explains: After …h5, Black has an aggressive plan, especially in blitz, but it is also viable in tournament play. Another strong option is …e5, immediately striking at White's center; if White takes, Black exchanges queens with tempo and ruins White's castling rights, and can later recapture with ...fxe5, giving Black a good game.
teaches: Striking at the center early can force favorable simplifications and disrupt the opponent's king safety.
plans: If White plays Be3, Black develops with ...Nd7 and ...Nf3, then pushes ...e4, gaining space.

explains: If White plays Bd3 to prevent ...e4, Black can play …d4, and after Bxd4, …Ne5 gives Black a good position. Black then plans ...Bh6, ...Rg8, and ...Bg4 to attack the weakness on g2.
teaches: When the opponent tries to prevent one pawn break, look for another central push that opens lines for your pieces.
plans: Black will target g2 with rook and bishop, creating pressure on White's kingside.

explains: White can challenge the e4 pawn with f3, but after …Qe7, fxe4 fxe4, and Bc4, Black can play …Nd6, and if White plays Qh5, Black can ignore the bishop and play …c5, opening the center. This variation requires aggressive and energetic play to justify the weakness on f4.
teaches: In sharp positions, you must be willing to sacrifice material for activity and keep the initiative.
plans: Black should play ...c5 to open the center and create counterplay.

explains: The main line after …Bf5 is c3, preparing ...e6 and ...Bg6, ...f5, ...Bg7 or ...Bh6, ...Nd7, ...Qc7, and ...O-O-O. After Nf3, White's main try is g3, and Black's main move is …Nd7. The engine may say Black is worse, but this is an unsound variation engine-wise, yet it was playable before engines; ignore the engines in the opening.
teaches: Some opening variations are practically playable even if engines dislike them; rely on your understanding and the practical chances.
plans: Black will fianchetto the bishop and castle kingside, with counterplay on the g-file.

explains: After g3, Black can play …Qb6, slowing down White's development of the c1 bishop. If White plays Bg2, Black can play …Qa6, forcing the bishop back to f1, and then ...Qb6 again, confusing White and taking him out of preparation.
teaches: Using queen moves to harass the opponent's pieces can disrupt their development and force them to lose time.
plans: Black aims to keep White's bishop on f1 and prevent the fianchetto, gaining a development edge.

explains: After White plays g3 and Bg2, Black can play Qb6 to hinder White's development of the c1 bishop and then Qa6 to prevent Bg2, forcing the bishop back to f1, after which Qb6 returns. This takes White out of book.
teaches: Use queen maneuvers to disrupt the opponent's planned fianchetto and force them out of their preparation.
plans: Black aims to develop with Be7, Nf6, and maintain pressure on the queenside, while White may try Qe2 to answer Qa6 with Bf1.

explains: If White plays c4, Black can play Bb4+ and after Be2, Nxe2, Black can still play Qb6, attacking d4 and b2. However, Black should not take on d4 because after Qxd1+ Kxd1, Black loses material and is busted.
teaches: When the opponent offers a pawn, check if the recapture is safe; here taking on d4 loses due to the queen trade and exposed king.
plans: Black should avoid material grabs and instead develop with Nd7 and Nf6, aiming for d5 or e4 outposts.

explains: In the resulting position, Black's structure has weaknesses (c4, d4) but Black has counterplay. The knights can go to d7 and f6, and rooks to d8 and g8, with h5-h4 to attack the kingside.
teaches: Even when the engine says the position is worse, human play can rely on king safety and attacking chances over static pawn structure.
plans: Black plays Nd7, Nf6, Rooks to d8 and g8, and pushes h5-h4 to open lines against the white king.

explains: Instead of the main move Bg7, Black can play Qc7, then after White castles, Black can play f5-f4 and Bg6 to break through on the kingside, giving Black attacking chances.
teaches: Choosing a less common move can lead to a different type of game with more attacking potential, even if objectively White is better.
plans: Black plays Qc7, castles, then f5-f4 and Bg6 to undermine White's kingside structure.

explains: In the Spanish, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5, Black chooses the Fianchetto Defense with ...g6 and ...Bg7 instead of main lines like ...a6 or ...Nf6. The bishop on g7 controls d4, making it hard for White to establish a strong center with d4.
teaches: When facing e4 e5, consider setups that challenge White's central pawn push d4. A fianchettoed bishop on g7 is a thematic way to restrain the d4 advance.
plans: Black aims to castle kingside and develop the bishop to g7, then challenge the center with ...d5 or ...exd4 depending on White's play.

explains: If White plays d4 immediately, Black takes with exd4, and after Bg5, Black should not weaken with f6 but instead play Be7, trading bishops. This leads to a safe position where Black has given up the dark-squared bishop but is not worse.
teaches: When facing an early d4 in the Spanish, it's often fine to trade off the dark-squared bishops to relieve pressure, even if it means a slight structural concession.
plans: After the bishop trade, Black recaptures with the queen, then develops the knight to f6 and castles, reaching an equal position.

explains: White's alternative plan is c3 followed by d4, which is more dangerous because White gets two central pawns. Black must be ready to handle that central pawn duo.
teaches: In the Spanish, White's c3 and d4 is a critical setup that gives a strong center. Black needs a concrete plan to challenge or undermine those pawns.
plans: Black will need to find a way to pressure the center, possibly with ...d5 or ...exd4 and piece play, depending on White's exact move order.

explains: The repertoire is built on the idea of playing ...g6 setups against many e4 e5 openings, not just the Spanish. This is a practical approach that avoids deep main-line theory.
teaches: A flexible setup like ...g6 can be applied across multiple openings, simplifying preparation and steering the game into positions you know well.
plans: Use the same ...g6 ideas against the Italian, Scotch, and other e4 e5 lines, adapting as needed.

explains: In this line of the Spanish, Black has played ...g6, leaving the pawn on g6 rather than g7, which is slightly awkward but acceptable. White's immediate d4 is a critical test, yet Black can still reach a playable, imbalanced position.
teaches: When facing a direct central push, look for active development (like Bg4) and counterplay in the center rather than passively defending.
plans: After d4, Black can play Bg4, and if White plays Nd2 and f3, Black can respond with c5, Qe3, and O-O-O, reaching a roughly equal position.

explains: Against the Spanish with c3, Black can fianchetto with Bg7, and after d4 exd4 cxd4, Black plays a6, the main move. White's bishop often ends up on b3, and Black's plan is to gain a tempo with ...Na5 if White plays d5.
teaches: In the Spanish, the placement of White's bishop (b3 vs c2) determines Black's response to d5: with the bishop on b3, ...Na5 gains a tempo; with it on c2, ...d5 is the way to challenge.
plans: Develop with ...Nf6, ...d6, and if White plays d5, meet it with ...Na5. If White plays Bc2, then ...d5 is the key move, leading to a complex but playable position.

explains: In the Spanish with ...g6, Black aims to break the pawn chain with ...c5. If White plays d6, Black can play ...d6, creating a potential passed pawn on the c-file, which is very comfortable for Black.
teaches: When facing a pawn chain, look for pawn breaks that undermine the base and create long-term structural advantages, such as a passed pawn.
plans: After ...c5, if White plays d6, Black plays ...d6 and then develops with ...Be6 and castles. If White plays Bc3, Black can play ...f6 to block the pawns.

explains: Against the Italian, the approach is different: Black should play the main lines with ...Bc5, as the ...g6 setup is riskier due to tactics on f7. In the Deuts Gambit (after c3 and d4), ...exd4 is bad, ...Nxd4 is losing, but ...Bxd4 is best.
teaches: Choose your opening setup based on the specific tactical features of the position; in the Italian, the f7 weakness makes the fianchetto less safe, so stick to classical development.
plans: Play ...Bc5 and enter the Giuoco Piano. If White plays the Deuts Gambit, capture on d4 with the bishop, ensuring a good position.

explains: In the Italian Game, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 d4, Black should meet the center challenge with …Bc5, entering the Giuoco Piano. If White plays the Evans Gambit (c3 and b4), Black should accept and maintain the extra pawn with accurate play.
teaches: Against the Evans Gambit, Black should aim to keep the extra pawn, as White often struggles to regain it if Black defends precisely.
plans: Develop naturally, castle kingside, and prepare to consolidate the extra pawn while neutralizing White's initiative.

explains: In the Giuoco Piano, White's c3 is a multi-purpose move: it prepares d4, allows the bishop to retreat to c2, enables Qb3, and supports b4 (the Evans Gambit). Black must be ready for various setups, but the main plan is to castle, place the bishop on a7, and prepare d5.
teaches: In the Italian, Black's typical plan is to castle kingside, put the bishop on a7, and aim for the central break d5, often after rerouting the knight to f4 via h5.
plans: Play ...O-O, ...Ba7, ...Be6, ...Nh5, ...Qf6, and ...Nf4, trading off the light-squared bishops and creating attacking chances.

explains: When White plays a4 to prevent b5, Black can still proceed with the standard setup. If White tries to occupy f5 with a knight (via Re1, Nf1, Ng3), Black should respond with g6 and h5 to start a kingside pawn storm.
teaches: In the Italian, Black should not be passive; if White aims for f5, Black can counter on the kingside with pawn advances, maintaining active play.
plans: Continue with ...O-O, ...Ba7, ...Be6, and then ...g6 and ...h5 to challenge White's kingside plans.

explains: In the setup with a bishop on a7, if White plays Nxe5, Black can punish with Qh4, as the rook has moved from f1. This tactical pattern is crucial to remember.
teaches: When the f1-rook is displaced, a knight on e5 can be vulnerable to a queen check on h4, winning material or creating a strong attack.
plans: After ...Nh5, if White plays Nxe5, respond with ...Qh4, exploiting the weakened kingside.

explains: In this Italian Game position, Black has set up a kingside attack with the knight on f4 and pawn on g6, preparing h5 and g5 to support it. The bishop on a7 is well placed, and White's typical sacrificial ideas against the knight are not effective because the rook on f1 can move away.
teaches: When building a kingside attack, it's important to have pieces supporting each other, like the knight on f4 being protected by the queen on f6, so that recaptures don't weaken your structure.
plans: Continue the attack with h5, g5, and possibly Kh8 and Rg8, or alternatively play for d5 to open the center and use the rook on e-file.

explains: Black has a choice between two plans: the direct kingside attack or playing for d5 in the center. If Black has a rook on e8, exchanging on e6 and recapturing with the rook keeps the f-pawn to cover f5, which is useful for controlling key squares.
teaches: When you have a choice between a wing attack and a central break, consider which plan gives you more long-term activity. Recapturing with the rook instead of the pawn can maintain control over important squares.
plans: If playing for d5, aim to play d5 at the right moment, and if White trades on d5, be ready to double rooks on the e-file.

explains: Against the Scotch Gambit (e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Bc4), Black should play the main line with Nf6, e5, d5, etc., which is forcing and theoretical.
teaches: In sharp openings like the Scotch Gambit, it's essential to know the main lines because they are forcing and any deviation can be punished.
plans: Follow the main line: Nf6, e5, d5, Bb5, Ne4, Nxd4, Bd7, Bxc6, bxc6, O-O, Bc5, and then respond to White's f3 with Ng5.

explains: After Nxd4, Black can play the sideline Qf6, which has been played by many strong players. The queen on f6 not only attacks the knight but also puts pressure on f2.
teaches: Sometimes a non-main move can be good if it has multiple purposes, like attacking a piece and creating threats against the opponent's weak points.
plans: After Qf6, if White plays c3, Black can transpose to a Bc5 Scotch with Qf6. Then develop with Nf6, Bc4, and instead of castling, play b6 to fianchetto the bishop, preparing queenside castling.

explains: In this Scotch Gambit line, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 d4, Black can avoid the main lines with an early b6, preparing to fianchetto the bishop. Since White hasn't played f4 yet, Black has time for this setup.
teaches: When facing aggressive openings, you can counter with a solid but flexible setup that avoids well-trodden paths. Delaying castling to complete development can be a valid strategy if the center is stable.
plans: Black will fianchetto the bishop on b7 and castle queenside, aiming for an aggressive but sound position.

explains: If White plays c3 to prevent Nb5, Black can respond with Bb4 and then Bc5, putting pressure on f2. The move c3 weakens White's control over d4 and gives Black a target.
teaches: Provoking a pawn move like c3 can restrict the opponent's knight from developing to its best square. Pressure on f2 is a common theme in these open games.
plans: Black will continue with h6 to prevent Bg5, then castle and play Ng7, maintaining pressure on the f2 square.

explains: If White plays Nb5, Black can ignore the attack on c7 because the knight is misplaced. Black can develop with Bc5, and if White takes on c7, the knight gets trapped after Kd8.
teaches: Sometimes you can allow a pawn to be attacked if the attacking piece becomes vulnerable. Tactical awareness of the opponent's piece activity is crucial.
plans: Black will continue developing, and if White takes on c7, Black will win the knight or gain a strong initiative.

explains: When White plays Qf6 after taking on c6, Black can choose to recapture with the b-pawn to keep the c-file open and maintain flexibility. This leads to a structure where Black aims for the d6 and e5 pawns.
teaches: Choosing which pawn to recapture with can have long-term structural implications. Keeping the c-file open can be useful for rook activity.
plans: Black will play d6, then a5, and aim to trade dark-squared bishops to reach a favorable endgame with a knight on f4.

explains: If White plays Qd2 instead, Black prefers to recapture with the c-pawn (dc6) to open the d-file for the rook. This allows Black to quickly play Rd8, pressuring the d4 pawn.
teaches: The placement of the opponent's queen can influence which pawn you recapture with. Opening a file for your rook is often worth a slight structural concession.
plans: Black will play Rd8, then Bf8 (or similar) to maintain pressure on d4 and prepare to challenge White's center.

explains: In the line with Bc5 and c3, White can sacrifice a pawn with Bxf2+ to expose the king. Black can accept the sacrifice, but must be careful about White's compensation.
teaches: Pawn sacrifices for initiative are common in open positions. You must evaluate whether the opponent's activity compensates for the material deficit.
