plans: After ...Nxg2 and ...c6, maintain the solid structure and prepare to challenge White's center with ...d5 or ...e5 breaks.

explains: In the main line with Bg5, Black again plays a5, Na6, and Nb4, not fearing d5 or e5. The knight on b4 is well placed, and White's bishop is misplaced if it goes to e4/d3.
teaches: The same setup (a5, Na6, Nb4) works against Bg5 as well, showing the value of a flexible, plan-based approach over memorizing specific lines.
plans: Continue with ...Nb4, and if White plays d5 or e5, exploit the resulting weaknesses (d5 square, misplaced bishop).

explains: In the Exchange Variation, White's setup differs based on the knight's placement: Ne2 prepares e4 and keeps the f-pawn free, while Nf3 signals a minority attack with b4. Black's setup is schematic: Be7, Nbd7, O-O, Re8, Nf8.
teaches: Recognize White's intentions by the knight's development: Ne2 indicates a central pawn push, Nf3 indicates a minority attack. Black's setup is flexible and can adapt to either plan.
plans: Develop with Be7, Nbd7, O-O, Re8, and Nf8, then respond to White's plan: if minority attack, consider ...a5 and dynamic counterplay; if e4, prepare to challenge the center.

explains: Against White's minority attack (Rb1, b4), Black plays ...a5 to slow it down. When White continues with a3, Black must fight dynamically, using the loose bishop on g5 (attacked twice) to play ...Nd4, distracting White from b4-b5.
teaches: In the Carlsbad structure, a loose bishop can be exploited tactically to create counterplay and divert White from the minority attack. Use tactical resources to gain time for your own plans.
plans: Play ...Nd4, and if White takes, recapture with the queen, defending e4. Then aim for ...f5, ...f4, and active rook play on the e-file, possibly with ...c5 or ...b6 to secure the queenside.

explains: In this Queen's Gambit Declined structure, Black has accepted the pawn on c4 and White is preparing to push e4. Black's plan involves counterplay against White's center, often with moves like b5, c5, or g6 to control key squares.
teaches: When facing a minority attack or central pawn push, it's crucial to have active counterplay rather than passively waiting. Weaknesses like a backward c-pawn are acceptable if you gain control over important central squares.
plans: Black can aim for moves like b6, c5, or g6 to undermine White's center and activate pieces. If White plays b5, Black should be ready with counterplay such as c5 or g6.

explains: After White plays h3 instead of Ra1, Black chooses g6 to control f5 and prepare a knight maneuver to e6-g7-f5. This setup also defends h7, preventing tactics on that diagonal.
teaches: A multi-purpose move like g6 can serve several functions: controlling key squares, preparing piece maneuvers, and defending weaknesses. It's important to consider all the benefits of a move before playing it.
plans: Black will develop the knight to e6, then g7, and finally f5, putting pressure on White's center and compensating for any minority attack.

explains: In the line where White plays b4, Black allows it and plays a6, forcing White to play a4 and open the a-file for Black's rook. Black then plays Bf5, fighting for the e4 and f5 squares.
teaches: Sometimes it's okay to allow the opponent's pawn advances if you can use them to open lines or create counterplay. The resulting weaknesses may be less important than the activity you gain.
plans: Black will continue to pressure White's center, possibly with moves like Nf5, and use the open a-file for the rook.

explains: After the exchange on b5 and d3, Black's knight reaches f5, and White's bishop is running out of squares. If White plays Bg5, Black can respond with h6, forcing the bishop to take or retreat.
teaches: When your pieces are well-placed, you can create threats that force the opponent to make concessions. A knight on f5 can be a powerful piece that restricts the opponent's bishop.
plans: Black will continue to improve piece placement, possibly bringing the knight to d6 or c4, and use the pressure on White's position to gain an advantage.

explains: In this Queen's Gambit Declined position, White has played e4, aiming for the Horwitz Attack. The key is to keep flexibility and avoid allowing White's knight to reach e4 and exchange on g5. Castling is a solid, flexible move that doesn't commit to a specific plan.
teaches: When facing flexible setups, prioritize moves that maintain options and avoid weakening your structure. Castling early is often a good way to improve king safety without committing to a pawn structure.
plans: After castling, Black will continue with b6 and Bb7, developing the bishop to the long diagonal, regardless of whether White plays Bf4 or Bg5.

explains: If White plays Bg5, Black should not play h6 immediately because the bishop is not on g5. Instead, Black can proceed with b6, developing the bishop to b7. The setup is the same whether White plays Bf4 or Bg5.
teaches: Don't make pawn moves like h6 unless they are necessary to prevent a pin or attack. Develop pieces according to your plan, not in reaction to every threat.
plans: Black will continue with Bb7 and c5, establishing the typical Tartakower structure.

explains: If White plays Bd3, Black can take on c4 and then play Ba6, trading off the light-squared bishop. This is a simple way to solve the problem of the bishop on c8, which is often passive.
teaches: When your bishop is blocked by your own pawns, look for opportunities to trade it off or activate it. Taking on c4 and then playing Ba6 is a common method in the QGD.
plans: After Ba6, Black will develop normally, aiming for the standard structure with c5.

explains: In the main line, White plays cxd5. If Black recaptures with the e-pawn, then b6 is wasted, and Ba6 can be met by Bxa6. Therefore, Black should play Nxd5, and after White takes the knight, recapture with the queen to keep the bishop's diagonal open.
teaches: When recapturing, consider which piece should do the recapturing to maintain flexibility and avoid blocking your own pieces. Here, recapturing with the queen keeps the bishop's diagonal open.
plans: After Qxd5, Black will play c5, defending c7 and opening the queenside, then follow with Bb7.

explains: In the Tartakower Defense, if White plays cxd5, Black recaptures with the knight. If White plays Bd3, Black should not take on c4 because the bishop can retreat to g3. Instead, Black plays Bb7, then Nbd7, and c5, sticking to the standard structure.
teaches: The correct response to a capture depends on the position of the pieces. In some lines, taking on c4 is good; in others, it allows the bishop to retreat to a better square. Always evaluate the resulting position.
plans: Black will develop with Bb7, Nbd7, and c5, aiming for the typical Tartakower structure.

explains: The critical line is when White plays Be2, and after Black takes on c4, White takes on f6. This forces Black to play e5, allowing White to play b4, preventing c5. Black must then play c6 to stop b5, and later a5 to challenge White's queenside pawns.
teaches: When your opponent creates a pawn majority or a strong pawn chain, you must find ways to counter it. Here, c6 and a5 are essential to prevent White from gaining space and to create counterplay.
plans: Black will play c6, then a5, and if White plays a3, Black can play b5 to close the position and reroute the bishop to a better diagonal.

explains: After White plays b4 to prevent c5, Black plays c6 to stop b5, then a5 to prepare b5, aiming to close the queenside and keep the position solid.
teaches: When White tries to prevent your freeing break, use pawn moves to secure your own space and prepare the break anyway.
plans: Play b5 to shut down the queenside, then develop the bishop to the long diagonal and the knight to d7.

explains: In the Tartakower structure, after White plays Ne5, Black plays cxd4, exd4, Be7, d5, and then ...d4, accepting a weak b6 pawn but gaining active piece play.
teaches: Sometimes you must accept a structural weakness to activate your pieces and create counterplay.
plans: Play Nc5, Nd7, Rc8, and Nc5 to challenge the knight on e5 and neutralize White's pressure.

explains: When White takes on f6, Black recaptures with the bishop, keeping the bishop on f8, which makes e5 an easy freeing move later.
teaches: Recapturing with the right piece can preserve flexibility and make future breaks easier.
plans: Play c6 to support the center, then develop the knight to d7 and prepare e5, possibly after exchanging on c4 to avoid an isolated queen's pawn.

explains: Before playing e5, Black exchanges on c4 to eliminate White's ability to take on d5 and isolate the pawn, then plays e5 with a comfortable position.
teaches: Exchange pawns to remove tactical threats before making a central break.
plans: After e5, if White plays h3, recapture on d4 and play Nb6, aiming for a position with the bishop pair against an IQP.

explains: After e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 h4 g4 Ne5 h5, Black's move …d6 attacks the knight and the g4-pawn. White's only reasonable response is to retreat the knight to d3, since blocking the bishop with a piece would be poor. The main line continues Nxd3 (or similar) and after …Nf6 Nxf6+ Qxf6 Nc3, White defends e4 and the position is equal in material (seven points each). White's pawn structure is arguably better, and although White's king is exposed, Black's king is also far from castling, making it double-edged.
teaches: In the King's Gambit, when Black returns the gambit pawn, White should often accept it and aim for a solid central setup, as material equality with a better pawn structure can be favorable.
plans: White should aim to consolidate the center, develop pieces, and put pressure on Black's weaknesses, especially the f4-pawn, while keeping the king safe.

explains: In the line after …d6, White can also play Bb5, pinning the knight on e5. Black's most popular response is …Kd8, breaking the pin, after which White captures on c6 and plays Qf3. Black may try ...Rg8 to threaten ...Bg4, but White can respond with d3 and then move the queen. The position remains equal, with neither side having full king safety or a perfect pawn structure, and the outcome depends on strategic play.
teaches: When facing a pin, it's often useful to move the king to break it, even if it delays castling, as long as the position remains tenable.
plans: White should continue developing, aiming to exploit Black's lack of king safety and the limited scope of Black's light-squared bishop, while Black should seek active counterplay.

explains: In the position after …d6, White can also consider Nxg4, winning back the pawn, but the main line is Nd3. Black's move …d6 is considered risky because it allows White to gain time and central control. Strong players have used it, but the main line is more precise.
teaches: When you have an extra pawn in the King's Gambit, it's often better to try to keep it rather than return it voluntarily, as the pawn can be a long-term asset.
plans: White should aim to maintain the extra pawn and build a strong center, while Black should seek active piece play to compensate.

explains: After …h5, Black protects the g4-pawn but leaves weaknesses. White can play Bc4, attacking f7, the main weakness. Black has two defenses: …Nh6 or …Rh7. The move …Rh7 is poor because after d4, White can sacrifice two pieces for a rook and emerge with a material advantage. For example, after …d6 Nxf7 Rxf7 Bxf7+ Kxf7 Bxf4, White has seven points to Black's six, and White stands better.
teaches: In open positions, attacking the weakest point (often f7) can create tactical opportunities, and sacrificing pieces for a rook can be favorable if the resulting material balance is in your favor.
plans: White should continue to pressure f7 and exploit Black's weakened kingside, while Black must find accurate defenses to avoid material loss.

explains: After …h5 Bc4, Black's better defense is …Nh6. White then plays d4, opening the center, which is the key idea of the King's Gambit: to create a broad pawn center after removing Black's e5-pawn. Black plays …d6, and White continues g3 (or similar), with the main line being …Be7. The move …g3? is bad because it gives White a huge edge, as Black has no attack and White can round up the weaknesses and pressure f7.
teaches: In the King's Gambit, White's goal is to build a strong center with pawns on d4 and e4, and to use that central control to launch an attack. Black must avoid weakening moves that give White a free hand.
plans: White should aim to consolidate the center, develop pieces, and prepare an attack on Black's king, while Black should try to undermine White's center and create counterplay.

explains: The Rosenthal Defense (Queen to e7) is a sounder sideline for Black. It puts pressure on the e4 pawn and often leads to queen exchanges, which dampens White's attacking ideas. After the exchanges, the position is normal, but Black's pawn structure is weak (the f4, g5, h5 pawns are targets).
teaches: Exchanging queens can be a good way to neutralize an aggressive opponent's attacking plans, but you must be careful about resulting pawn weaknesses.
plans: White can target Black's weak pawns, especially f4, and use the f3 square for a knight. Black must defend these weaknesses carefully.

explains: Another sideline after g5 is Bishop to g7 (the Paulsen Defense), which puts pressure on the knight. This is a sideline for a reason, as it doesn't address Black's fundamental issues.
teaches: When choosing a defense, prioritize moves that address the key weaknesses and maintain activity, rather than just developing pieces.
plans: White should continue with natural development and maintain pressure on Black's position.

explains: After e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 h4 g4 Ne5, Black's …Qe7 is dubious because White gets a strong outpost on e5 or an even bigger target if the pawn moves. White's pieces can easily come to the center, with f3 as a perfect square for the knight.
teaches: In sharp gambit lines, central outposts and piece activity often outweigh material. A queen move that doesn't challenge the opponent's plan can leave you worse.
plans: White should aim to consolidate the center, possibly with d4, and use the f3 square for the knight to pressure Black's position.

explains: In the line after d4 Bxd4 Qxd4 d6 Nc3, White has not regained the pawn but has a favorable position: the f4 pawn can be rounded up, and White can castle long. Black's pawn on g4 is weak, and if Black plays ...d5, White can respond with e5, keeping the center closed.
teaches: Sometimes it's worth sacrificing a pawn for long-term positional compensation, such as a safer king, better pawn structure, and active pieces.
plans: White should aim to capture the f4 pawn, castle long, and possibly play f5 to liquidate the isolated king's pawn if Black's king stays in the center.

explains: In the Kieseritzky Gambit, after …Nf6 (Berlin Defense), the move Nxg4 is too risky because after …Nxe4 d3, Black gets good play, and in many variations Black can win the rook but then lose, so it's a bluff. The main move is Nc3 or d4, with Nc3 being solid.
teaches: Avoid speculative sacrifices that rely on the opponent not knowing the theory. In sharp openings, it's better to play principled moves that maintain the initiative without unnecessary risk.
plans: White should choose a solid continuation like Nc3, keeping the center stable and preparing to develop, rather than grabbing the g4 pawn.

explains: In the main line after Nc3, if Black plays …Nxg4, White can play Nxe4, and if Black plays …d5, White can respond with Ng3, exchanging the awkward knight. After …Bxf4 Qe7 Be2, Black's best is …Rg8, because the knight on g3 is hanging due to the pin on the bishop. If Black takes on h1, White has a strong move Bg5, which almost forces the win of the queen.
teaches: In tactical positions, pins and discovered attacks can lead to decisive material gains. Even if the opponent wins a rook, a strong move like Bg5 can turn the tables.
plans: White should aim to maintain the pin and use the threat of Bg5 to win material or force a favorable simplification.

explains: In this Kieseritzky Gambit position, the knight on e5 is hanging because the bishop on c4 is pinned by the rook on h7. If Black plays Be2, then Nxh1 wins material, but White has a strong resource: Bg5, which threatens to win the queen by attacking the pinned knight and the queen simultaneously.
teaches: When a piece is pinned, it cannot defend other pieces. Use tactical motifs like pins to create threats that overload the opponent's defenses.
plans: After Be2 Nxh1, White should play Bg5, forcing Black to deal with the threat of winning the queen. If Black plays h6, White can continue with Nf6+ or other aggressive moves to maintain the initiative.

explains: Black has several defensive tries after Bg5, such as Qb4+ or Qa5, but White can meet them with c3 and Nf6+ checks, leading to a decisive attack. The engine suggests h6 as best, but it is not human-friendly; White's attack is overwhelming.
teaches: In sharp tactical positions, concrete calculation is essential. Even if the engine finds a defense, it may be impractical for humans; trust the attack when the opponent's king is exposed.
plans: If Black tries to defend the queen, White should continue with checks and threats, such as Nf6+ and Bxe7, to win material or deliver mate.

explains: The line with Nxd4 is not good for White. After Nxg4 is a sideline, and Nxe4 leads to a position where Black can choose to take on h1 or play Rg8, leaving White with a poor position. The best move is Bxg3, exchanging pieces, but Black ends up with a safer king and better pawn structure.
teaches: When considering a gambit, ensure that the compensation is real. If the opponent can return material and reach a safe position, the gambit may be unsound.
plans: White should avoid the Nxd4 line and instead play the main move Bc4, which gives Black less time to consolidate.

explains: After …Nf6 (the Berlin defense), if White plays d4 instead of Bc4, Black can force the exchange of White's e-pawn for Black's doubled f-pawn, which is unfavorable for White. This allows Black to eliminate his main weakness and leaves White with a worse position.
teaches: In the King's Gambit, the center pawns are valuable. Trading your central pawn for a doubled pawn is usually bad because it relieves the opponent's weakness and gives up central control.
plans: White should play the main move Bc4, which attacks f7 and prevents Black from playing d6 easily. Black's best response is d5, similar to the Two Knights Defense, to counterattack in the center.

explains: In the main line of the Kieseritzky Gambit, Bc4 is the critical move because it attacks f7, forcing Black to respond. Black's best is d5, challenging the bishop and opening lines for development. Other moves like Bd6 or Nc6 are possible but inferior.
teaches: In sharp openings, the main move is often the one that creates immediate threats and limits the opponent's options. Attack the weakest point (f7) to gain time.
plans: After Bc4 d5, the game continues with Bxd5 or other moves, leading to complex play. White should aim to maintain pressure on f7 and develop quickly.

explains: In the Kieseritzky Gambit, Bc4 is the main move because it immediately attacks f7, preventing Black from playing d6. Black's best response is d5, mirroring the Italian Game's knight attack on f7.
teaches: When your bishop attacks a weak point like f7, it restricts the opponent's development options. Always consider such direct threats before developing further.
plans: After d5, Black can play Bd6 to attack the knight on e4, while White aims to castle and prepare an attack on the kingside.

explains: In the main line after Bc4 d5, Black castles, and White can choose between taking on f4 with the bishop or the rook. Taking with the rook is safer because it avoids the dangerous line where Black's queen takes on h4 and White lacks the resource g3.
teaches: When deciding which piece to recapture with, consider the resulting tactical motifs. A recapture that allows a strong defensive move like g3 is often preferable to one that leaves your king exposed.
plans: After Rxf4, White can develop pieces, keep the queen eyeing g4, and aim to solidify the center before launching an attack.

explains: Taking with the bishop on f4 is too risky because after Qxh4, Black has Bh6, and White has no good defense against the threats, often losing the queen. The engine evaluates such lines as clearly better for Black.
teaches: Before grabbing material, check if the opponent can create a decisive attack. If your king is exposed and the opponent can bring pieces to bear, material may not compensate.
plans: Avoid this line; instead, prefer the safer recapture with the rook.

explains: After the safer recapture, White is an exchange down but has the bishop pair and active pieces. The engine gives Black a slight edge, but White's position is playable, with chances to attack if Black errs.
teaches: In gambit lines, being down material is acceptable if you have compensation in activity and attacking chances. The opponent must play precisely to convert.
plans: White should continue developing, keep the queen pressuring g4, and look for opportunities to exploit Black's weaknesses.

explains: The Kieseritzky Gambit is a highly theoretical line where Black has many chances to go wrong. White's practical chances come from the pressure Black faces over the next 10-15 moves.
teaches: When playing sharp gambits, rely on the opponent's potential mistakes. Even if the engine says the position is better for Black, practical play can favor the attacker.
plans: Prepare the main lines and be ready to punish any inaccuracies from Black.

explains: This position arises from the main line of the Kieseritzky Gambit, a highly theoretical branch of the King's Gambit. Black's setup with ...h5 and ...Bh6 is the most solid defensive arrangement, but every move offers chances for Black to err.
teaches: In sharp gambit lines, the defender must be precise for many moves; one inaccuracy can be punished. The attacker should be patient and wait for that mistake.
plans: White continues developing and building pressure, aiming to exploit any slip in Black's precise defensive sequence.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: In the Van der Wiel Attack, Nc3 serves a dual purpose: it defends the e4 square, so that when White later plays g4, the bishop on f5 cannot retreat to e4, and it supports the central pawn structure. However, this move also blocks the c2-pawn, which is a significant drawback because Black's main pawn break c5 can no longer be met by c3.
teaches: When choosing a developing move, consider both its defensive benefits and how it affects your ability to respond to your opponent's typical pawn breaks. A move that strengthens one part of the center may weaken another.
plans: White aims to play g4 to harass the bishop, while Black should prioritize the c5 break to undermine White's center.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: If White plays Nc3 without following up with the aggressive g4 plan, Black can quickly achieve a comfortable position. For example, if White develops normally with Nf3 and Be3, Black can play c5, Nc6, and Qc7, and even have tactical ideas like Bxc2 followed by d4 to win back the piece.
teaches: When your opponent plays a move that has a specific aggressive idea, if they fail to follow through, you should be alert to seize the initiative and exploit the lack of pressure.
plans: Black should develop harmoniously, aim for c5, and look for tactical opportunities to punish White's slow play.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: Black has a choice after Nc3: either play e6, allowing White's plan of g4, or wait with moves like Qb6 or a6 to avoid committing the bishop. If Black delays e6 and White plays g4, the bishop can retreat to d7, transposing to a French Defense structure where White's g4 is less effective.
teaches: When facing a plan that targets a piece, you can either accept the challenge or find a way to sidestep it. Sometimes delaying a pawn move can change the nature of the position to one you prefer.
plans: Black can choose between e6 (entering the main line) or a waiting move like Qb6, depending on the desired type of position.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: In the main line, after e6, White plays g4, forcing the bishop to g6. White then prepares h4-h5 with the maneuver Ne2-f4. The knight on f4 is crucial because it threatens Nxg6, and if Black recaptures with the f-pawn, White can play Bd3 and Qf3, attacking the weak f-pawn and winning material.
teaches: A well-placed knight can create a decisive threat that forces weaknesses in the opponent's pawn structure. When a piece is pinned to a weakness, the opponent's defensive options become limited.
plans: White will continue with h4-h5 to provoke a weakness, while Black must find a way to avoid allowing Nxg6 and the subsequent attack.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: After g4 Bg6, White threatens Nf4, attacking the bishop. If Black plays h6 or h5, White can take on g6, forcing Black to recapture with the f-pawn, which weakens the kingside and leaves the h-pawn vulnerable. Then White plays Bd3, attacking the h-pawn, and if Black defends with Qf7, White plays Qf3, creating a decisive attack.
teaches: When a bishop is pinned or attacked, forcing the opponent to recapture with a pawn can create weaknesses. Look for tactical sequences that exploit the resulting weak squares and open lines.
plans: White aims to play Nf4, forcing the bishop to retreat, then exploit the weakened kingside with Bd3 and Qf3.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: Black's most active response is c5, immediately attacking White's d4 pawn. If White plays Nf4, Black plays Nc6, gaining a tempo against the queen when it recaptures on d4. After h4 and h5, White plays Nf4, forcing the bishop back, and then White wins the h-pawn. Black gets compensation: the knight on f4 is offside, White's king is unsafe, and Black has a strong pawn on d4.
teaches: When giving up a pawn, seek compensation in dynamic factors: piece activity, king safety, and a strong central pawn. A misplaced knight can be a long-term weakness.
plans: Black will castle queenside, use the d4 pawn to restrict White's pieces, and target the weak g7 pawn if White captures on h5.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: In this Caro-Kann advance with Nc3, White's g4 is a key idea, but the presence of the knight on c3 controls e4, so Black cannot play Bg4. The bishop on f5 is a target; White wants to gain time against it and eventually trap it with h4-h5.
teaches: When a knight on c3 controls e4, Black's bishop cannot safely go to g4. White's g4 is a typical way to challenge the bishop, but the bishop can retreat to g6 if h4 is not yet played.
plans: White aims to play h4 and then Nf4, attacking the bishop on g6, forcing ...Bxf4 or ...gxf4, ruining Black's kingside structure. Black should play actively with ...c5 to counter in the center.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: Black's main move is ...e6, which is best because it prevents the bishop from retreating to d7 and keeps the position solid. After ...e6, White plays g4, and the bishop must go to g6. White then plays Nge2, preparing Nf4 to attack the bishop.
teaches: In this structure, ...e6 is the most natural developing move, but it allows White to gain time against the bishop. The knight on e2 is heading to f4 to increase pressure on the bishop on g6.
plans: Black should not waste time; the most active plan is ...c5, attacking d4, because the c3 knight blocks the c2 pawn, leaving d4 vulnerable. Black can follow with ...Nc6 and ...Qc7, pressuring e5.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: White must play h4 before Nf4, because if White plays Nf4 immediately, Black can play ...cxd4, and after Qxd4, ...Nc6 wins a tempo, leaving White's position losing. So h4 is necessary to make Nf4 a real threat.
teaches: Sometimes a move like h4 is a prerequisite for a later threat; playing the threat too early allows the opponent to counter in the center. Timing is crucial.
plans: After h4, White threatens Nf4, so Black must respond. Black's ...c5 is still the best way to create counterplay.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: White has an alternative in Be3, which is tricky: it defends d4, attacks the c5 pawn, and prepares to recapture on d4 with the bishop if Black takes. It also frees d4 for the knight on e2, and later White can play Bb5 with tempo.
teaches: A move like Be3 can serve multiple purposes: defense, attack, and preparation for piece maneuvers. It's important to see the hidden ideas behind such moves.
plans: If Black allows ...dxc5, White can play Nd4 followed by Bb5, which is almost decisive. Black must be careful not to fall into this trap.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: White's plan with Bc1–e3 is to pressure the c5 pawn and, if Black takes on d4, recapture with the bishop and then bring the knight to d4, followed by Bb5 with tempo. This exploits the weakened a4–e8 diagonal, which Black cannot defend adequately even with Nc6 because that knight can be captured.
teaches: When a pawn chain gives you a space advantage, look for ways to use the extra space to transfer pieces to strong central outposts (like d4) and create tactical threats along open diagonals.
plans: White aims to play dxc5, then Nd4, and Bb5, pressuring Black's king side and the weakened diagonal. Black must find a solid defensive setup to avoid falling into these threats.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: After White takes on c5 and Black recaptures with the knight, White's knight goes to d4, creating threats along the a4–e8 diagonal. Black must respond with Nd7, blocking the diagonal and putting pressure on c5. The position remains balanced, with Black having central pawns that help compensate for the pawn structure.
teaches: When your opponent has a strong outpost, you often need to challenge it directly or block the lines that give it power. Central pawns can be a valuable asset in maintaining equality.
plans: Black plays Nd7, then b4 to defend the c5 pawn, followed by Be7 and h6 (or a5) to stabilize the position. The game is roughly equal, and Black should aim to complete development and castle.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: In the Van der Wiel Attack, after e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nc3 e6 g4 Bg6 Nge2 c5, Black should prefer …Ne7 over …Nc6. The knight on e7 supports the c5 break and avoids immediate pressure on d4.
teaches: When facing a space-gaining advance, develop pieces to squares that support central pawn breaks and avoid creating targets for the opponent's pieces.
plans: Black aims to play ...cxd4 and ...Nec6, pressuring e5 and preparing ...Nd7 to win the e5 pawn.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: After White plays f4 to defend e5, Black plays ...Be7, fixing White's pawn structure. White's pawns on e5 and f4 become targets, and Black has good piece play.
teaches: Fixing the opponent's pawn structure can create long-term weaknesses, even if the opponent gains space.
plans: Black will continue with ...Nh5 or ...h5 to challenge the g4 pawn, aiming to undermine White's center.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: The move ...h5 is the most common reply, leading to a justified pawn sacrifice. White plays Nf4, and if Black tries to save the h5 pawn, White can take on g6 and win. Black must retreat the bishop, allowing Nxh5.
teaches: Sometimes it is correct to sacrifice a pawn to activate pieces and create long-term compensation, especially when the opponent's knight becomes offside.
plans: Black accepts the pawn sacrifice, gaining time and harmonious piece play, with the knight on h5 offside.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: After the pawn sacrifice, Black is equal despite being down a pawn. The knight on h5 is offside, and Black gains time. All of Black's pieces work harmoniously.
teaches: Material is not the only factor; piece activity and coordination can compensate for a pawn deficit.
plans: Black will develop quickly, targeting White's center and exploiting the misplaced knight.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: The sideline g5 is playable but committal, giving away the f5 square. If White plays g5, Black can play …cxd4, and if Qxd4, then …Nc6 wins a huge tempo.
teaches: Avoid weakening key squares like f5 unless you have concrete compensation; such moves can give the opponent long-term targets.
plans: Black gains a tempo and can develop with ...Ne7-f5, putting pressure on White's center.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: After …Nc6, White often plays Bb5, pinning the knight, but the critical move is Bg2, which is more challenging. The main line is Bb5, but Bg2 is the most interesting option.
teaches: In sharp openings, the most critical moves are often those that develop with a threat or prepare a central break, even if they are not the most common.
plans: Black must be prepared for both Bb5 and Bg2, as they lead to different types of positions.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: The move Nxg7+ is a bad move for White. After …Kf8, the knight must retreat, and Black wins the e5 pawn. White's position becomes very dangerous, with many tactical threats.
teaches: Avoid greedy captures that leave your pieces hanging; calculate the consequences before taking material.
plans: Black will pick up the e5 pawn and maintain a strong initiative, with White's pieces scattered.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: In the line with Nxg7+, after …Kf8 Nh5 d4 Na6? (or similar), White's knight is trapped, and Black wins the e5 pawn. Even with best play, White is close to equal but slightly worse, and any mistake is fatal.
teaches: When the opponent's pieces are offside, look for ways to trap them or win material while maintaining the initiative.
plans: Black will continue to attack White's weaknesses, especially the e5 pawn, and create threats against the king.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: In this Caro-Kann Advance with Nc3, after ...c5, White has several tries. Taking on g7 with the knight is a mistake because Black can respond with ...Nb5, ...a6, ...Na3, ...Ne5, and ...Rh3, leading to a decisive attack. The position is very problematic for White, so this move is easily refuted.
teaches: When a piece captures a pawn on g7, it can become trapped or the king can be exposed. Always check if the capturing piece can be harassed or if the opponent can generate a strong initiative.
plans: Black should aim to exploit the misplaced knight and the open h-file, with moves like ...Rh3 and ...d3 to break through.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: White's favorite move is Bg2, which prevents Black's typical ...d4 and ...Qd5 ideas. After Bg2, Black should play ...Kf8 to defend, and then develop with ...Bf4, ...Rc8, ...Bg3, and ...Ng7. The bishop on g2 strengthens White's position because it controls the d5 square and supports the e5 pawn, making it mobile.
teaches: A fianchettoed bishop can be a powerful defensive and offensive piece, especially when it controls key central squares and supports a pawn break.
plans: White can aim for ideas like Rh3, Qd2, and if the d5 pawn falls, the e-pawn becomes mobile with threats like Qf3 or Nf4-e6. Black must be careful about tactics on d5 and e6.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: After Bg2 and ...Kf8, if White plays Bg5, Black should not play ...Qb6 because of Nf4 and e6 ideas. Instead, Black should retreat the bishop to e7. Even though Black is technically down material, this is the best way to defend because the king on f8 is vulnerable to tactics on d5 and e6.
teaches: When your king is stuck in the center, prioritize safety and piece coordination over material. Avoid moves that loosen your position or allow tactical shots.
plans: Black should aim to complete development and castle quickly, while keeping an eye on the d5 and e6 squares.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: The alternative Bg5 is also playable. Against Bg5, Black can play ...Qb6, and if White plays Na4, Black has tactics with ...Bxb4+ and ...Qxb2. White must defend with Qd2, and then Black can play ...Rb1, ...Qxc2, ...Qxc2, ...Bxc2, and if White takes on b7, ...Nxe5 wins. So Bg5 is not dangerous for Black.
teaches: When a bishop pins a knight, the pinned piece can often be attacked with tempo, and the defender must be careful about tactics on the b-file and the f2 square.
plans: Black can aim to create counterplay on the queenside and exploit the pin on the knight.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: After Bb5, ...Qc7, White plays Qf3 to defend against ...d4. Black castles queenside, which is good because Qxf7 doesn't work due to ...d4. White then plays Nxg7, picking up a second pawn, but Black has great compensation with ...Ne7, ...Bg5, and ...d4, sacrificing an exchange and trading queens. Black's pieces and the d4 pawn are superior.
teaches: Sometimes it's worth sacrificing material to activate your pieces and create a strong pawn center. Even when down an exchange, dynamic factors can outweigh the material deficit.
plans: Black should aim to trade queens and use the d4 pawn and active pieces to create a winning endgame or middlegame attack.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: In this line, black sacrifices the exchange and trades queens, relying on the superior pawn structure and piece activity to compensate. The d4 pawn is strong, and black's pieces are well placed.
teaches: When sacrificing the exchange, ensure you have concrete compensation: active pieces, a strong pawn center, or attacking chances.
plans: Black should focus on exploiting the weak white pawns and the offside knight, while maintaining pressure on the c2 pawn.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: After the queens are traded and the exchange is sacrificed, black has a very dangerous endgame with the bishop pair and a potential passed pawn. White's knight is offside, and any pawn weakness could be fatal.
teaches: In endgames, the bishop pair and a passed pawn can outweigh a material deficit if the opponent's pieces are poorly placed.
plans: Black should aim to create a passed pawn on the c-file, supported by the bishops, and target the weak white pawns.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: After e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nc3 e6 g4 Bg6 Nge2 c5, black has alternatives to c5, such as f6 and Ne7. The move f6 is weak because it allows white a massive space advantage after h4 and f4, while Ne7 is more flexible, preparing to meet h4 with h5 and occupy f5.
teaches: When choosing a setup, consider flexibility and the opponent's possible plans. Avoid moves that give the opponent a free space advantage.
plans: If black plays Ne7, white should avoid h4 and instead play Nf4, leading to similar positions as the main line. Black must be prepared to handle the pressure.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: In the line with Ne7, after Nf4, black can play c5 and then Nd7, aiming to provoke f3 and then play a6 to prevent the knight from using d4. The bishop is not trapped because it can retreat to e4.
teaches: In sharp positions, look for tactical resources like a6 to restrict the opponent's knight, and be willing to play cold-bloodedly to maintain the initiative.
plans: Black should continue with h5, Be4, provoking f3, then a6, forcing the knight to d6, after which black can capture and maintain pressure.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: In this line, after g4 Bg6, if Black plays Nd7, White can try to provoke weaknesses with h5 and Bf3. Black can respond with a6, making the bishop safe because if the knight takes on d4, the queen recaptures and both bishops are attacking f3 and c2.
teaches: When a piece is attacked, look for counterattacks or ways to keep it defended rather than immediately retreating or giving it up.
plans: Black can continue with Nd6, and after White takes, Black plays g5 to drive the knight back, then h6 to eventually give up the bishop while maintaining a solid pawn structure.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: After the bishop is given up, Black has all pawns intact while White has sacrificed two or three pawns. The position is equal, but Black's pawns and activity give a slight preference.
teaches: Material imbalances can be compensated by pawn structure and piece activity; sometimes giving up a piece for a lasting pawn advantage is fine.
plans: Black should defend the d6 pawn and consider castling, with ideas like f5 and ef5 to open lines.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: Against the Van der Wiel, Black has alternatives to e6. Playing h5 to prevent g4 leads to a weakened g5 square and a bad version of the Tal variation. White can then play Bd3, forcing the trade of the light-squared bishop, and later Nf3 to exploit the weak g5 square.
teaches: Preventing a pawn push like g4 can create permanent weaknesses; sometimes it's better to allow the push and handle it.
plans: If Black plays h5, White should play Bd3, and after Black takes, White recaptures with the queen, then Nf3, targeting g5. Black's knight on h6 heading to f5 can be met by White's plan to exchange it.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: In the line with h5, Black's knight on f5 is active, but White can play Ne2 to exchange the knight on c3 for Black's active piece. If Black tries h4 to keep the knight, the h4 pawn becomes a permanent weakness, tying down Black's pieces.
teaches: When a piece is active but can be exchanged, it's often better to trade it off than to keep it at the cost of a weak pawn.
plans: White will play Ne2, Ng3, and then solidify the kingside with g3 and hg3, preventing Black's pawn breaks.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: Alternatives to e6 include a6 and Qb6, which invite a French Defense. If White plays g4, Black can enter a French with a white pawn on g4, which may be better for Black than the normal French. However, White can also switch plans and punish Qb6 with Bd3, attacking the d4 pawn and gaining a lead in development.
teaches: When your opponent makes a waiting move, consider changing your plan to exploit the loss of time.
plans: Against Qb6, White should play Bd3, and if Black takes on d4, White plays Nf3, attacking the queen and the bishop, gaining time.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: After Black plays Qb6 in the Van der Wiel, White should not automatically play g4. Instead, Bd3 is strong because the d4 pawn is protected; if Black takes on d4, the queen gets chased by Nf3 and loses time while the f5 bishop is also hanging.
teaches: When the opponent plays a queen move that attacks a pawn, consider whether the pawn is truly weak. Often the queen becomes a target and you can gain time by developing with tempo.
plans: Play Bd3, and if Black takes on d4, follow up with Nf3 attacking the queen, then continue development. If Black doesn't take, trade bishops and proceed with normal development.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: In the line with Bd3, if Black takes on d3 with the queen, White recaptures with the c-pawn, and after ...e6, White can play Ng2, reaching a favorable version of the French where Black's queen is misplaced on d3.
teaches: Sometimes allowing the opponent to win a pawn is fine if you get a lead in development and a better pawn structure. Compare the activity of pieces rather than counting material.
plans: Continue with Ng2, aiming to castle and exploit the lead in development.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: Against the waiting move ...a6, White can also consider g4 to transpose into a French, but a more interesting idea is Be3, which makes it hard for Black to play ...c5. If Black then plays ...e6, White can proceed with g4 and Ng2, reaching a position where Black's ...a6 is not useful.
teaches: When the opponent plays a waiting move, look for moves that restrict their main freeing break. Here Be3 prevents ...c5, so Black is forced into a passive setup.
plans: After Be3 and ...e6, play g4 and Ng2, transposing to a favorable version of the Van der Wiel where Black's ...a6 is a wasted move.

opening: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Van der Wiel Attack
explains: The Van der Wiel Attack leads to positions where strategic understanding and attacking skill matter more than rote memorization. Black must be very precise to avoid losing, and the line with Bg2 offers rich attacking chances.
teaches: To master an opening, study model games and analyze the typical plans and attacking motifs, not just the moves. This builds the 'feel' needed to handle unfamiliar positions.
plans: Study games from the Van der Wiel, especially those with Bg2, to learn the typical attacking patterns and strategic ideas.

explains: In this line, White aims for a Benoni structure without Black's d6 pawn, which means White's e4-e5 break is not hindered. This is an improvement over the standard Benoni where the d6 pawn blocks that expansion.
teaches: When the opponent lacks a central pawn that normally restrains your pawn break, prioritize that break as a key plan.
plans: Develop naturally and prepare e4-e5, using the absence of d6 to gain space.

explains: White also seeks an Open Sicilian structure with an open d-file and a lead in development. In the normal Open Sicilian, Black's d6 pawn prevents queen recaptures on d4, but here that pawn is absent, so White can recapture with the queen and avoid losing tempo to Nc6.
teaches: In structures where the opponent lacks a key defensive pawn, consider recaptures that would normally be bad due to tempo loss.
plans: After ...cxd4, recapture with the queen to maintain development advantage and prevent ...Nc6 with tempo.

explains: White's rule is to delay d4 or e4 until Black commits in the center. By playing Nf3 first, White can respond appropriately to Black's central pawn moves, gaining more information about Black's setup.
teaches: In flexible opening positions, wait for the opponent to commit before choosing your central pawn break.
plans: Play Nf3, then meet ...e6 or ...c5 with d4, and if Black delays, proceed with d4 anyway.

explains: If Black plays ...e6 and ...c5, White heads for a Sicilian-type position by playing e4 instead of taking on c5. After ...cxd4, White recaptures with the queen, and if ...Nc6, White trades, leaving Black with a worse pawn structure and White with a development lead.
teaches: In Open Sicilian structures without queens, keeping the king in the center is safe, and a lead in development is more important than material.
plans: Develop pieces to natural squares like Be3, Nf3, and consider castling queenside to use the d-file and pressure d5.

explains: In the resulting position, Black must play ...a6 to prevent Nb5, and then White can build pressure on the d5 square, potentially creating a passed pawn. Black's light-squared bishop is often blocked, so White can target the e6 square.
teaches: When the opponent has a weak pawn on d5 and a blocked bishop, aim to control the d5 square and undermine the pawn structure.
plans: Play Be2, castle queenside, and look for Nd5 infiltration, possibly creating a passed pawn.

explains: After c4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Nf3 c5 e3 e6, Black's queen on d8 is not a concern; White should continue developing with Nf3 and not commit to a specific plan prematurely.
teaches: In the opening, avoid committing to a plan until Black reveals their intentions; develop naturally and keep options open.
plans: Continue with natural development, aiming to control d5 and possibly create a passed pawn there.

explains: If Black plays Qa5, a second sideline, White should again continue with Nf3 and wait. If Black plays e5, White must react to the central expansion with e4, but should not open the center with d4 because the queen on a5 pins the knight and leaves the king's diagonal vulnerable.
teaches: When the opponent expands in the center, respond by challenging it, but avoid opening the position if it exposes your king or weakens your pawns.
plans: After e4, play Bc4, aiming for Qb3 to target f7, since Black's queen on a5 prevents the typical ...Na5 defense.

explains: Against Black's e5, after White plays e4, the move Bc4 is a key motif: because the black queen is on a5, Black cannot play ...Na5 to double-attack the bishop and queen, so White can constantly threaten Qb3 and the f7 pawn.
teaches: Exploit the opponent's queen placement to create tactical threats that are otherwise unavailable; here, the queen on a5 removes a defensive resource.
plans: If Black plays ...Be6, White is better; if ...Nf6, Qb3 wins; if ...Be7, Qb3 forces ...Nh6. White should avoid d4 for now.

explains: If Black chooses a Benoni-type setup with g6, White has a great position. After d4 c5, White plays d5, punishing Black for allowing the expansion. Then, with ...Nf6, White can unpin with Bd2 (preferable to Nd2) and follow with e4, gaining a pleasant space advantage.
teaches: When the opponent gives you the option to expand in the center, take it; then unpin your knight efficiently to maintain the pawn chain.
plans: Play Bd2, then e4, and later develop with Bd3 or Bc4, aiming for a standard Benoni plan with a strong center.

explains: If Black plays c5 immediately, White should play e4, and after ...Nc6, d4 is justified because Black has no pawn on e5, so White must fight for the d4 square. After dxc5, Nxc5, Nf6, White can play Bxc6 to ruin Black's pawn structure, and then Bc4, with Qb3 ideas since Black lacks the e5 pawn.
teaches: In positions where the opponent has no central pawn, fight for key central squares; exploiting a missing pawn can lead to structural weaknesses.
plans: After Bxc6 and Bc4, Black must play ...e6, leaving White with a lead in development and a weak black pawn on c5.

explains: After c4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Nf3 c5 e3 e6, White should not play d3, which is too passive. Instead, White should fight for the d4-square immediately with d4, challenging Black's c5-pawn.
teaches: In the opening, when you have a chance to fight for a key central square, take it rather than playing passively. Central space and activity matter more than solidity.
plans: Play d4, and if Black captures, recapture with the knight, then consider Bc4 to pressure f7 and potentially ruin Black's pawn structure with Bxc6.

explains: If Black plays ...Qd6, White should prefer Nf3 over d4. The move d4 allows ...e5 with tempo, leading to complications where White's extra pawn is weak and Black gets good play. With Nf3, White prevents ...e5 and maintains a solid advantage.
teaches: Sometimes a waiting move that prevents your opponent's freeing break is better than an immediate central advance. Patience in the center can be a virtue.
plans: After Nf3, if Black plays ...e5, White can play e4 to stop the pawn from advancing further, maintaining a favorable center.

explains: In the line with ...Nc6, d4, and ...Nxd4, if Black recaptures with the e-pawn, White has a decisive tactic: Nxd5, threatening Bf4 and winning material. Black's best is to recapture with the queen, but then White gets a better endgame after trades.
teaches: When your opponent makes a natural recapture, always check if a tactical shot like a knight fork or a pin can win material. In endgames, a better pawn structure and active pieces can be worth a pawn.
plans: If Black takes with the e-pawn, play Nxd5 and then Bf4. If Black takes with the queen, trade queens, play Nb5, and regain the pawn with a superior position.

explains: If Black plays ...c6 instead of taking on d5, White should take with the knight and then play Nc3, entering a gambit line. Black's best is ...e5, but if Black delays, White can play f4 to prevent ...e5 and keep a pawn up with a strong center.
teaches: When your opponent gives up a pawn for activity, you can often accept the pawn and then solidify your center. A move like f4 can be a strong prophylactic against your opponent's freeing break.
plans: After ...c6, take with the knight, then Nc3. If Black doesn't play ...e5, play f4, then develop with Nf3, e3, and possibly d4 and Bd3, enjoying a pawn-up position with central control.

explains: After c4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Nf3 c5 e3 e6, White has a pawn majority in the center and controls e5. Black's best try is to play e5 immediately, challenging White's central dominance.
teaches: In reversed openings, controlling the center with a pawn majority is key; if the opponent can play e5, it undermines your central control, so you must be ready to meet it.
plans: If Black plays e5, White can take on e5 and follow up with d4 and e4, gaining tempo and a huge center. If Black delays e5, White can play f4, maintaining a Dutch-like setup with a pawn up.

explains: In this gambit line, Black's best move is e5. If White instead plays e3 and d3, Black can play e4, forcing White to take and allowing Black to regain the pawn with active play, e.g., after d3, Bb4, Be2, O-O, Nf3, e4, dxe4, Nxe4, Black is at least equal.
teaches: Avoid setting up a passive pawn structure (e3/d3) in reversed Sicilian positions, as it allows the opponent to strike in the center with e4 and seize the initiative.
plans: Against e5, White should adopt a setup with g3, avoiding allowing e4 with tempo. This leads to a favorable reversed Sicilian with a pawn on c4 and control of e5.

explains: In the variation where Black plays e5 and White plays g3, if Black tries e4, White can simply retreat the knight to g5, attacking the pawn and opening the bishop, so Black's pawn sacrifice is not dangerous.
teaches: When the opponent sacrifices a pawn to gain time, you can often return the knight to a square where it attacks the pawn and improves your piece activity, neutralizing the initiative.
plans: White should continue with Bg2 and maintain the pawn on c4, keeping a comfortable advantage.

explains: In the Schultz Gambit (c4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5), Black tries to recapture with the knight. White should not hold onto the pawn with e4, because after Nxc3, Qa4+ wins the knight. Instead, White should play Nf3, transposing to a favorable Neo-Grünfeld structure.
teaches: Don't cling to a pawn if it costs you positional weaknesses; it's often better to return the pawn and develop harmoniously, especially when the opponent's recapture would give them active play.
plans: After Nf3, if Black plays c6, White can transpose to main lines with e5 and g3. If Black takes with the queen, White can still play d4 and maintain a good position.

explains: In the Neo-Grünfeld-like positions arising from the Schultz Gambit, White gets a favorable version because there is no knight on c3, so Black cannot play Nxc3. White can aim for a solid setup with Nf3 and g3, controlling the center.
teaches: Recognize when a transposition leads to a favorable version of a known opening; the absence of a piece on c3 can be a significant plus.
plans: White should continue with Nf3, g3, Bg2, and d4, aiming for a comfortable advantage with central control.

explains: After c4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Nf3 c5 e3 e6, Black has played ...Nf6 and ...c5, and White has not committed the knight to c3. Taking on d5 with the queen is unnatural because Black has already developed the knight to f6, so the queen on d5 is misplaced and gives Black transpositional options.
teaches: In the Anglo-Scandinavian, if Black has already played ...Nf6, recapturing on d5 with the queen is inferior; the knight recapture is natural. White should keep flexibility by not committing the knight to c3 too early.
plans: White should play d4 and then e4 to build a broad center, avoiding knight to c3 to maintain support of e4.

explains: After White plays d4, Black must prevent e4. If Black plays ...g6, then e4 follows, and the knight on d5 has no good square: it either blocks the bishop and later gets hit by e5, or goes offside to b6. The only good move for Black is ...Bf5, pinning the e-pawn.
teaches: When facing a broad center, the defender must immediately challenge the advance of the central pawns. A knight on d5 can become a liability if it has to retreat awkwardly.
plans: White should reinforce e4 with Nb1-d2, threatening e4. If Black plays ...e6, then e4 wins a piece because the knight is trapped.

explains: After Nb1-d2, Black's best is ...Nf6, which saves the knight and prevents e4. Now the knight has left d5 and the bishop has left c8, leaving b7 weak. White can play Qb3, forcing ...Qc8 to defend b7, since ...b6 would be weakening.
teaches: When the opponent's pieces leave key squares, look for weaknesses to target. A queen sortie to b3 can create concrete threats and force passive moves.
plans: After ...Qc8, White plays g3, preparing Bg2 and a strong setup. If Black plays natural moves like ...e6, White can exploit the weak e5 square with Nc4, grabbing the bishop pair and dominating.

explains: In the resulting position, White has a huge advantage: the b7 and c6 squares are weak, Black's pieces are tied down, and White can break open the center with f4, e4, e5 at will. White also has the bishop pair.
teaches: When you have a space advantage and the opponent has weaknesses, you can often choose the moment to open the position. The bishop pair and central pawn majority are long-term assets.
plans: White should continue developing with Bg2, then look to play f4 and e4-e5 to blast open the position, while exploiting the weak b7 and c6 squares.

explains: In this English Opening line, after c4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 Nf3 c5 e3 e6, White can try to regain the pawn or play dynamically. One idea is to allow Black to keep the pawn while White gets active piece play.
teaches: When behind in material, look for dynamic compensation: active pieces, pressure on weak squares, and long-term structural advantages rather than forcing immediate material equality.
plans: White can consider moves like Qa4+ or Na3 to regain the pawn, or play for pressure on the c-file and dark squares.

explains: The move Na3 is a sideline that aims to recapture on c4 with the knight, preventing ...b5. If Black doesn't take the knight, White gets a pleasant advantage with the bishop on g2 dominating.
teaches: A knight on the rim can be justified if it supports a key outpost or prevents a useful pawn break. Here Na3 prepares Nxc4 and controls b5.
plans: After Na3, if Black plays ...Bxa3, White recaptures with bxa3, opening the b-file and aiming for a powerful bishop on b2 or a3.

explains: In the Na3 line, White often gives up the pawn but gets long-term compensation: weak black pawns, a weak diagonal, and control of c4. Even if White doesn't regain the pawn, the position is playable.
teaches: Material is not always the most important factor. Weak squares, pawn weaknesses, and piece activity can outweigh a pawn deficit.
plans: White can play a4 to undermine Black's queenside, then place the bishop on b2 or a3 to pressure g7 or a8. If Black plays ...c6, White continues with a4 and Qc2, preparing to regain the pawn.

explains: If Black plays ...Nc6 instead of ...c6, White can try Qa4 to regain the pawn, but must be careful about ...b5 tricks. If the bishop is on b2, taking the pawn can run into ...b5, ...Rxb8, etc.
teaches: When trying to regain a pawn, watch for tactical tricks like ...b5 to deflect the queen or attack the bishop. Sometimes it's better to improve your position first.
plans: White can play Qc2 instead, which avoids ...b5 with tempo, and after ...Bf8, Qxc4 regains the pawn with pressure on the c-file.

explains: The main line is Qa4+ check, forcing Black to block with ...Nc6 or ...Bd7. After ...Nc6, White takes on e4, regaining the pawn and maintaining pressure.
teaches: A check can force a useful developing move for the opponent, but it also gains time for White to improve their position. Here Qa4+ forces Black to commit a piece to defend.
plans: After Qa4+ Nc6, White plays Qxe4, regaining the pawn, with a comfortable position and active pieces.

explains: In this English Opening line, White has given up a pawn but has the bishop pair and excellent bishops. The knight on a3 prepares to develop the bishop to b2, creating a powerful fianchetto. Even if the pawn is not regained, White has compensation.
teaches: When you sacrifice a pawn for development and the bishop pair, you should aim to activate your bishops along open diagonals, especially the long diagonal.
plans: Develop the bishop to b2 and aim to regain the pawn or maintain pressure with active piece play.

explains: After Black plays Qxd4, Black's main responses are c5 or a6. If Black plays a6, they intend to play b5 later with tempo on the queen. White should anticipate this by moving the queen to c2, avoiding threats.
teaches: When your queen is attacked by a pawn advance, move it preemptively to a safe square to avoid losing time.
plans: After Qc2, continue development with Nf6, c5, castling, and prepare to challenge Black's structure.

explains: In the Qxc4 lines, Black often tries to expand with b5. White's powerful resource is a4, attacking the b5 pawn and forcing Black to respond. This is a key pattern to remember.
teaches: When the opponent has a pawn on b5 that is supported, a4 can be a strong move to undermine it and create weaknesses.
plans: After a4, if Black plays bxa4, White can recapture with the rook and then apply pressure on the a-file and the b-pawn.

explains: Black can also play c5 instead of a6, leading to a setup with b6 and Bb7, similar to a double fianchetto. White's knight is on d7 instead of c6 due to the check on a4. White should aim for the same double fianchetto setup with b3 and Bb2.
teaches: In these structures, both sides often aim for double fianchetto setups, controlling the center with bishops.
plans: Develop with b3, Bb2, and then play d3, Nbd2, and castle, with the bishops cutting across the board.

explains: When Black plays Nf6 and Be7, White's setup is to get a double fianchetto with b3 and Bb2. A key rule is that whenever Black tries to fianchetto the bishop (with b6), White should take on d5 if possible, to prevent it.
teaches: If your opponent wants to fianchetto a bishop, you can often prevent it by exchanging the pawn that supports it.
plans: Develop with b3, Bb2, and if Black plays b6, take on d5 to stop the bishop from coming to b7.

explains: In this English Opening setup, Black often tries to fianchetto the light-squared bishop with ...b6. The key is to decide whether to capture on d5 immediately or keep flexibility.
teaches: When Black plays ...b6, you have two main options: take on d5 to create a double fianchetto, or keep the tension and develop with Bb2. The flexible approach is often better because it avoids simplifying and keeps more pieces on the board.
plans: Against ...b6, prefer Bb2, then e3, Nc3, and only later consider taking on d5. This maintains central control and prepares the d4 break.

explains: If White takes on d5 early, Black can recapture with the knight, which opposes White's bishop on b2. This can lead to a blocked position where White's bishop is less active.
teaches: Avoid premature captures that allow your opponent to develop with tempo or trade off your active pieces. Keeping the tension often preserves your advantage.
plans: Instead of taking on d5 immediately, develop with Bb2 and prepare d4. If Black plays ...c5, you can still take on d5 later after ...Bb7, forcing Black to recapture with the queen, which is a slight concession.

explains: After ...c5 and ...Bb7, taking on d5 with the knight is possible. If Black recaptures with the pawn, White plays d4, blocking the bishop. If Black recaptures with the queen, White gains time by attacking the queen with moves like Ne5.
teaches: When your opponent's queen is forced to recapture, you can often gain a tempo by developing with threats. This is a common theme in the English Opening.
plans: After ...c5, play Bb2, e3, Nc3, and only after ...Bb7, take on d5. If Black recaptures with the queen, play d4, and if the queen goes to d6, consider dxc5 to ruin Black's pawn structure.

explains: In this line, Black might try ...Qxd5, but that is bad because after ...Qxg2, White can play Kxg2 and Ne5, winning material. The correct move for Black is ...Qd6, but then White can play dxc5, ruining Black's pawn structure.
teaches: Sometimes your opponent's natural-looking captures are actually mistakes. Always check if you can exploit the queen's exposure with tactics.
plans: If Black plays ...Qxd5, be alert for tactics like Ne5. If Black plays ...Qd6, consider dxc5 to damage Black's pawns, and then follow up with moves like Nd7 or Rc1 to maintain pressure.

explains: In this position, White must be careful about playing d4 because the bishop on b7 is hanging. If White plays a quiet move, d4 doesn't work due to tactical issues: the queen cannot recapture on d4, and after pawn takes, Black has threats like Nb5 or Ne5. Taking on d4 immediately with the queen also fails because Black can play Na4 and the queen must retreat.
teaches: Always check if central pawn breaks are tactically sound, especially when your opponent has a bishop on b7 eyeing the center. A pawn break is only good if you can recapture or if the resulting tactics favor you.
plans: Instead of d4, White should develop with b3 and Bb2, preparing to eventually take on d5. This setup avoids the tactical issues and maintains pressure.

explains: Black's triangle of pawns (c5, d5, e6) can lead to several openings, often the Semi-Slav. White chooses to play Nf3, and if Black plays dxc4, White can either castle or play Ng1 to transpose to known lines. After dxc4, castling is recommended, and if Black plays b5, White plays d3, creating pressure on c6 and d3 with Ne5.
teaches: When facing a flexible pawn structure, it's important to have a clear plan. Here, White's idea is to castle quickly and then use Ne5 to pressure Black's queenside, even if it means giving up a pawn for activity.
plans: After dxc4 and b5, play d3, then Ne5, aiming to pressure c6 and d3. If Black plays Bb7, White can take on d3, accepting a pawn deficit for a safer king and active pieces.

explains: In this English Opening setup, White has played c4, Nc3, Nf3, and e3, while Black has a pawn triangle on d5, e6, and c5. The e4-square is a key central outpost that White can control with pawns on d3 and b3, preventing Black's knight from jumping to e4.
teaches: When facing a Stonewall-like pawn structure, controlling the e4-square with pawns (b3 and d3) is a simple and effective way to neutralize Black's main central counterplay.
plans: Develop the bishop to b2, castle, and prepare the e4 pawn break to gain a central advantage.

explains: If Black tries to block the dark-squared bishop with an early d4, Black will likely follow with c5 and e5 to grip the dark squares. White can respond by playing d3 to block the pawn, e3 to attack it, and a3-b4 to break the bind on c5.
teaches: When facing a pawn chain that restricts your bishop, use multiple pawn breaks (e3 and b4) to undermine the chain and open lines for your pieces.
plans: After achieving both e3 and b4, White's position resembles a reversed Benoni with the bishop becoming strong on the long diagonal.

explains: In the reversed Benoni structure, White aims to prevent Black's e5 break while preparing his own e4 push. Black often plays ...Nd7 and ...a5 to control b4, but White can still proceed with a3 and b4 to undermine the d4 pawn.
teaches: In a reversed Benoni, the side with the extra tempo should strive to execute their central break (e4) while preventing the opponent's corresponding break (e5).
plans: Continue with a3, b4, and then prepare e4, keeping the d4 pawn under pressure and maintaining active piece play.

explains: Against the g6 system (Gurgenidze), Black develops the bishop to g7, so White must play d4 to blunt that bishop and then aim for the e4 break. Black will try to counter on the queenside with b6, a5, or c5.
teaches: When facing a fianchettoed bishop, it's important to challenge it with a central pawn advance (d4) and then follow up with the other central break (e4) to gain space.
plans: Play d4, develop the bishop to the long diagonal, and prepare e4 while keeping an eye on Black's queenside pawn advances.

explains: In this English Opening setup, Black aims for a kingside fianchetto with ...Bg7, which can be powerful. White must blunt that bishop by playing d4 at the right moment, allowing White's own bishop to occupy the long diagonal.
teaches: When facing a fianchettoed bishop, contest the same diagonal with your own bishop and central pawn breaks to reduce its influence.
plans: Play d4 to blunt the g7-bishop, then aim for the e4 pawn break to gain central space.

explains: Black may choose ...Nc6 to block the c-pawn, signaling they are not playing ...c5 immediately. Alternatively, ...Nd7 followed by ...c5 is possible but less effective. White should not overcommit; a flexible setup with e3 and Qc2 is appropriate.
teaches: Recognize opponent's pawn-structure intentions from piece placement; keep flexibility to adapt to different plans.
plans: Develop with e3, Qc2, and prepare to meet ...c5 or ...b6 appropriately.

explains: When Black plays ...b6, White should take on d5 with the c-pawn (cxd5) and then develop the bishop to b2, claiming that White's bishop on b2 is stronger than Black's on b7. This is a key positional idea in this system.
teaches: In symmetrical fianchetto positions, the bishop that is more active or better supported can be a long-term asset; trade or neutralize the opponent's counterpart.
plans: After ...b6, play cxd5, then Bb2, and prepare to pressure the c-file with Qc2 and Rc1.

explains: White's pressure down the c-file is a major asset. The targets at the end of the file (like the c7-pawn or the knight on c6) force Black to either move pieces or keep them tied down. If the knight on c6 moves, White can occupy e5; if the bishop takes on e5, White recaptures with d5, creating pressure on d5.
teaches: A semi-open file with targets can be a long-term advantage; line up heavy pieces to control it and exploit the opponent's piece coordination.
plans: Build pressure on the c-file with Qc2, Bb2, and Rc1, and be ready to exploit any piece movement to gain central squares.

explains: In the e3 setup, if Black plays ...c5, White can take on d5 and then play d4, transposing to a Tarrasch-like structure. If Black tries ...d4 themselves, it fails because White can recapture and gain an edge with an isolated pawn to play against.
teaches: When facing a central pawn break, consider transposing to known structures; an isolated queen's pawn can be a target if you can blockade it.
plans: Against ...c5, play cxd5 and d4; if Black plays ...d4, capture and use the resulting isolated pawn as a target.

explains: After d4 Nf6 Bg5 e6 e4 h6, White's center is under pressure. The move e5 opens the center prematurely, allowing Black to simplify and leave White with nothing special. Instead, Nc3 is a solid developing move that keeps the tension and gives White the best chances.
teaches: In sharp openings, don't rush to push the central pawn if it releases the tension without clear gain. Develop pieces and maintain the central pawn mass.
plans: White should continue with Nc3, preparing to support the center and develop harmoniously.

explains: The move Bxf6 is the theoretical choice, doubling Black's pawns on f6. This is better than exf6, which gives Black counterplay. After Bxf6 gxf6, White has a strong central pawn duo on d4 and e4, and Black's pawn structure is compromised.
teaches: Doubling the opponent's pawns can be a long-term positional advantage, even if it means giving up the bishop pair. Keep the center intact and avoid moves that allow Black easy development.
plans: White will play Nc3, then e3, g3, Bg2, putting pressure on the d5 square and the weak pawns. Black will have to defend passively with Be6.

explains: In the line after Bxf6 gxf6, Black often plays Qb6, forcing White to defend the b2 pawn. White can play Qc1, and Black then has the option of f5 or Bh6. The move Bh6 is an interesting alternative, aiming to provoke weaknesses and create tactical chances.
teaches: When the opponent's queen is on c1, a bishop to h6 can be a strong resource, similar to ideas in the London System. Be aware of tactical motifs like Qb2 if the bishop is taken.
plans: White should respond with e3 to block the bishop's diagonal, then continue with c4 and f4, maintaining the center. Black will play f5 and f4, leading to sharp play.

explains: In the sharp line after Bh6, e3, f5, c4, f4, exf4, Bxf4, Black can play Qxf4 and then Qxb2. However, with the c-pawn moved, White has the resource Ne2, and the queen can defend the b2 square. This shows the importance of pawn moves in creating defensive resources.
teaches: Sometimes a pawn move that seems to weaken the center can provide crucial defensive squares for pieces. Always consider how pawn structure affects piece placement and defense.
plans: White will play Ne2, then Nc3, d6, Qd2, developing while keeping the queen safe. Black must be careful not to trap the queen prematurely.

explains: In the game continuation, Black played a6, b5, and then Nb7, aiming to activate the pieces and create threats against the white queen. White's queen got trapped, and Black won material. This shows that even in a line where the queen seems safe, Black can generate strong counterplay.
teaches: When the opponent's queen is misplaced, look for ways to harass it with pawns and pieces. Sometimes sacrificing a pawn (like b5) can open lines and activate your pieces.
plans: Black will continue to develop with Be7, Bf5, and create threats against the white king. White must be careful to extricate the queen and coordinate pieces.

explains: In the Trompowsky after …c5, White has two main approaches: capturing on f6 for a positional edge, or playing d5/Nc3 to head for the Vaganian Gambit or a quick queenside castling attack. The position after …Qxf6 Nc3 d6 Qd2 Nd7 is a typical setup where White aims to pressure Black's structure.
teaches: When facing the Trompowsky, be prepared for the sharp …Bh6 idea, which requires deep preparation. The main line with ...f5 leads to thematic positions where White pressures the f5 pawn and Black seeks counterplay on the queenside.
plans: White should develop with c4, Nc3, e3, and Bd3, keeping the central tension and preparing to attack Black's weaknesses. Black should maintain the tension and try to generate queenside play.

explains: In the typical structure with White's pawn on e3 and Black's on f5, White has pressure on the f5 pawn. Black's option to advance ...e5 is important because it closes the e-file and gives Black central space. The key is for White to keep the tension and for Black to seek dynamic compensation.
teaches: When you have a structural weakness like a backward pawn or a hole, you must seek dynamic play to compensate. The side with the better pawn structure should aim to trade pieces, while the side with the bishop pair should keep the position complex.
plans: White should consider e4 to break open the center if Black castles kingside. If Black castles queenside, White should play a3 and b4 to start a queenside attack, while Black should counterattack on the kingside.

explains: In the game example, Black castled queenside and White played h3 and Rc1, which were slow. Black then played ...h5 and ...Rd2, activating all his pieces and winning. White should have played a3 and b4 immediately to start his own attack.
teaches: In opposite-side castling positions, every tempo matters. Do not waste time on unnecessary moves like h3; instead, push your pawns to attack the enemy king. The side that starts the attack first often wins.
plans: If White had played a3 and then Rfd1, he would have been ready to meet Black's attack with his own. Black's attack is dangerous, but White's should be faster if played accurately.

explains: After Black castles queenside, the position is risky for Black because White's queenside attack can be very strong. If Black castles kingside, he is not worse but must be careful not to lose quickly.
teaches: When choosing which side to castle, consider the pawn structure and the opponent's attacking potential. In these structures, queenside castling can be dangerous if White is prepared to push his a- and b-pawns.
plans: White should aim to keep the initiative and punish Black's structural weaknesses. Black should look for dynamic counterplay to avoid being overrun.

explains: Black can deviate early with Nc6 instead of Nf6. This move develops a piece and keeps the g8-knight flexible, but it abandons the support of the d5-pawn with c6.
teaches: A slightly imprecise move can be a practical weapon because it takes the opponent out of book, even if it gives a small theoretical edge.
plans: Black aims to develop quickly, possibly castle queenside, and use the bishop pair to attack the white king.

explains: After …Nc6, White can play Bb5, pinning the knight. Black should accept doubled pawns if White takes, and then develop with Bd6, preparing queenside castling.
teaches: Accepting structural weaknesses can be worth it for active piece play and attacking chances.
plans: Black can castle queenside, play Nge7, c4, and aim for a kingside attack with the bishop pair.

explains: Alternatively, White can play Bd3, aiming for a setup with c3, Be3, 0-0, Re1, Qc2 to attack h7. Black can counter by developing the bishop to d7, playing Qf6, and then castling queenside.
teaches: When the opponent sets up a standard attacking formation, you can disrupt it by choosing a different development order and castling to the opposite side.
plans: Black's bishop pair on the long diagonal can pressure the white king, and the knight can come to f5 or g4 for a menacing attack.

explains: In the Exchange French, black can deviate from the main line with Nc6 instead of Nf6, avoiding the passive setup with c6. This keeps the f6 square free for the queen and creates dynamic possibilities.
teaches: Consider early deviations that avoid passive structures and keep pieces flexible, especially when the opponent's setup is aimed at a specific plan.
plans: If white plays Bg5, black can play Bg4, pinning the knight, and later Qf6, threatening to double white's pawns with Bxf3. Black may castle queenside to create opposite-side castling and attacking chances.
